Description: Transcribed from IFP transcript T0017A, which was copied from a manuscript belonging to M. K. S. Bhattar of Madurai.
It comprises pages up to 635; the remainder of the manuscript is contained in transcript T0017-B.
See the Muktabodha IFP online catalog for bibliographic details.
Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski.
Revision 0: February 5, 2012.
Country of Publication: India || Śrīḥ ||
Oṃ.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
O wise ones, devoted to that [goal], listen to how those gods are situated:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva himself. (1)
That which is even beyond that is the supreme, the ultimate limit.
It consists of the letter A, the letter U, the letter M, and the Bindu.
Śiva is beyond that, and beyond him is that which is higher than the high. (3)
The letter *a* is remembered as Brahmā, and the letter *u* is indeed Viṣṇu;
they say the letter *m* is Rudra, and the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is Īśvara himself. (4)
Since Nāda is to be known as Śiva, all-pervading, and higher than the highest;
for even those principles (tattvas) that exist beyond the highest are indeed contained within it. || 15 ||
"The goddesses who are to be understood in their true nature, as well as those presiding over the *bindu* and *nāda*, [and] those which are the imperishable syllables... The Goddess said: [6]
"How do they, by resorting to oneness, go to the supreme state? The Lord said:
"The syllable Om, conjoined with the Bindu, is remembered as the mouth of the Vedas. (7)
The letter *a* belongs to that god Śiva, the Supreme Self;
through the union of *a* and *u*, the syllable *oṃ* is proclaimed. (8)
The letter *ma* arises when joined with the two lips; and the moon (*i*) is situated immediately after it, above the *ma*. (9)
One should know it as having four parts, adorned with the fourfold knowledge:
namely, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti.
These are declared to be the digits (kalās) of the Bindu-deity, O wise one;
when the letter 'ma' is touched by the syllable 'oṃ', it indeed resounds.
Then the Bindu quickly touches the head of the letter *ma*;
the twenty-four *kalās* are traditionally taught as beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*. (12)
They say that these, established and situated in three locations, are always to be known as the characteristics of the deity Bindu, appearing in the form of a white mustard seed. (13)
O Goddess, that which is common to all tantras has been declared to you:
it has a form resembling the letter *ma* at the top of the syllable *oṃ*.
Resembling a half-moon and situated beyond the Bindu is that which is even higher than it: Sadāśiva in the form of Nāda. || 15 ||
The Nāda exists pervading that which is beyond the highest, beyond the furthermost;
there is nothing higher than this, nor anything beyond Śiva.
By knowing the god Parijñāna, a man is liberated from all [bondage].
[The mantra consists of] the beginning, the middle, and the end, with three and five [syllables] along with the *visarga*. 17.
In the Grandfather (Brahmā), they are established in the reality of the Self, residing within the body;
from the fourth [element] onwards, they are indeed grasped up to the seventh beyond. (18)
One should also point out that which is the supreme of him, as well as that of Keśava;
that which is the beginning and the end, and that which is below and the eleventh.
One should designate the first five Vaiśeṣas as portions of Rudra.
Indeed, whatever the nature of each [letter], it consists of that very essence.
The letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *kṣa* are established within the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*).
The Goddess Mātṛkā is said to be established within the syllable Oṃ;
by her, one is liberated from all fetters and goes to the stainless Śiva.
The Goddess said: "O Lord, regarding this which has been told, that the syllable Om (Oṃkāra) is the embodiment of all deities," || 23 ||
"How then, O Lord, is it said that the gods and the yogis who contemplate reality meditate upon that?
The Lord said:
"The mind (citta), the consciousness (cetas), as well as thought (cintā), the object of thought (cintya), and the thinker (cintaka) are distinct. (24)
"Having understood this pentad, one should then practice yoga.
The Goddess said:
"What is the nature of the mind (citta), and what is the nature of the thinker (cetana)? (25)
What kind of thought is said to be, and how is the object of thought related to the thinker?
O Supreme Lord, tell me all of this again according to the truth. (26)
O Mahādeva, wielder of the trident, source of grace, I have a doubt. O Īśvara,
[grant] attention, mindfulness, consciousness, intellect, and the various modes of awakening.
Thus, having understood it in these five ways, the Supreme Goddess— || 28 ||
"Therefore, one should apply oneself to yoga; otherwise, never at any time.
The Goddess said:
"O God, O Supreme Lord, even now there remains a doubt regarding yoga. (29)
"O Lord, please tell me truly what kind of yoga that would be. (p. 8) The Lord said:
Thus has this supreme yoga of the yogins been fully explained.
It is proclaimed to be of two kinds: that which has become the target and that which is not a target.
Having correctly perceived the target, the knower should indeed apply himself to that which resides therein.
Having become absorbed in that and being composed of it, one who practices yoga is liberated;
he experiences pleasure and pain while being devoid of the [ordinary] senses.
But when it has become motionless and steady, it is declared to be "unperceivable" (alakṣa).
This yoga, which is both supreme and most excellent, has been explained to you. (33)
To anyone who has become absorbed in that [state], one should impart the yoga:
"Oṃ; intellect, mind, ego, and the individual soul as the fifth. (34)
(9) Resting upon the plane of the fourth (turya), the Praṇava is firmly established;
for the Praṇava is bound to the Bindu within the domain of the Nāda of the Suṣumnā. 35.
Abiding at the emission (visarga) at the end of the sixteen, liberation is held to be beyond that.
This very god, consisting of speech, is the imperishable fivefold portion of mantra. (36)
It is proclaimed by all established doctrines that the supreme station of the Imperishable (Akṣara) is situated there;
it abides as its own nature and is renowned by the name of Brahman.
When it is uttered aloud, Brahmā is the presiding deity therein;
when it is uttered in a whisper, Viṣṇu is the presiding deity therein.
One should remember [the mantra] with the mind without uttering it; Śiva is the presiding deity therein.
The self is the meditator, the mind is the meditation, and the object of meditation is the pure Maheśvara. (39)
O Goddess of gods, one should, through meditation, unite the Self with that which is supreme sovereignty, the all-pervading Maheśvara, within one's own body. (40)
Having made the *praṇava* partless and devoid of vowels and *mātrās*,
and having placed Śiva at its end, that which is thus united bestows the state of liberation.
He for whom this supreme rarity has thus arisen as a distinction shall go to the highest abode, accompanied by hundreds of millions of his kinsmen.
O Goddess, even if one has reached every possible state or is joined with all sins, he is necessarily liberated, for [this mantra] is capable of bestowing grace upon everyone. (43)
O Goddess, this supreme [teaching] must be guarded with great effort;
behold, O Queen of the Gods, how one is liberated by a means that is free from all constraints.
(11) Furthermore, I shall again explain its higher and lower divisions;
it is to be known by yogins through vision, touch, movement, and meditation. (45)
For even by mere remembrance, the supreme state is attained;
O Goddess, I shall describe that which is difficult even for the gods to obtain. (46)
That which consists of the thirty-eight kalās and is "Śivo'm" is indeed the embodiment of the Vedas; it is certainly the savior from the ocean of saṃsāra.
The Goddess said:
"Tell me, what is this procedure for the auspicious Oṃkāra like? Again, a doubt has arisen: how is it that Śiva is remembered as 'Oṃ'? (48)
When the Lord (Īśvara), who is the beginning of all principles (tattvas) and so forth, is above the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta) of the deity; (p. 12)
And Śiva is likewise ordained as being endowed with three and five. || 49 ||
The Goddess said:
"In which locations are the thirty-eight kalās established? Please tell me their names according to the distinction of their places."
Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Svadhā, Sthiti, Rajā, Rakṣā, Arati, Pālyā, Kāmā, Saṃyaminī, and Kriyā. (51)
You are the intellect, the creator, the rustic woman, and the deluder;
you are darkness, delusion, hunger, sleep, death, illusion, fear, and old age.
Manifestation and establishment, knowledge and likewise peace;
Śaśinī, Aṅgadā, Iṣṭā, Marīci, and Jvālinī. (53)
The half-moon and the spear, along with the digits (kalās), belong to the Knower. || 54 ||
The power that ceases the half-moon and the sound (nāda), which does not go upward and is situated within the Śakti, has been described by me; one should designate it as the Pervasive One (Vyāpinī).

The utterance of the Praṇava is its [nature]... [omitted]. Of that sound which has arisen as the dual [nāda], whatever sound is heard constantly, that indeed is the upward-moving [aspect] of the nāda, situated both within and without. (57)
When the Śakti is being observed, that radiance which is perceived is indeed the all-pervasive one, situated both within and without the Śakti. (58)
In brief, the thirty-eight digits (kalās) of the Praṇava have been declared;
they should always be known by those who follow the Śiva Tantras. (59)
That great god who is all-pervading and heard of by all, is indefinable and nameless, equal and established everywhere. (60)
The contemplation that "it exists" is indeed its first stage;
even by the gods, it was not known what that contemplation of existence actually is. (61)
The very notion regarding that [power] has arisen; it is designated as "Śakti.
It is perceived directly in all worlds and is seen existing everywhere. (62)
But that which is its state as fruit is directly perceived everywhere;
O Goddess, it is heard constantly and is renowned by the name "Sound" (nāda). (63)
The other [aspect] of that state is called cessation;
it is declared to be the half-moon, pervasive and situated externally at the end.
For indeed, whatever syllable is enjoined elsewhere through conjunction, it obstructs all yogins; this is renowned as the "Half-Moon" (ardhacandra). || 65 ||
Knowledge is that which is born of yoga and is to be meditated upon; it is the auspicious practice and ritual action.
He who is to be known as the most supreme abides within all the senses and so forth.
O Lord, you previously declared that the Goddess is the partless *praṇava*, situated everywhere within all the stalks, lotuses, and other parts [of the body]. (67)
Furthermore, O Lord of the Gods, for what reason does the Sovereign [act] toward those who possess blemishes?
Abiding in the form of mantra, he sustains all beings.
Having first grasped the form of the mantra, knowledge subsequently shines forth;
the world, which is the root of bondage for the bound soul (paśu), is known to consist of both the bound soul and its fetters (pāśa). (69)
And Maheśvara, whose form is the mantra,
compassionate toward all beings and resplendent like ten thousand suns, became the cause for its uprooting.
The Lord, who is Śiva, the imperishable, having assumed the form of mantra out of compassion;
and [the goddess] Vyāpinī, whose form is space, the infinite, the sovereign, and the supportless (anāśritā). 71.
The form of the God is renowned as the Praṇava, joined with the Brahmans; it comprises Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, Sadyojāta, and the others. (72)
He is the source of immeasurable qualities for all that is moving and unmoving; he is the Praṇava, the manifest God, the sovereign lord of all knowledge.
The indestructible, perfectly full, the drop of splendor, the supreme Śiva;
the Praṇava is His body, the Lord Īśāna, who is held as the Lord of the lords of mantras. (74)
Having known the great [power], the Lord [acted].
O lady of excellent vows, as many vowels and consonants as there are residing in the Praṇava,
so many hosts of gods become manifested for you.
These [energies] abide within the Praṇava; in truth, they reside in the Praṇava.
The Praṇava is the self of all dharmas for those whose minds are attached to the Praṇava.
The *praṇava*, which possesses infinite forms, is the support of all yet is itself without support;
within the *praṇava* resides the entire universe, as well as that which is beyond sound and the other sense objects. (77)
The Praṇava is the life-breath of all life-breaths, devoid of all means of valid cognition.
Maheśvara, whose essence is the Praṇava, is the supreme lord of Brahmā and the other creators;
yet Śiva is even beyond that, being the collection of all mantra-forms and their ultimate essential nature. || 79 ||
Understand in accordance with reality that the entire world, from the realm of Brahmā down to the earth, originates from the Praṇava, and that the entire world dissolves back into it.
But whatever form it has at the beginning, such it remains even at the ends of the kalās; because of its eternity and its inner nature, as previously stated in the recollection of the Praṇava.
O virtuous one, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Śiva, and Śānta perform the *praṇava* for Him; therefore, He is remembered as *Praṇava*. (82)
Pure, all-pervading, and eternal, Śiva is established in the Praṇava;
he is the supreme, pure body of knowledge, the primordial and sovereign Lord.
Whatever is contained within the Praṇava, established in the light, serves for the purification of the form and its characteristics; and that is the cause of liberation.
The supreme god Praṇava, who pervades all, is established as the remainder of the names of the gods and of the entire world; he is the creator of all creators. (85)
The Praṇava is the soul of all dharmas, residing in the hearts of living beings;
consisting of three measures and a half-measure, the Praṇava is beginningless in its origin.
The *praṇava* is Maheśvara himself, residing in the hearts of all beings; he is to be known, he is to be worshipped, he is to be meditated upon, and he is indeed to be recited. (87)
The Soul of the Universe, the one who becomes the universe, the means of attaining the Bindu, and the means of individual attainment—the Praṇava should always be meditated upon as such. 88.
Sovereignty, mastery, and likewise greatness—O Goddess of gods, O fair-faced one, these are attained without doubt through meditation alone. (89)
When meditated upon, the Lord of All, the Divine, bestows omniscience;
all deities reside within the heart, established in the vital breath (prāṇa) within the heart.
All lights are in the heart; this Praṇava resides in the heart. Endowed with these three, it is established within all beings.

The goddess Citta is superior to the mind (cetas); she knows the self in its true essence. The mind is declared to be the body, while the conscious one (cetā) is proclaimed to be power (śakti). || 92 ||
When one perceives oneself as being devoid of these, as if fallen asleep from poison,
even so, O Goddess, is consciousness perceived when it is bereft of them.
Form, touch, and likewise sound—these three aspects are everywhere present as the subtle part;
the supreme *praṇava* is the most subtle, devoid of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The origin of all principles consists of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas;
among these, the Praṇava is to be known as the charioteer of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
What is that consciousness which is the Lord residing within this body and pervading all beings?
That sound should be known as the Praṇava; it stands filling everything.
That supreme, subtle Prakṛti creates that which is of the nature of Śiva;
O Goddess, she is proclaimed as the fifty Praṇavas through a single division. (97)
This should be constantly understood by yogins who follow the knowledge of Śiva, as it is found in the Vedas, Sāṃkhya, Purāṇas, Pāñcarātra, and Itihāsas. (98)
Likewise, other Smṛtis and others speak of various [mantras] in succession;
all yogis declare that "Om" is the single-syllabled Brahman.
"They speak without knowing," thus [is] Māyā, whose essence is Śiva. The Goddess said:
"O Lord, the fifty Praṇavas have been understood by me through your grace. (100)
Within that, O God, the phonemes (varṇas) are situated, as well as the Bindu and the Nāda.
O Maheśvara, I wish to hear further; I have a doubt.
Īśāna, Puruṣa, Ghora, Vāma, and likewise Sadyojāta; the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), the Guardians of the Quarters (Lokapālas), and the Weapons, in their proper order. 103.
"Tell me the extraction of the mantras for these [deities] without distinction.
The Lord said: "Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret, the most excellent true essence of the mantras. (104)
O fair-faced one, I shall now declare all the mantras within the Praṇava; that which was proclaimed first as the letter 'A' constitutes its end. (105)

The second [syllable] is indeed *dha* from *dharmādi*, and likewise the *cchādanāni*; one should conceive the third as the lotus (*padma*) together with the *anusvāra*, and it should truly exist [thus]. (106)
One should assign the nine Śaktis using the seed-syllable *cathrtha*;
the letter *ma* is declared to be the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of that lotus eternally.
In this regard, the parts beginning with the syllable *u* have been briefly explained;
O Goddess of the Gods, one should arrange them up to the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *puṣkara*.
Those [vowels] beginning with *ḷ* and ending with *e* that have been mentioned should be known as the filaments of that lotus, O beautiful one. (109)
Having thus arranged [the deities] with effort and having arranged the Mūrti as before, one should likewise place Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti. (110)
O Mistress of the Gods, Śāntyatīta and the others are proclaimed as the five Brahmans;
beginning with Vāyavya and ending with Śaka, they are established [in the directions]. (111)
The limbs of Śiva should be understood as they have been described in brief:
the letter *ṣa* shall be the eye, and she is proclaimed to be Gāyatrī. (112)
O fair-faced one, in this tantra, Kṣassāvitrī should always be known;
O Goddess of the lords of gods, having worshipped Sadāśiva, who is named Haṃsa. (113)
The supreme imperishable one is the transcendent deity, endowed with all scriptures;
having meditated upon that Lord of Devas, one should worship him according to the prescribed sequence.
One should place the embryo in the first [square], the universal monarchs in the second,
the world-protectors in the third, and the weapons in the fourth.
The eight universal monarchs (cakravartin) are those beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with *ja*;
those beginning with *jha* and ending with *ta* are proclaimed to be the world-protectors (lokapāla). (116)
The weapons, beginning with the letter *tha* and ending with the letter *bha*, are joined respectively with the vowel *a*; these are proclaimed as the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*). (117)

One should join the world-protectors with the *bindu* (the nasal drop) and the weapons with the *visarga* (the final sibilant); for all of them, however, one should proceed according to the ritual sequence of perfumes and incense, preceded by the *praṇava* (the syllable Om).

O Goddess, all that has been prescribed must be performed with effort in the proper sequence and in every way; indeed, all those rites which have been mentioned are to be performed with the syllable Om (praṇava).
O noble lady, all duties must be performed without conceptual differentiation;
this applies to all the principles (tattvas) proclaimed to exist, from earth up to Śiva.
(27) By means of the *praṇava*, however, the worship, the performance of the fire-offering (*homa*), and all ritual actions— indeed,
all activities such as recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*)— must be performed. 121.
One should offer oblations thirty times, followed by the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in due order.
This Mātṛkā sacrifice is difficult to attain even for the gods.
This sacrifice to the Mātṛkās has fulfilled its purpose for you; with doubts severed, stainless and free from fever, he attains union with Śiva.
O Goddess, that which is designated as the Supreme Imperishable was explained by me from the very beginning;
O beautiful one, such a sacrifice for it has also been proclaimed by the Lord.
This division of the mantra of the *praṇava* has been declared;
thereafter [follows that which] consists of victory.
In a very short time, he shall conquer timely death;
one month is said to be equal to a hundred years, and two months [are equal to] ... || 126 ||
Through the procedure of recitation and worship, one attains perfection in a single year. || 127 ||
Henceforth, O Goddess of the gods, I shall explain the sequence of the wheel of ritual placement (nyāsacakra), beginning from the east, until everything is completed. 128.
Thus, with a well-concentrated mind, one should arrange [the letters] according to the sequence of the classes;
the letter *kṣa* alone should be applied sevenfold.
It is joined with the seed-syllable of Rudra and endowed with the six limbs.
Having placed the syllable *juṃ* at the beginning, O beautiful one, and ending with the letter *sa*,
some [call] the *mṛtyuñjaya* among them, consisting briefly of sixty-four [syllables]. (131)
The knower of yoga should perform the recitation (japa) with the excrement in due order;
and established in the wheel, the knower of the path should constantly practice meditation (dhyāna). || 132 ||
The collection of mantras should indeed be known as resembling pure crystal;
through meditation and the mind, [this is achieved], of this there is no doubt. || 133 ||
When a yogin seeking victory over death goes to the field of time (kālakṣetra),
he should contemplate the *saṃpuṭa* [mantra] and a second one above it.
Having done this, O Goddess of the Gods, one should always traverse the path;
one recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times. || 135 ||
(30) "O Goddess, because it destroys the object [of death] by means of the power that opposes death, this Cakramṛtyuñjaya has been described to you. (136)
One is liberated from all diseases and becomes equal to Amṛteśa.
O fair-faced one, I shall now further explain the initiation into the wheel (cakra).
Having withdrawn [the ritual] free from all distraction, one should perform the procedure for universal withdrawal in brief. || 138 ||
O Goddess of the gods, sprinkling and protection are said to be performed by means of the supreme syllable;
likewise, for the sake of purifying the consecration of those to be worshipped, there is the seizing of the bound souls (paśus). || 139 ||
Everything must be performed by him; having observed the sequence with a focused mind, he should meditate according to that very order. 140.
O Goddess of the gods, having meditated upon the wheel as it exists specifically within the body of the bound soul (paśu), one should perform the ritual actions in their proper sequence. (141)
Starting from the first leaf until everything is completed,
one should join [the visualization] with the heart-cakra and then commence the fire offering (homa) there;
one hundred oblations each should be offered in sequence, concluding with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Having joined [the disciple] by means of the path of the channels, he who enters [the state] with a concentrated mind—there, the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) should be offered; then one should join him again to others. || 144 ||
Having drawn [the breath] in this manner by means of *pūraka*, one should cause it to enter the wheel of the heart; O lady of good vows, it should be joined to the channels in this sequence.
This procedure for the sacrifice, however, one should not give to just anyone. || 146 ||
He attains equality with the gods in my presence; of this there is no doubt.
This entire secret core is incomparable, [O] Āpremi. || 148 ||
One should carefully draw an eight-petaled lotus, having inscribed the mantra with diligence.

In the heart-cakra, one should perform all this according to the previously stated procedure; whatever is desired, the practitioner of mantra should worship that, and there is no doubt that he will attain success. || 150 ||
O Goddess of gods, by means of non-conceptualization he shall become a partaker of the fruit of accomplishment.
O fair-faced one, having first performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the deities in the heart-cakra, (151)
O Dear One, one should perform the arrangement of the mandalas as before;
O Goddess, this is proclaimed as the most secret [teaching] and must not be given away. 152.
Having examined [the recipient], one should give; not to an atheist or a slanderer.
But by means of the intellect of reasoning and inference, one should grasp the teaching as if it were a desired object. 153.
What has been accepted will not succeed; therefore, one should avoid him.
Whether he possesses the three qualities or is endowed with qualities, and regardless of his state, such is the teacher (deśika). || 154 ||
This [rite] should always be honored by those who know the principle of Śiva; the placement (nyāsa) was previously taught by me in the Sūtra known as the Uttara. 155.
(34) That very thing is to be known therein; those alone are proclaimed as the mudrās.
One should not act otherwise, O Goddess; this is the command of the Supreme Lord. 156.
But he who, out of delusion, fails to understand this unsurpassed ritual for the purpose of destroying death, shall merely partake of oily fruits. (157)

One who knows the procedure for nourishment, who understands the application of the rules for ritual placement (nyāsa), and who knows the reality of the movement of the channels (nāḍī)—he shall conquer death. (158)
Exhausted by burning and dehydration, he departed with half his body;
by means of the excellent smoke, his head was split open at the crown.
Whoever, through such distinctions as these, knows the reality is to be known as liberated; all others are impostors who know only themselves, beginning with Śeṣa.
He who understands the principles and the supreme pervasion of those principles is not stained by merit or demerit; he is capable of bestowing grace upon all. (161)
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, when he knows reality,
no distinction whatsoever exists, for he is indeed like fire within fire.
Just as milk poured into milk, or water placed into water, no distinction can be found; so too, when one is permeated by the Lord, reality becomes unified.
For just as all rivers, once they have reached their resting place in the ocean, cannot be distinguished by their individual flavors or natures, [so too is the case for these beings]. (164)

In the same way, O Goddess, whether one belongs to a caste and stage of life or is an initiated animal-sacrificer (paśu), if they are endowed with the state of Śiva, these two are equal; of this there is no doubt. || 165 ||
He who, relying upon the Śiva-tantra, should perform a ritual division [of the body],
that man shall be cooked in the thirty-two terrible hells. (166)
A man is purified by penance for five days of Brahmā, five days of Keśava, and three days of Rudra. || 167 ||
Therefore, with every effort, one should always remain undiscriminating;
for the discriminating person goes downward, while the undiscriminating person conquers.
Thus, O Goddess, this supreme pervasion of the principles has been told to you;
it must be kept strictly secret by you and should not be given to one who has not received initiation from another.
Through ten, twelve, six, or three [perfections], one attains the unsurpassed state from among the castes;
or rather, it occurs when truth alone has been realized through worship.

Īśvara said:
When the *jīva* is joined with all things, both auspicious and inauspicious, and by it all beings live, therefore it is celebrated here as the *jīva*. (20)
Bound by manifold fetters from the beginning up to Kālarudra, the bound soul (paśu) wanders about; it is for this very reason that he is celebrated as "the wandering one. (21)

In the aggregates whose nature is consciousness, sentience is the state of being conscious;

on the path originating from the Sun, the circle of light (jyotirmaṇḍala) is to be meditated upon.
When that very [light] is present before one's eyes, it is proclaimed as death;
having caused that radiance to disappear within by means of inhalation (pūraka), one should enter one's own path.
The mouth, the two nostrils, and the two ears are the four causal [sites];
endowed with the five [sites] including the crest-lock (śikhā), it should always be meditated upon by yogins. (34)
One should contemplate divine nectar flowing from the center of the crest-lock;
it falls indeed into the smokeless fire and remains there again and again. (35)
In this way, they undergo desiccation from all sides, down to the base of the lotus;

There, the hollow space is seen, awakened by the lamp-seed;
then, by that very path, one should slowly perform exhalation (recaka), O virtuous lady. (37)
Then, O Goddess of the Gods, one should cut the first knot with a cutting instrument in this sequence until [the cord] reaches the head.
Then one should utter the syllable *huṃ* and exhale the upward-moving breath (*ūrdhvavāyu*) forcefully; by casting it forth with speed, fainting and trembling arise therein. (39)
Having fallen into a state of delusion, the knower of yoga, having regained his consciousness, should perform a restoration once more and destroy the fainting and trembling. (40)

By means of a downward-facing lotus and by circumambulation with lamps,

O Goddess, this supreme nectar of practice must not be given away;

But when it is certain, O Goddess of gods, even one who has a hundred years of life may depart [from the body];

In the case of hiccup, one should press upon the ears and turn the tongue;

"Established in the mantra along with its attendants, the Lord is the imperishable essence of mantra.

65) Therefore, I shall fully explain the definitive teaching on Bindudeva—[the reality] that is without syllables, unutterable, imperishable, and characterized by its own nature. || 4 ||

Because it is free from the impurity of manifold forms and because of its dissolution, it is called *bindu*;

Whichever seed of birth is seen in the eyes, the self (ātman) would be in the middle of that eye; the shadow of the living being is seen there.

yellow, red, and yellow again, tawny, and even smoky.
The tenth is like crystal; their respective fruits are as follows:
for the destruction of Piśācas, the black variety is declared by Śiva himself to be the best;
for the destruction of all seizing spirits (grahas), the blue variety is indeed proclaimed.
A cloud-colored [stone] is for the destruction of diseases; yellow and red for killing;
that which is smoke-colored and resembles crystal performs all rites and bestows liberation.
They declare that the deities of all [the mantras], beginning with Śveta, are as follows. || 50 ||
Beginning with Ananteśa and ending with Śikhaṇḍin, they are proclaimed; Kālāgnirudra is the ninth, and Sadāśiva is the tenth.
This is the primary characteristic of the deity Bindu, known as Śiva;
it should be understood by wise practitioners, sages, and those desiring liberation. 52.
The first point (bindu) is called "Void" (śūnya), and the second is the "Supreme Void" (paraśūnya);
therefore, they say that the third alone is the profound state that is the true meaning of reality (tattvārtha). || 53 ||
Akṣobhya is the supreme drop (bindu), the sixth, beyond doubt;
the seventh is the more empty (śūnyatara), and the eighth is the appearance of emptiness (śūnyābhāsa). (54)
The ninth is the Nirābhāsa (the non-manifest), while the tenth is the Ābhāsaka (the illuminator).
The eleventh is declared to be Sukānta (the beautiful end), and the twelfth is remembered as Suśiva (the most auspicious).
The thirteenth is Sunāda, the fourteenth is named Tāra;
the fifteenth is Varābhāsa, and the sixteenth is Dhruva-Bindu.
Ten times seven are said to be the imperishables (avyayas), established in the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva);
and Śiva is the one who is imperishable—thus, in sequence, there are eighteen.
One should diligently know that Bindudeva is both the supreme and the non-supreme;
by means of the single-rooted ladder, one should ascend to the highest state. 58.
The Goddess said:
How can there be the non-utterance of the *bindu*, or how might its utterance occur?
From the void, a voider void was spoken; thus, eighteen [voids] were taught in sequence. (59)
Thus, by means of this classification of names, the principles (tattvas) have been proclaimed.
That shadow which rests upon the eyes emerges from the middle of the eyebrows. (60)
"O Blessed One, you should tell me what the signs of that [state] would be.
"Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret concerning that which you have asked about; he is the Lord (Īśvara). (61)
Therefore, O Goddess, I shall fully explain that unsurpassed nectar of the *lakṣmā*, which is designated as the single *bindu*. (62)
That which is beyond utterance is to be known as Śiva; it is remembered as the unmanifest (avyakta).
Devoid of phonemes, it is nothing whatsoever; therefore, it is called the immutable (kūṭastha). (63)
Possessing a body endowed with color, it moves within the range of Brahmā and others;
having produced everything through its nature as a dense web, it departs.
O beautiful one, this is said to be the utterance of the deity Bindu;
therefore, one should utter it joined with others in all ritual acts.
At the time of initiation, during recitation, in the fire sacrifice, and likewise in the ritual worship of the phonemes,
it should be performed joined with the nasal drop (bindu) for the successful accomplishment of all rites.
O fair-faced one, that which I have described to you as the invocation by means of the word "Śūnya" is to be understood through the division of the elements, beginning with earth. (67)
(78) Its production occurs through one [element], O beautiful one;
one hundred and one oblations should be offered, and one should join reality with reality. 68.
That which is liberated from the sixth vowel and is the first among the seven principles—
by means of that single seed-syllable, the entire path should be offered as an oblation without exception.
The *pūrṇāhuti* offerings should be given for every hundred oblations;
one should cause the syllables to be pronounced with a protracted sound and joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*).
Then, when it is joined with the bindu, the preceptor must indeed produce the nāda;
at its conclusion, the Goddess should again cause the full oblations (pūrṇāhuti) to be poured.
In this way, one attains union with each reality (tattva) by means of that very reality; of this there is no doubt.
Now, I shall describe the target (lakṣa) for the shadow that rests upon the eyes. || 72 ||
By the mere knowledge of which one is liberated from the bondage of birth—
all that has been proclaimed in other treatises is here fully described. (73)
But the news is told, O Goddess, and this is indeed evident:
all yogins, O Mistress of the Gods, speak of "bindu, bindu. (74)
They do not recognize such a direct perception as that which proceeds by a wrong path, like [attacking] a sword from the front. (75)
With divine vision, one should see the supreme orb of light;
covering the face, it stands resembling the color of lac. || 76 ||
Resembling the rising sun and appearing as if produced from saffron dye,
it stands like a mass of smokeless glowing coals gathered into a single heap.
O Goddess, he who practices the supreme one hundred thousand [recitations] day after day is not afflicted by diseases within six months. (78)
Strengthened by the splendor of Śiva, he performs even the purification of the murder of a Brahmin without the ignition of fire; of this there is no doubt. (79)
Through the yoga of constant practice, when well-performed for six months,
the fulfillment of all desires arises— a goal sought even by the gods.
Within a year, the lord of yogis, whose self is disciplined and who is permeated by Śiva,
perceives directly whatever proceeds within the three worlds.
Enveloped by this body within the midst of his splendor as a mere sport, he creates and withdraws the universe; like Śiva, he attains mastery over his own will.
I shall now tell you how a *lakṣa* will arise even within that splendor; listen now, and not otherwise. (83)
Just as that lakṣa of power exists within the midst of that very fire, so too,
O beautiful one, that lakṣa of power is to be known and understood by them.
For those desiring the second accomplishment, there is only one [method], namely *vijñaptimātra*;
it involves eighty lakhs and a great lakh, and knowledge of the time for molten metal. (85)
Just as it has been seen through direct perception, and likewise through divine vision,
I shall proclaim the supreme true nature of yoga, which is itself direct perception.
Pressing the breast with the left hand, one should extend half the hand;
all the fingers should be extended, releasing only one [finger] there. || 87 ||
O Goddess of the gods, one should fix the *lakṣya* there at the center of the couch;
having established it directly in front of that, one should withdraw it through practice. (88)
One should meditate with a single gaze; when it wavers, one must certainly steady it. Very gradually, one should draw that focal point toward the face.
One should contemplate it entering [the body], resembling the milk of a white cow, with a most cool touch to the face, incomparable and unsurpassed. (90)
O Goddess, as soon as its taste is obtained, one attains success; there is no doubt about this.
Within just one month, one becomes endowed with intelligence and splendor; of this there is no doubt. (91)
His body will especially arise; there is no doubt in this matter.
O Lord of practitioners, he becomes omnipresent like Śakti.
Even though he had not yet entered the hall of a hundred thousand [verses], he was fortunate and pleasing to behold;
he was a knower of all scriptures, like the Lord of Speech himself—of this there is no doubt. (93)
O beautiful one, the characteristics of this [target], which is like direct perception, have been told to you;
now hear in brief the perfection that comes from its divine vision. 94.
O Goddess, when it is seen motionless, pride brings joy to men;
one should recognize this as the Great Lakṣa, which bestows all perfections.
Whatever exists in the three worlds becomes directly perceptible to him;
like fire, the yogi blazes forth, freed from old age and death.
Whatever it touches with its hand, whatever it beholds with its eye—
all of it blazes like fire, becoming unbearable even for the gods of the thirty-three realms.

One who knows yoga is not defiled by what is fit or unfit to eat; he may even initiate those who have committed the most heinous crimes, such as the killing of a Brahmin, for he is never tainted by such sins. (98)
One should observe the remaining group situated in three places like a garland:
in the direct perception [of the signs], white and yellow, and blue, black, and white.
One should observe such qualities as these within the midst of the white;
just as a gem pierced by a thread shines brilliantly in its purity. (100)
Thus that garland shines, strung together with the threads of the *nāda*.
O Goddess, this true nature of reality has been declared to you. (101)
Now I shall describe the supreme characteristic of the *bindu*;
it is situated above the forehead in the center of its mandala. (102)
O Goddess of Gods, it resembles a water bubble, as pure as clear crystal, smoke-colored, and blazing with many rays of light. (103)
O fair-faced one, this *lakṣa* increases day by day;
within a single month, whatever direction the lord of yogins gazes upon, [it prospers]. 104.
The yogi perceives a flash of lightning resembling Śiva; there is no doubt about this.
He should contemplate the dripping bindu through the movement of the fourth state (turya). 105.
Through the path of the uvula and the palate, into the expansive and auspicious heart-lotus—this should always be meditated upon by yogis for the sake of conquering death. (106)
By the very flow of the iḍā, everything is certainly nourished;
O lady of excellent hips, it is remembered as the bringer of all accomplishments through its various [aspects]. (107)
This divine [mantra], characterized by these [qualities], brings about all accomplishments:
the knowledge of hearing from afar, mental cognition, and vision. (108)
There is no doubt that it is born through this well-formed body;
all those forms previously mentioned are established within it. 109.
O Goddess of gods, that which is characterized by direct perception is remembered as the bringer of all accomplishments;
for accomplishments exist everywhere within the well-guarded illuminations of reality.
O Goddess, this supreme essence of knowledge must not be given to one who is ill-informed, deceitful, cruel, or who walks the path of injustice. 111.
To one who is self-controlled, tranquil, and devoted to the worship of Śiva,
who stands upon the path of Śiva, one should [appoint] a teacher who has reached the further shore of reality.
This knowledge should be imparted to one whose devotion to the Guru is always greater than that toward Śiva; otherwise, it should never be given under any circumstances. (113)
The Goddess said:

O Mahādeva, O Lord, explain to me according to the proper method the path of the parts (kalādhvan), which consists of the fourfold [categories] and comprises the entire world of moving and non-moving beings. 114.
O Lord, I shall explain the path of Kalā in brief; listen to me as to how creation proceeds through Nivṛtti and how it occurs through Pratiṣṭhā.
O Goddess of the gods, I shall explain the Vidyā for Peace in brief, and I shall also explain that which transcends Peace in brief. || 116 ||
(88) But for the *nivṛtti* [kalā], one should offer oblations in the sequence beginning with earth;
O Goddess of the gods, its emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) is declared to end with *prakṛti*. || 117 ||
O Maheśvarī, having first performed the *pauruṣa* [rite] and last the *māyātattva*, one should offer oblations into the *pratiṣṭhā* at the time of initiation.
Beginning from the Vidyā-tattva up to the Tattva of Sadāśiva,
the practitioner of mantras should perform oblations for the Vidyā at the time of initiation during the Śiva-sacrifice.
One should offer oblations for the Śānti [rite] and likewise for the Śivatattva in due order;
O Goddess of the Gods, one should then gradually offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Śāntyatīta [mantra].
Having performed the illumination from the syllable Oṃ, as well as the salutation (namaskāra),
the short Haṃsa shall be Nivṛtti, while that differentiated by the long vowel is Pratiṣṭhā.
The preceptor should indeed join it with the *vidyā* and the *bindu*;
joined with the *visarga*, it is proclaimed as peace (*śānti*). || 122 ||
It is joined with the syllable *haṃsa* and the sound *ukāra*, endowed with the ending *vauṣaṭ*,
conjoined with the crescent moon and the *nāda*, and accompanied by the syllable *ū*.
O Goddess, this has been fully explained as the cause for transcending peace (śāntyatīta).
Therefore, one who desires union with Śiva (śivasāyujya) should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
In the Nivṛtti-kalā, the eight and three principles (tattvas) should be offered as oblations by the preceptors;
however, in the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā, only seven should be offered by those who are composed in mind.
One should offer into the fire the three principles (tattvas) preceded by Vidyā;
above that, the principle of Śiva is declared to be for the sake of pacification (śānti).
(90) O Goddess, this is declared to be the pervasion of emanation within the path of the *kalās*.
Having known this, one is liberated and can liberate others; of this there is no doubt. (127)
The Goddess said:
"The vowels and all the deities alike are dependent upon the Bindu. By what is that Nāda—which possesses the brilliance and resonance of the Bindus—distinguished? (128)
Īśvara said:
Within its pericarp, the seed-vitality (bījajīva) is declared to exist;
resembling a thread of lotus fiber, it is pierced by the void of sound (nāda).
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, you have described Maheśvara as the partless Bindudeva;
I wish to hear how he is both with parts and without parts. (130)
Furthermore, O Lord, there is doubt regarding Bindudeva Maheśvara; O Īśāna, tell me here of his supreme and inferior divisions. (131)
O Goddess, listen, O beautiful one, as I shall fully declare that supreme secret of the Lord of the Bindu, which is both with parts and without parts.
The manifestation of the fifty principles, which effects the continuous process of bondage and liberation, exists within this principle of withdrawal as the manifest form of Svayambhū himself. (133)
The God situated on the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha) is proclaimed as "with parts" (sakala);
moreover, O Goddess, that which transcends it is described to you as "without parts" (niṣkala).
The Goddess said: (p.
92) Of what nature is his body, and by what seeds is it said to be known?
I wish to understand this, O Blessed One; you should deign to explain it.
The Lord (Īśvara) is so called because he is described as being under the control of Īśāna and others; likewise, in the case of other mantras,
he is worshipped due to the greatness of his qualities, as he is the Great One arising from all principles and so forth.
The fourteen [vowels] are beyond sound, beyond the parts [of phonemes], and beyond the senses;
they should be known together with the neuter [consonants] as the fifteen syllables.
But another, beyond the three pentads, is liberated into the state of the Bindu as the sixteenth;
he is to be known as Śiva with parts (sakala), for that Śiva creates the kalā.
Bound by the end of the *bindu* and emerging from the mass of sound, the *bindu* expands within the knot; from that, the arising of sound occurs. (139)
The five [elements], which are the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the aggregate (*saṅghāta*), are well-perfumed by the seed-source;
then, consecrated by the water of power (*śakti*), there arises the great sprout of the light of the drop (*bindu*).
The Goddess said:
"What is the meaning of the name 'Binduteja' (Light of the Bindu), and what is this 'bindu' that is spoken of here?
Īśvara replied:
Therefore, O Great Goddess, by your grace I shall explain it to you. (141)
This is your Lord Bindu, the one who leads all the world;
he dwells in the midst of Nāda, and is neither of the nature of origination nor of dissolution. || 142 ||
It is neither a constellation nor a seed, and no agent for it is found;
it is never diminished, nor does it become even slightly small, nor is it ever censurable, nor does it increase anywhere. (143)
Unmanifest yet abiding within the unmanifest, he is exceedingly subtle yet not possessed of subtlety;
like the wind, he eternally wanders with his ten forms.
The protector of the eight worlds, with eyes like lotuses, he is this very Lord Bindu, the teacher of all the worlds and the universe. 145.
He is the fierce one who brings about the end of the eon, filling the seven continents and more;
he leaves only the seven oceans remaining and is the destroyer of the twelve suns.
The entire world here exists as a single mass, like a lump of clay, with its base in the netherworld, its support in the serpent's body, and its crushing pressure from the serpent's limbs. 147.
With the subtle balance of yoga, Śiva weighs this entire world of the moving and the unmoving, like a jewel on the half-and-half notch of a chin-string. (148)
He is Time, who by means of his illusory power (māyā) causes the world to revolve like the wheel of a water-wheel;
he is indeed Death, and he is Indra, Varuṇa, and the Moon.
He is Anala, Nīla, Āditya, and Ākāśa in succession;
he is Brahmā, he is Viṣṇu, Rudra, and indeed Īśvara. (150)
Hrī, Śrī, Smṛti, Dhṛti, Medhā, Kānti, Sarasvatī, Prakṛti, Puruṣa, Niyati, and Kāla. (151)
This Lord is Māyā and Vidyā; from the Bindu, this entire world arises.
He is likewise the Veda, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Buddhism, and Jainism. || 152 ||
Whatever treatises there may be, all have issued forth from the Bindu.
One should know that everything consists of the Bindu—mind, consciousness, and form. (153)
He is the supreme one who delights all the immortals, the bearer of the burden of all scriptures;
he is immeasurable, subtle, unmanifest, and eternal.
Whether walking, throbbing, sleeping, eating, or even waking, for those whose nature is permeated by Śiva, the Bindu-deity is eternally their very self. 155.
Then, with his body divided as Ardhanārī, he is remembered by you as Sakala (with parts);
then, through the yoga of the absorption of his partial portions, he is remembered as Niṣkala (without parts).
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā. The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear the definitive explanation of the sound of Nāda."
It is proclaimed to be of two kinds, distinguished as gross and subtle. || 1 ||
O Maheśvara, how does the nāda become gross or even subtle?
How is it to be known within the body in its true essence? Please tell me this.
O Goddess, listen, for I shall declare to you that supreme secret which you have asked about— the unsurpassed knowledge of Nāda.
That sound which is heard perfectly full from within the body—
therein Prakṛti has arisen, clothed in a great net.
One should report that he stands there in the midst of that sound;
the person born therein has transcended all qualities and is stainless. (5)
The third, however, was the Great Sound (Mahacchabda), abiding like the resonance of a bell;
from that, Rudra was born, the Lord and leader of the three worlds.
That which is declared as the peaceful sound, the supreme cause,
stands like a staff for striking the wicked, resembling a mass of moonlight.
Within that [egg] arose the Lord, a mass of splendor belonging to the Great Soul—
he who is the perfected Śiva, subtle, perfectly tranquil, and facing in all directions.
For he is indeed immeasurable and inexpressible; he is proclaimed as being of the nature of sound (nāda).
And that very state is proclaimed by the knowers of reality as the station of dissolution (layasthāna). || 9 ||
The supreme deity is beyond the state of dissolution, indefinable, and free from affliction;
knowing this, the wise one is liberated even while enjoying sense objects. (10)
"This supreme secret knowledge has not been told to just anyone.
The Goddess said:
"What is this Nāda? What is its measure, what is its form, and from where has it flowed? (11)
"For what purpose and by whom was this uttered, and how does it proceed?
The Lord said:
"O fair-faced one, this is my supreme form, designated as Sound (Nāda)."
It is constantly contemplated by yogins who desire the state of non-rebirth;
because it is all-pervasive, no measure for this liberation can be found. (13)
Because it is beginningless, there is no origination; and because it is eternal, there is no fixed destiny.
Just as it exists in conventional reality, it cannot be uttered, being devoid of words and syllables. (14)
That is attained with ease; I shall tell you the means for it:
having covered both of one's ears with the two thumbs, the practitioner [should proceed]. (15)
Then he hears that sound, which has a resonance like the roar of a rain-cloud;
O Goddess, O large-eyed one, from hearing this sound—
Having severed the bonds of the fetters, he attains supreme nirvāṇa;
this subtle body of mine is designated as "sound. (17)
This wonderful [teaching] has been made manifest for the purpose of removing the bonds of the bound soul (paśu); beyond this, there is no other object of meditation that is taught. (18)
And this supreme, unutterable, and stainless potency of his is not obtained by the Goddess when I am not pleased. (p. 101) 19.
He who correctly perceives this attains identity with it;
thus has this Nāda, which is most difficult to obtain, been fully explained to you. (20)
Now listen to that which is beyond reproach, wherein this [soul] attains dissolution—
this fourth state known as Turya, which transcends the preceding stages.
One should perceive the fifth state as space, established in equilibrium;
it is immovable, indefinable, infinite, unborn, and undecaying.
Without beginning, middle, or end, one, without return, free from conceptual proliferation, tranquil in mind, beyond the senses, and free from affliction. (23)
Extensive, uninterrupted in its middle and ends, facing in all directions,
stainless, pure, circular, lofty, pervasive, and eternal. (24)
The ether known as Sadāśiva is described as having such qualities;
this subtle, imperishable supreme ether is the seed of the universe. (25)
Here, the sound (nāda) attains dissolution when all activity has ceased;
having reached the state of dissolution into supreme peace, one who is counted among the perfected ones indeed attains this station.
By his will, these beings once again become embodied in sound;
thereafter, they remain in the position of universal sovereigns with bodies composed of sound.
By the will of the Lord, they perform the act of bestowing grace upon the worlds;
having thus assumed their office, they do so through the expenditure of this time.
"They again attain a state that is unattainable by nature, empty and free from ego. Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
O Great Lord Śiva, tell me specifically about the Goddess Śakti and the characteristics of Śakti.
Is this power (śakti) in the cause declared to be different from it, or non-different? (1)
Whether they are identical or different, I ask this question regarding my doubt:
if the power were not distinct from those two, tell me what the difference between them is.
Or else, there might be another power [distinct] from Śiva; therefore, he would not be the uncaused [cause].
Through the state of being either non-different or different, there arises the doubt as to whether he exists or does not exist. (3)
(104) "The scriptures have various opposing views; one who is of a doubting nature perishes.
Therefore, O Supreme Lord, speak without concealment so that I may be free from doubt. (4)
The Lord is the non-different cause; His power is characterized by presiding over [the world].
He is omniscient, conscious, pure, and the illuminator of all principles.
Abiding therein among all principles, it reveals those various states according to their qualities and defects, among living beings who are both pure and impure.
Likewise, the power that pervades all beings, as well as their essential nature and the senses,
eternally abides within them all.
Just as the power of burning exists in fire and the quality of coldness in water, so too do these six powers of the Lord exist within the Supreme Self. (8)
Just as there is the supporting of the earth, just as there are rays in the sun,
and just as there is space in the sky— such are the powers of the Lord.
Just as fragrance is in the earth, form in fire, taste in water, touch in the lordly wind, and sound in space, so too are the powers of the Lord.
Just as rays belong to the sun, or as the radiance belongs to jewels,
so too is the beginninglessness of power and its possessor accepted here.
Just as the light of jewels, fire, the moon, and so forth are inseparable from the sun,
so too do the powers (śakti) residing within one's own body belong to the Supreme Śiva.
Whether undivided or divided, characterized as either a property or its locus,
the property, by its own will, presides over the activity of the locus. (13)
When the substratum (dharmin) is absent, the property (dharma) cannot attain establishment;
when the substratum is maintained, that property is said here to have a valid cause.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord Maheśvara, even now there remains a doubt regarding knowledge and the object of knowledge."
Tell me in its entirety the distinction between reality, both supreme and inferior.
How do the principles (tattvas) perform the activities of embodied beings within the body?
And how do those principles experience the waters of dreams while lying down?
Whether standing or walking, speaking or even laughing, the principles (tattvas) reside in the breathing; they abide within the long breath as it moves. (3)
And what principles (tattvas) are proclaimed for him during the middle and the conclusion [of the ritual], while he is dancing and singing, filled with passion and longing for compassion? (4)
And who abide in the signless (animitta), and who indeed remain in the state of contemplation?
What is the destiny for those attached to ritual actions when they give up their lives? (5)
Tell me, by what are these principles impelled to perform their activities?
And how are the principles understood to be established in eight or nine ways?
How is there uniformity among the groups ending in the final consonants, and how is the flavor equal? And how is it that those devoid of internal organs are established within the body? (7)
(108) "O Mahādeva, please graciously explain this secret.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret regarding how the principles (tattvas) reside within the body.
And hear how they perform their activities when presided over by another— the true nature of knowledge, the distinction between the principles, and that which is supreme and inferior.
Exaltation, mental agitation, the prowess of the sun, as well as intoxication with joy and delusion—these have been described by Surasundarī. (10)
All this has been declared as full of essence and should be understood by those who contemplate reality;
likewise, there is the upward-flowing power and the influence on the left and right sides.
Steady up to the ears and tranquil, the supreme partless [reality] has been described;
with the gaze fixed on the causeless, it is placed upon the lower lip of the mouth of speech. (12)
Laughing, the state residing within the heart shines forth in eight ways when the desired [state] is described;
having thus known it in these eight ways, this indeed is the characteristic of emptiness.
The palate [is characterized] by the taste of delight; cough, breath, and the hanging tongue;
joined with the mental application of the syllable *huṃ*—this is declared to be the eightfold [mantra] rich in artistic refinement (*kalā*). 14.
One should observe the face as it manifests sweetness, the *halāhala* poison, radiance, fear, terror, trembling, and the union of anger and compassion. (15)
O Goddess, it is fragile like a child's [toy], turned away, and beautifully adorned;
it is scattered by fire and wind, and its song is accompanied by the sound of tinkling ornaments. (16)
That which is named Kṣapaṇa is declared to be the supreme knowledge. One should recognize the states of Āghūrmita, Vighūrmita, Suṣupta, and Supta. (17)
O beautiful one, awakening is indeed the cessation of the continuity of the blow of a dream;
these qualities, which end with destruction, must be understood by those who contemplate reality. 18.
A gentle and steady gait, swift movement, as well as leaping and shifting;
the sound "huṃ," harsh speech, and the eightfold Vedas at the throat and lips—[these are the signs]. (19)
O Goddess, pervasiveness has been described; now understand the nature of sound as well:
the deity with parts (sakala) resides in the udāna breath, while the supreme partless one (niṣkala) resides in the agitated state. 20.
One should understand that in the state devoid of thought, the piercing of the heart has been described by me;
in the secret [teaching], however, the essence of the Kalās is known as the impurity of Vikrama.
O beautiful lady, it should be understood by one who knows the knowledge that *kṣepaṇa* is said to occur in *harṣa*; likewise, understand that it occurs in *unmāda*, ending in *kṣaya*. (22)
Then, in the state of delusion (moha), there is that which is produced from the throat and lips; this indeed is the first group of eight.
Above that is the union of all parts, which is partless (niṣkala), sustaining, and trembling.
That which is without appearance is said to be "emptiness"; it should be observed with great effort.
On the left is the principle (tattva) of Kalesvara, and on the right is Bhujamalin.
O Goddess, the mendicant (kṣapaṇa) should be known by his application to the heart up to the ear;
O lady of excellent hips, he is characterized by the body as being partless (niṣkala) at the end of decay.
In the Śānta-tattva, the second characteristic of division has been declared to me:
the Sakala [form] is in the path of the mouth, while the Niṣkala [form] is in the left path.

In the state of emptiness, when there is distraction regarding the support, it is conceptualized as the absence of intrinsic nature; in the signless state, however, one who is rich in creative power perceives [reality] as the stainless sky. (27)
The destruction [of defilements] should be understood as occurring in laughter; one should observe it within the mind itself.
O you who abide within, I shall explain to you the internal destruction that resides in the heart. 28.
The Lord Īśāna is established in the throat and lips; there is no further [higher] stride.
Thus, the eightfold impurity (malāṣṭaka) is to be understood through the threefold division of knowledge.
O lady of excellent limbs, the third supreme division has been described:
the deity with parts (sakala) is within the heart, while the partless (niṣkala) is unperceived.
One should know the palate to be empty; one should observe the state of existence within its own nature.
When it is illuminated, one should know it as enriched with its digits; when the palate is void, it is shaken by the breath.
O Goddess, when [the breath] is suspended, it should be known as *pralaṃba*; this is declared by the term *svarita*.
O lady of excellent limbs, one should recognize that which has been exhausted by means of the sound *huṃ*. (32)
Likewise, O Goddess, that which is joined with *na* is proclaimed as the gutturo-labial;
this, O beautiful lady of the gods, is declared to be the fourth division.

O beautiful lady, when it is sweet and complete, one should know that the eternal state is reached; having gone to the station of Ananta, it is characterized by the meaning of emptiness in its laughter.
When one is afraid, Kāleśvara is to be known; when terrified, Khamala is remembered;
when trembling, Kṣapaṇa is proclaimed—thus it has been told in due order.
The other [aspect] is the abiding reality, compassion, and the eightfold nectar;
this is indeed declared to be the fifth division, explained in due order.
In movement, it is the support of the three steps; in that which is fragile, it is the partless supreme.
In pervasiveness, they call it the Void. This is your [nature], O Wreath-armed One. (37)
O Aparājitā, one should always understand that these elements— earth, water, fire, air, and space— are distinct entities existing within the body.
O lady of excellent hips, maintain the thread within the house until its end;
O beautiful goddess, [recite] that which is produced from the throat and lips, joined with the sound of the *jhaṅkāra*.
The six varieties have been explained in due order according to their application:
in the state without waves (aghūrmita), it is the support of the parts (kalādhāra); in the state with waves (vighūrma), it consists of the partless (niṣkalātman).
They say that in deep sleep it is empty; one should perceive it as being veiled.
But in the dream state, time arises from mental construction, while at the end of the dream, the void is remembered as pure.
O Goddess, in the case of *vighāta* there is *kṣapaṇā*, and in the case of *santāna* there is *kṣayamantaka*;
in *vibodha* there is *kaṇṭhoṣṭhya*; and *subheda* is the seventh in sequence. (42)
In the Saumya [state], they say there is a gentle movement; in the Sthira [state], indeed, it is the supreme, partless [state].
One should know the Śīghra [state] to be void, and one should observe its own movement.
In leaping, the deity known as Kālatattva is invoked; in moving about, Kha mala is remembered; in the utterance of "huṃ," the god Kṣapaṇa is present—he should reverse all of this.
At the end of the destruction, the *jharjhara* sound is proclaimed; one should observe it in what is called the "Auspicious" [note].
In speech, when the words are coarse and bright, the gutturo-labial [sound] is present everywhere. (45)

O Goddess, having thoroughly understood this supreme reality— which is stainless due to its eightfold division— along with its divisions of principles (tattva), one realizes it in its partless (niṣkala) state according to the prescribed rule.
Thus, for one who knows the distinctions of consciousness, there is no doubt regarding his liberation. (p.
117) In that which is called Haṃsa are Bindu and Nāda; in the Half-moon is Nirodhikā.
The pervasive one, the upward-moving, and the power (śakti) are the great state of peace;
all that is imperishable within the imperishable is to be understood in its proper sequence. (48)
Thus, he who knows this in its true essence shall become that supreme goal.
In this way, indeed, the eightfold division has been explained to you, O beautiful one. (49)
Furthermore, I shall later explain it again in its ninefold form as it truly is.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā. The Lord said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed knowledge of sound (śabdajñāna), which resides within sentences, within the heart, and is established even while bestowing [itself]. 1.
In the three locations, the entire deity brings about the destruction of the bonds of bondage;
one should know Śiva as the follower, while the prowess belongs to the Queen of Knowledge (Vidyārājñī). || 2 ||
O Goddess, that which follows the breath should be designated as the partless (niṣkala);
it is divine, born of the lower abdomen (apāka), and devoid of the limits of the navel and the ears.
It is eternally situated in the midst of the void, the liberator from all bonds within;
it is the palate located between the ears and the navel, curved like the stalk of a lotus.
That which is designated by the name Kalāḍhya is the creator of all forms;
it casts both of those [principles] into that reality (tattva), the tranquil reality (śāntatattva), along with all the others.
One should always contemplate with the mind the entire [mantra] together with the void-seeds (khapadas),
along with the upward-flowing fire (ūrdhvavāhamanau) and the blazing abode (gāram), in brief.
(119) Well-applied and perfectly tranquil, it removes the bonds of the *kṣapaṇa* and *upāśa*;
[it is applied] from the heart-lotus to the region of the navel, and between the ears and the palate. || 7 ||
For in these aforementioned locations, the auspicious destruction that ends the fetters occurs;
[it occurs] in the udāna at the station of immobility, and in all stations, O Sulocanā.
Everything should be consumed with the word "sarva"; the eighth is the immutable word "śabda.
O Goddess, this group of eight words has been proclaimed for the sake of welfare.
Nor should the highest good be given away, for there is no knowledge beyond this:
the meditation on emptiness, which is difficult to perceive due to its beginningless and endless non-existence.
Therefore, with every effort, one should characterize it through existence and non-existence;
by that, O fair-hipped one, this is known: "He whose state of being consists of my own state. (11)
For the sake of protecting non-existence, I have composed this discourse on existence for one whose mind has abandoned non-existence and turned toward existence. (12)
One wanders in saṃsāra as long as one does not find the true state of being, even through the words of the meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti, and through the beauties of poetry and rhetoric. (13)
One who is deluded by the contemplation of the treatises on grammar goes to a downward state;
non-existence leads to emptiness, and that which is empty is called non-existence.
Liberation is said to be non-existence, while bondage is the conceptualization of existence.
Through non-existence, the mind attains immovability within the eternally empty.
Then the embodied soul, going toward nirvāṇa, attains the abode that is free from all affliction.
I contemplate that which is without state or word, inaccessible, the pure emptiness of nirvāṇa, the vast sky above, all-pervading.
By which [means] a person who has practiced the non-dual emptiness is not born again here in a womb;
the net of bonds is severed, primordial nature (prakṛti) ceases its creative activity, and he is withdrawn from the state of manifestation. || 16½ ||
Behold the solitary void, devoid of the impurities of worldly existence; behold this state here described by those liberated from all bonds as the emptiness of Nirvana.
This is empty, this is empty; from emptiness comes emptiness, the supreme and the inferior.
And that which is empty even from emptiness—that emptiness is indeed free from affliction. || 17 1/2 ||
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"O Knower of the Vedas, Sāṃkhya, Purāṇas, Pañcarātra, and Itihāsas..."
And likewise other yogins, as well as those who abide even on wrong paths. || 1 ||
Having deluded them with their circle of breasts, they show them their own bodies;
and they too say here, "Whence else could there be a way [to liberation]? (2).
"There would either be partiality on your part, or liberation would exist everywhere.
O Lord, this is my doubt; tell me what is the truth. (3)
Īśvara said:
"O large-eyed one, both you and I are the root of all people;
as Mātṛkā in the form of Śiva, we are the tree born of the intellect."
a) From the realm of Brahmā down to the very foundations of the earth, the entire world of moving and unmoving beings— all have originated from my seed and emerged from your womb. (5)
The five which are proclaimed on earth as the great sciences beginning with the Vedas are: Sanskrit, Prākṛta, Apabhraṃśa, and Anunāsika.
Whatever verbal expression there may be, whether divine or non-divine, it is born from your progeny;
you are the goddess who is always proud, eternally devoted to egoism.
Since everything is established in you, modifications arise from you;
therefore, the world perceives me as being subject to modification, though I am free from it.
Those who are deluded regarding fundamental knowledge do not attain the supreme state;
for all living beings die even while consuming food of six flavors.
Having consumed the root of the *mṛtasañjīvanī* plant, they do not die;
just as a jar [is not distinct] from a lump of clay, and a cloth [is not distinct] from its threads. (10)
The phonemes, existing in the form of power (śakti), attain manifestation by the will of Śiva.
The Goddess said:
"Having recited the root-knowledge (mūlajñāna), the yogis, being disciplined, meditate. (11)
Having their every desire fulfilled, they enter the auspicious state; O Maheśvara, liberation is attained through renunciation and through the practice of ascetic conduct.
O Lord, that liberation which is obtained through contentment by those veiled by ignorance is likewise obtained through knowledge;
you are the illuminator of that knowledge.
O Lord of Gods, tell me how worship, knowledge, and the object of knowledge may come to be; O Lord of Gods, I have a great doubt regarding this. (14)

Through the practices of renunciation and non-renunciation, through contentment and self-restraint, and indeed through the emaciation of the body, the unintelligent desire for liberation from the Lord. (15)
Cold, wind, heat, fire, the ten, and the eleven;
likewise hunger, thirst, and rain—the wise seeker of liberation should endure these. (16)
"Celibacy, austerity, charity, compassion, patience, and non-violence—this speech regarding birth does not lead to pervading the world, nor to liberation. (17)
Liberation does not come through charity, nor through austerities, nor through the Vedas or sacrifices;
liberation comes through knowledge alone for the embodied soul when it is completely freed.

Even one whose senses and mind are restrained—what could such a person do, since knowledge is so difficult to attain? He would be like a charioteer mounted on a well-trained chariot who lacks the power of sight. (19)
The Goddess said:
Those Brahmins who are exponents of the Vedas, those who know the Sāṃkhya, those who know Yoga,
and those who are learned in the Pañcarātra, [if they associate] with other sinful people— || 20 ||
They speak thus, O Mahādeva; I shall declare their knowledge:
it is like fire cast into fire, or water poured into water. (21)

Just as a clod of earth is devoid of pleasure and lacks consciousness when struck by a staff or a stone, so too should Nirvana be understood as being entirely free from both pleasure and pain. || 22 ||
"O Lord, this which was known by me has been told to you. Īśvara said: p. 126) [The Lord said: "O God, this which was known by me has been told to you. Īśvara said:
All are thus thoroughly afflicted because they do not know the reality of liberation. || 23 ||
I shall tell you; listen to what liberation is like:
where there is the destruction of the living soul, devoid of happiness and devoid of consciousness. (24)
For them, liberation is like the dissolution of a lump of clay; it is not called liberation at all.
Their "liberation" is merely the belly of Māyā, whereas true liberation is consciousness through its various states.
One should remain like a corpse, free from the duality of deep sleep, through the liberation that consists of being devoid of consciousness. || 26 ||

Thus, even though it is the very essence, it remains [hidden] from one whose mind is attached to sense objects, in this auspicious great knowledge of Śiva, which is a city of realized wisdom. || 27 ||
The Lord is omniscient in mind, all-pervading, subtle, auspicious, and immutable;
indeed, he attains the state of equality with the nature of the Master for the one possessed of knowledge. (28)
He becomes omniscient and perfect, all-pervading and imperishable;
there is no arrival of sufferings, and therein happiness is uninterrupted. (29)

The cessation of all latent tendencies and the state of peace is designated as liberation; liberation belongs to both consciousness and its absence, but not to those who are merely freed from delusion.
When consciousness is pervasive and free from delusion, it is designated as liberation;
having become Śiva, the stainless one, he remains devoid of passion. || 31 ||
The wise one, whose mode of existence is self-dependent, who sits in bliss and bestows happiness,
becomes either bodiless or embodied according to his own will.
Becoming grosser than the gross and likewise subtler than the subtle, he enjoys sovereignty over all worlds according to his pleasure. (33)
They are indeed free from obstruction, devoid of passion and greed;
having attained the supreme Śiva-knowledge, which is beyond qualities and fulfills all desires. || 34 ||
Having become the peerless Great Self, he creates himself within himself;
pervading all, they remain established, dwelling within all beings.
There is nothing unknown to her, nothing unseen, and nothing unresorted to; nor is there ever any movement of hers anywhere in all the worlds that is not preceded by her arrival. (36)

Through their inherent power, they always grasp the objects of the principles (tattvas), as well as the modifications of primordial nature (prakṛti), both those devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and those possessing qualities (saguṇa). || 37 ||
Having been sustained by the Cause, they grasp their respective objects;
and all those qualities of sovereignty abide in the eternal Śiva. (38)
Even among those who have been initiated and who know the reality, he alone—endowed with immeasurable power, omniscient, and indeed the giver of all—is [the true teacher]. (39)
He is remembered as the doer of all, the lord of all yogas, and equal to Śiva;
he possesses the power of hearing from afar, as well as knowledge, reflection, and vision.
Free from the forms of the mind, intellect, ego, and the causal principle,
the slayer of Bali is self-dependent in all his undertakings.
The Sustainer, the Impeller, the Overseer, the Striker, the Subduer of all beings, the Mind, and indeed the Transmental (Unmanā). || 42 ||
The Lord of All, the Soul of All, the Sovereign of All, and the Great Refuge; he is undecaying, immortal, inexhaustible, and the agitator of all. (43)
Whatever qualities belong to those born of bondage—the sufferings of conception, birth, and old age—all these arise from ignorance; there is only one absolute bliss. (44)
Just as fire, though produced by friction while residing within wood, does not enter the fire-drill again once it has become extinguished; so too [is the nature of the Self]. (45)
Just as that which has attained the state of clarified butter cannot become curd again, so too, having realized perfect knowledge, one does not become a bound soul (paśu) again. || 46 ||
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"Without having attained supreme perfection, even one who is initiated and endowed with knowledge..."
Having understood the true nature of the scriptures, one is nonetheless tormented by the sufferings of death.
O Lord, O Supreme Sovereign, tell me: what would be the cause for [the fruits of action] regarding living beings while they are acting, since their destiny is imperceptible?
The Lord is two fingers above that place where he would be during salutation;
that [place] is the trident, which, by the force of the wind, is above the right breast.
For seven nights, people listen to [the recitation] by name and by oneself, including the short, long, and protracted vowels, as well as the *sādhārita* and *sakauśaka* [styles]. (4)
From the moment of vibration until the end of the month belonging to one's own lunar fortnight,
the *Tantriṇī* conjoined with the eighth [digit] is known as the nectar (*amṛta*). (5)
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā—these are the five worldly [tithis] that recur every three nights; now hear from me regarding those belonging to Śiva.
The lunar day (tithi) is Amṛtā, and by its very nature it is the second; the asterism (nakṣatra) is Abhijit, and above that is Jayantikā.
The moment known as Piṅgala consists of the two stars Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
it repeatedly licks the moonlight of the cluster of Dhruva stars like a wheel.
When the sun of immeasurable life has risen and shines intensely, licking [the end of life], then one falls under the power of death at the completion of the year; of this there is no doubt.
Having understood this, the wise person should perform acts of giving, recitation, and meditation on the day of immortality; all of that shall become a bestower of liberation. (10)
Whatever action one performs under the constellation named Abhijit, or during the victories [of the planets] presided over by Rudra and Viṣṇu, all that bestows the attainment of liberation.
Whatever action a man performs during the Piṅgala Muhūrta,
having understood the day of the week and the lunar date, all that bestows both success and liberation.
