The two fortnights consist of truth and untruth, and the third is indeed the fixed (dhruva).
When joined with the nectar (amṛta), liberation is granted by one of these two.
Through recitation and the yoga of meditation, success shall be achieved in a single day;
for thus indeed does one who understands this supreme secret [attain it]. (14)
He shall become equal to Śiva and rejoices together with Śiva;
his dead body shall not decay—this is the supreme conviction. (15)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"O God, those who were created by you in the past have been separated from their respective rites."
The Brahmins, endowed with the eight forms, perform sacrifices with various rites.
Why are those very people who have been initiated by various officiants with abundant sacrificial fees not liberated by those same mantras? (2)
If you speak the truth, [then] they lead the castes to union;
yet why do those Vedas, which are composed of the very same castes, not grant liberation? (3)
The masters say: some know it as the Praṇava, others know it as the letter *M*;
it is the arrangement of fifty syllables, the Puruṣa whose form is the Bindu.
A certain sixteenth digit of the moon is of nectar-like luster;
it is the source of trees, shrubs, creepers, and medicinal herbs.
The glorious one, who is the best among all sustainers of beings, is like nectar and the speaker of nectar;
some say he is the syllable *ya*, while others say he is the breath and so forth, facing in all directions.
In all things, the All-Knowing Creator is that wherein He manifests;
the wise declare that the letter *ra* here signifies fire. (7)
The withdrawal of all principles is renowned as being like the fire of time;
that consumer, whose fuel is food and drink, is called the individual self (jīvātman). (8)
Some praise Indu, who is honored by gods and asuras;
others call him Vibhū, who is worshipped by Śakra. (9)
All those before you offer salutation to the syllable *la*, the supreme state,
which resembles the kunda flower dripping with nectar and is as cool as the rays of the moon.
Some say that the seed-syllable of Varuṇa, which is eternal and bestows life upon living beings, is the supreme;
others, however, declare the unsurpassed seed-syllable of space (Vyoman) to be so.
Space is the support of all beings, providing them with room;
some say this is the most excellent, established as half of half of fifty.
The letter *ma* is the supreme reality; standing with arms raised, he is the Puruṣa consisting of twelve syllables, which the elders learned in the three Vedas possess. (13)
He is Agni, the lord of sacrifice, the sacrifice itself, the *vaṣaṭ* call, and the *svadhā* offering;
he is the Sun, the end-maker, who shines forth in the east. (14)
The waking state, preceded by the letter *a*, which sets all phonemes in motion, is the *Ṛgveda* and the *Āhavanīya* fire; it is said to be the *sāttvika* quality. (15)
The letter *A* is proclaimed as the Brahman of the earth element among all beings;
the letter *U* has Viṣṇu as its deity, is characterized by passion (*rajas*), and has the nature of liquidity. (16)
For this Dakṣiṇāgni is traditionally known as consisting of the Yajurveda;
they call the inner self (antarātman) the dream state, which is the supreme abode.
The letter *ma* has Rudra as its deity and is proclaimed to be characterized by *tamas*.
The *Sāman* is indeed the *gārhapatya* fire; it is characterized by the quality of *tamas*. (18)
They call deep sleep the state; that indeed is the supreme state.
The letter *ha* is truly without measure; that is the fourth state, the supreme state.
The *sañjīva* is the essence of the mantras of the Atharvaveda for all embodied beings;
it transcends the *guṇas*, is supreme peace, and by knowing which one attains immortality. (20)
"The stainless, divine space, all-pervading, the Lord, and imperishable"—this is the supreme Brahman, the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), which is eternally of the nature of existence. || 21 ||
Some call this the manifest Śiva, the tenfold seed-container;
it is remembered as the abode of all vidyās, the "Vidyālaya."
Regarding that, others speak of what is expressed through the syllables of the three principles;
some, relying on the knowledge of the Savior (Tāraka), [speak of] the Lord of a million [verses]. || 23 ||
The Lord of the Six Nines (Kārttikeya), the destroyer of the noose of hair (Śiva), and likewise the withdrawal of the fifty seeds (the fifty letters)—this is considered the supreme cause. (24)
They say that Nāda, the cause of all beings, is Sadāśiva;
he alone, existing in five states, is Śiva, both with parts and without parts.
Likewise, other people who know the knowledge of Śiva conceive of it in this [heart] as having the coiled form of a serpent—unutterable and free from ailment. (26)
First, among all the scriptures, this is written but not recited;
thus, it is devoid of salutation with joined palms, chanting, and meditation. (27)

(140) That which is devoid of the instruments [of perception]—smell, form, taste, touch, sound, and so forth—and in which the mind is restrained from conceptual construction (saṅkalpa); this indeed is the supreme state. || 28 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva—
thus the Praṇava is proclaimed to have five aspects and five deities.
Śiva, whose form is fivefold, consists of one measure, two measures, three measures, more than that, and that which is situated in half a measure.
Those who know the Vedas and proponents of Sāṃkhya who are thus deluded regarding these matters, being confused by the section on knowledge, do not arrive at a certain conclusion. (31)
Deprived of the supreme reality and devoid of primordial origination, those deluded ones do not understand that the *ṛc*s alone possess the pervasiveness of the mantra. (32)
(149) By means of pride in the Purāṇas and Vedas, and likewise by the Smṛtis,
men whose souls are well-sprinkled with gross states of being remain devoted to the knowledge of cattle. 33.
They defile the Śaiva knowledge of Śiva, which brings about all auspiciousness;
being firmly established in their own faction, they revile the factions of others. (34)
Not knowing the pervasion of the *varṇas*, nor likewise the pervasion of the *tattvas*, and not knowing the supreme reality (*paratattva*), they desire the fruits of gross knowledge. (35)
For this reason, O Goddess, in that [system] the castes do not grant liberation;
all, their views being unsettled, dispute with one another. (36)
In this manner, they mutually revile one another through the use of formal debate, informal chatter, and cavil.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Manner of the Confusion of Knowledge," in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
It is traditionally held that action alone is innate to the principles of Pradhāna, Ātman, and Īśa.
For what purpose does the Lord perform creation, which is born from Pradhāna? (1)
O Śaṅkara, how does this bound soul (paśu) become one who has accomplished his purpose?
Is the body derived from primordial matter (pradhāna), or what is its ultimate nature? || 2 ||
What are the characteristics of one who is awakening, and how do the awakened and the unawakened differ?
Regarding Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśāna, who possesses agency and of what nature is it? (3)
Having reached the state of the *kalala*, how does the person remain?
For what purpose is there bondage, O Lord of the Gods, and what indeed is bondage? (4)
What is the nature of bondage, or who is bound by bondage?
Is it the individual soul (paśu) that is joined with or separated from primordial matter (prakṛti)? (5)
And how is the creation of the principles (tattvas) brought about, and what is the nature of the various ritual actions?
[Tell me] truly of that which possesses qualities and that which is devoid of qualities, as well as the different types of yoga.
O Lord, tell me all this again in due order;
O Goddess, embodied beings have been submerged in the beginningless stream of existence. (7)
Like a boat for crossing over, these three principles are taught;
they have been declared to you, O Goddess of Gods, as the supreme and primary quality.
The individual soul (aṇu) is devoid of qualities, yet it possesses form; though all-pervading, it is powerless and imperishable;
its conduct is downward, its nature is insatiable, it is the enjoyer of the qualities (guṇas), and it remains within the sphere of bondage. || 9 ||

The individual soul (puruṣa) is traditionally held to be powerless, a creator of cattle, possessed of passion, ignorant, other [than the Supreme], not all-knowing, incomplete, and indifferent. || 10 ||
Such a thing characterized by these marks would be a state of non-awakening;
[it would be] devoid of qualities, yet all-knowing, the agent, and independent with respect to its entire range of objects. (11)
Complete, imperishable, peaceful, subtle, vital energy, supreme, and bodiless—this is declared to be the characteristic of the Supreme Goddess as she is being awakened to. 12.
The self is eternally awakened and pure, the cause whose form is beyond the reach of the intellect;
it is infinite, immovable, eternally satisfied, and without support. || 13 ||
The immutably stable one, the Lord of creatures, the Lord of all, he of measured luster, the beginningless, the unique, the unshakable, the conscious, the sustainer of all— Śiva. (14)
O beautiful-eyed one,
the well-known Smṛtis declare that there is indeed a single primordial principle (pradhāna) everywhere, designated as the field (kṣetra), which is insentient.
And among all these, the one Puruṣa is traditionally known as the conscious enjoyer of the field;
because it is insentient, the unmanifest does not act of its own accord.
Since volition as well lacks independence, there is a conjunction of both;
the union of these two principles is a great cause of delusion. (17)
Existing in the form of dissolution and origination, these two are beginningless and unperceived;
both consciousness and unconsciousness are likewise without a lord.
They undergo manifold division through the desire for the differentiation of syllables;
Īśvara, presiding over that [differentiation], governs the two principles of Pradhāna and Puruṣa. (19)
Having uprooted the entities in their successive order of principles,
the Lord, having perceived the name and the object, effects the creation born of Pradhāna.
This [treatise] on the waters is proclaimed for the sake of liberating the bound soul (paśu) from its fetters (pāśa).
Though solitary, the bound soul is powerless when stained by innate fetters. (21)

And because the existence of the principles beginning with the Unmanifest has not been understood, it remains unawakened from this state due to its reliance on the qualities of the Unmanifest. || 22 ||
Having attained that state, he experiences the arising of the fruits of pleasure and pain;
for although the Lord is capable of bestowing grace upon the individual soul (paśu) alone, [he does not do so]. (23)
The Lord indeed does not act impulsely, for he would otherwise destroy what has already been accomplished;
because he lacks any external cause, he does not perceive [the world] within his own self as being distinct from the Puruṣa. (24)
Therefore, Maheśvara brings about the conjunction of its causes;
they say that the unmanifest is the instrument (karaṇa), and the effect has ten characteristics.
Under the influence of another, that [Prakṛti] effects the purpose of the Puruṣa in many ways;
therein, however, the purpose of the Puruṣa is proclaimed to be pure consciousness alone. (26)
The person (puruṣa) is designated by the name "all-encompassing reality" (sakalatattva) and so forth;
for through the knowledge of reality, bondage comes to an absolute end. || 27 ||
And through the destruction of the bonds, he does not enter into saṃsāra again;
for the person who has turned away from saṃsāra, there is no further falling away. || 28 ||
He becomes one who possesses absolute happiness and is born indeed as independent. || 28½ ||
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
Then, the Lord [proceeds] with the complete and concise determination of the three principles (tritatva).
Out of compassion for living beings, this marvelous [teaching] is being fully revealed. || 1 ||
That which was called "the unmanifest" is now said to be the manifest sense-faculty;
while it is self-cognizable, the unmanifest is understood through its object by implication.
The elements consist of that [Prakṛti], and that [Prakṛti] consists of the five elements;
the manifoldness and unity arising from the elements are thus proclaimed. (3)

a) That which begins with the earthly principle (pārthiva) and extends up to Āśiva— this entire collection has been declared to be "prākṛta" (of the nature of primordial matter) many times by those who know the principles (tattva). || 4 ||

The ordinary elements, being undifferentiated, are not described as having the distinction of being divine or non-divine, nor as pure or impure, because their essential nature is not of the form of a self.
The principles (tattvas), even though they are composed of consciousness, attain purity;
yet, when pure, they bind those embodied beings who are ignorant.
But for the ignorant, who are intent upon the effects of existence and perform virtuous deeds,
those auspicious principles bind embodied beings.
Whatever consists of modification is taught as being *tattva*;
this is undoubtedly declared by those who know the true meaning to be *prakṛta*. (8)
Because it is all-pervading, because it is both subtle and manifest, and because its qualities are unproduced,
many maintain that the imperishable Supreme Self is the Void. (9)
Some declare the vital breath (prāṇa), others fire, and likewise other people the moon, as the supreme Brahman; thus they instruct one another.

With reference to a specific purpose, and due to the weight of the inherent nature and qualities of beings, this was spoken for the sake of conventional usage, not from the perspective of ultimate reality. (11)
One, two, three, four, and five qualities were previously conceived by the sages as the successive distinctions of the void and the other [tattvas]. (12)

That which is here described as the one, immeasurable, empty, liberated, and immutable is further proclaimed to be twofold by way of the distinction between the supreme (para) and the non-supreme (apara).
That from which sound proceeds is called the supreme void;
the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra) has arisen therefrom—that is the primordial, supreme state. (14)
The distinction between the two spaces has been made by means of the method of the single reality;
it is the supreme concealed by Māyā, yet devoid of even the highest Māyā.
Neither pure nor impure, devoid of both purity and impurity,
empty of the innate and acquired fetters, it has an unmanifest form.
That which is reckoned as space— unborn and undecaying— is composed of entities both gross and subtler, and possesses the nature of both existence and non-existence.
This form of sound proceeds, having the nature of being like milk;
from sound comes the perfect accomplishment of the body, and its cause is characterized by space.
It proceeds in two ways by way of the nature of knowledge and ignorance. Knowledge creates the body; this is the perception of the Puruṣa and the Unmanifest. (19)
And for men, delusion regarding existence and non-existence is contrary;
though consisting of knowledge, it resorts to a contrary basis for the sake of the [five] categories. (20)
This [element] manifests sound in two ways for living beings as ordained:
because it makes known the void which has sound as its quality to those who are deluded. (21)
It is taught that it brings about the purity and impurity of another;
this world is of the nature of mantra and is remembered as consisting of the sound of mantra. (22)
It is declared that sound is of the nature of emptiness, and emptiness is designated as the unmanifest;
from that, as soon as it arises, [the breath] is impelled by the mantra-wind.
It manifests through the two ears; therefore, it is remembered as "gross" (sthūlaka).
That which has the nature of sound arising from the void and so forth is designated as possessing immeasurable splendor. (24)
This is said to be the Supreme Śiva with attributes (saguṇa) or as impure;
thus, the elements along with their own qualities are mutually unreal.
In due course, they come into being and manifest all phenomena through great grossness and subtle pervasiveness on every side.
Existing as both the pervaded and the pervader, they are one yet manifold;
for this [reality] consists of all the *tattvas* and likewise consists of equanimity.
The body composed of the five elements is declared to be material;
yet that which abides as all-encompassing knowledge is this powerful body.
It is taught that [the body] consists of the elements and is the cause of excellent enjoyments and pleasures.
This aggregate, consisting of the five elements, is designated as the unmanifest (*avyakta*). (29)
Having understood that all things arise from [the mind], one is completely liberated from bondage. || 29 1/2 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter of the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear [the distinction] between those whose intellects are awakened and those whose are unawakened."
Tell me, why was it not previously taught by me in the seven crores of great tantras?
How is one to be known as unawakened, and how does one become awakened? Tell me truly about the process of awakening for one who is seeking knowledge.
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme, pure [reality], and that which is impure, enveloped by the qualities (guṇas).
That reality is proclaimed as pertaining to the Person (puruṣa); it is unborn, yet it falls within the sphere of worldly existence.
Though formless, because it is unawakened, this [Self] plays with enjoyments whose nature is illusion, due to its connection with the Unmanifest, like a child with toys. (4)
The insentient, which consists of the qualities (guṇas), is enveloped by that sentient one who is devoid of qualities;
the manifest is enveloped by the unmanifest, and that [unmanifest] is likewise enveloped by Him.
It does not perish when [the body] perishes, nor is it born by that which is born;
the immutable Self remains with the manifest states produced by human effort, as if they were its own.
On this earth, men of unrefined intellect declare that this person—who is unborn and undecayed—is indeed "born," even though he has already been made so. (7)
(155) One indeed goes to destruction, while another undergoes suffering;
here, yet another remains as the Lord, liberated from suffering and unperceived. || 8 ||
O blameless one, although this bound soul (paśu) is but one, it exists in three forms: the unawakened, the awakened, and likewise the awakening.
When one does not perceive the difference between the self and primordial nature, then this person is called "unawakened" by those who know the truth; such a one is a bound soul (paśu). || 10 ||
The Puruṣa, when not yet distinguished from the unmanifest, is called "becoming conscious" (budhyamāna);
he who is eternally awakened, the Lord of Pradhāna, is remembered as the Supreme Lord of Puruṣas. || 11 ||
Because it is unawakened by the natural qualities (guṇas), it binds itself; from that, passion arises, and through attachment to those qualities, the bound soul (paśu) perceives what is inauspicious.
Stained by passion, one subsequently pursues sense objects;
being addicted to them, one wanders here among beings merely through thought. (13)
As he meditates on sense objects day after day,
emaciation overcomes his strength and proceeds irresistibly.
Then, for one overcome by desire, fierce anger arises;
and for that deluded embodied being, the destruction of his intellect ensues. (15)
Through the destruction of the intellect, the fourfold group beginning with the senses proceeds;
through attachment born of ignorance, the person goes to take refuge in the unmanifest.
Due to taking refuge in the unmanifest, birth and again terrible karma proceed for the embodied soul, even though it is devoid of qualities, through attachment born of delusion. 17.
(157) Straight, born of qualities, and yet possessing a body composed of both the past and the future, the Imperishable One moves upward and downward like a water-wheel.
Who am I, and of what nature am I? Am I the agent, or is it the action?
It is said that one is strong because of sins; who here experiences sufferings for whomsoever? (19)
The Goddess said:
What is the cause of pleasure and pain that they are experienced so suddenly?
To whom do these forms—childhood, youth, old age, and so forth—belong? (20)
Who is it here that is born or dies, or who even exists? Or who, having abandoned the house, departs from the bodies? (21)
O Blessed One, you should explain this task in its entirety. (p.
158) Īśvara:
I shall relate these [matters] concerning a man who has been carried away by illusion.
Through association with ignorance, he deludes himself; even though seeing, he does not see, being accompanied by disease, birth, old age, death, and suffering along with all its trappings. (23)
Even though he knows this, that deluded soul does not experience agitation,
being thus enamored by the qualities born of the unmanifest.
Even another who has forcibly uncovered [the truth] is deprived by the power of illusion;
that entire retinue is born and grows only for the sake of suffering. (25)
And by means of the rope, its gross nature is destroyed;
this is another quality of the Puruṣa who is free from bondage. (26)
Now listen; I shall speak of the arising of the qualities of the one who is awakening.
His innate state of ignorance [is removed] through the impulsion of the Lord's grace. (27)
This state of awakening arises for the embodied soul;
through that engagement, this wise one becomes free from the suffering of the great sleep.
The beast beholds before him the inexhaustible ocean of worldly existence,
completely filled with hot water and agitated by waves in the form of the snares of desire.
It is thick with great delusion, covered with the bubbles of passion,
defiled by desire, hatred, and the like, and agitated by the winds of mental activity.
It is bitter-sweet with the violence of desire, terrifying with the roar of anger,
strewn with the whirlpools of the womb, and thick with the mire of illusion.
(160) It is frequented by the great multitude of disease, birth, old age, and death;
it is characterized by pleasure, pain, and fear at their appointed times, and is bounded by the limits of time. (32)
It was filled with flocks of beasts and swans crying out here and there;
from food, blood, flesh, phlegm, and semen are produced in succession.
Beings arise from the pure [essence]; therefore, the world consists of food.
That food is consumed by embodied beings in the form of morsels, mouthfuls, and gulps. (34)
The *prāṇa* gradually establishes itself in the thick inner receptacle (*antasthūlāśaya*);
then it divides the food and drink that have been consumed into two parts. (35)
Having entered into the midst of the food, [one should place] the food separately and the water separately;
having placed the water above the fire, that food should be placed upon the water.
p.
161) The vital breath (prāṇa), itself abiding above the flame, gently fans the fire;
the fire, being fanned by the wind, makes the water exceedingly hot. || 37 ||
That food is then cooked on all sides by hot water;
once cooked, it becomes twofold: the waste matter separately and the nutrient essence separately.
The ears, eyes, nose, tongue, teeth, penis, anus, and nails, along with phlegm, sweat, feces, and urine, are known as the twelve seats of impurity. (39)
All the channels are connected on all sides to the heart-lotus;
moreover, the vital breath places the subtle essence at their openings.
The vital breath (prāṇa) then fills those channels with that essence; once they are completely filled, it thoroughly nourishes the entire body from all sides. || 41 ||
Then that [substance], situated within the middle of the channels, is cooked by the heat of the body; and while being cooked, it undergoes two further stages of digestion. (42)
From all around the skin, marrow, and bones, the sinews are produced;
likewise, blood, body hair, flesh, head hair, and fat arise. (43)
The channels, fat, pus, marrow, and phlegm—these arise from food, as does the semen which is the essence of procreation. (44)
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā:
"The Lord [states] that because semen, conjoined with the vital fluids (rasa), is the source of the body’s origin."
When, during the period favorable for conception, the flawless semen is situated within the womb. (1)
Then, rubbed by that wind, it attains oneness with the female blood;
at the time of the emission of the semen, the *jīva* becomes conjoined with its cause. (2)

Whichever latent disposition, through its ripening, extends toward the enjoyment of a particular enjoyer, he finds delight therein alone, having been previously colored by that very [disposition]. (3)
Or even if he is capable of discernment, he should not carry out what has been deliberated;
becoming one whose mind is fixed on that and absorbed in it, he enjoys objects of pleasure like one who is hungry.
Having transcended the life-force and the rising and falling of states of existence,
the transmigrating soul enters a womb according to the constraints of its differentiated karma.
That white and red [elements], united together, become the *kalala* in one day;
after five nights, the *kalala* attains the form of a bubble (*budbuda*). (6)
After seven nights, the bubble then becomes a mass of flesh;
after two weeks, from that mass of flesh, blood and flesh then become firm.
Just as sprouts arise from a seed, within twenty-five nights it becomes a *peśī*;
furthermore, after another month, it develops fivefold.
The neck, the head, the shoulders, the spinal column, and likewise the abdomen—
all these indeed arise from Tamas within two months.
In three months, all the limbs and joints are fully formed;
in four months, the fingers and toes are produced in their proper order.
The mouth, the nose, and the two ears are formed in five months;
likewise, the rows of teeth, the tongue, and the nails and so forth are produced. (11)
The lips and cheeks are formed within six months;
the wind, the penis, the generative organ, and the navel likewise come into being.
All the joints are formed within seven months, along with the limbs and minor members fully developed, and the head provided with hair. (13)
Furthermore, with its parts fully differentiated, it remains fully matured for eight months, endowed with the five groups of five [aggregates]. || 14 ||
Through the potency of the mother's food and by means of the sixfold tastes,
bound to the root of the navel, it grows day by day.
Then, when this subtle body is complete, the individual soul (jīva) regains its memory;
it perceives pleasure and pain, as well as sleep and dreams resulting from past actions. (16)
I have died and been born again; I have been born and died again.
While being born, thousands of various wombs have been seen by me. (17)
"Having been born just now and having already received the purificatory rites, I shall perform there that which is beneficial, by which a future conception may not occur. (18)
Remaining in the womb, he thought: "Once I have emerged from the womb, I shall study the knowledge of Śiva, which brings an end to saṃsāra. (19)
Thus, that living being, intensely tormented by the great suffering of the womb,
remains there under the power of karma, not contemplating the means of liberation.
Just as someone trapped within a great mountain remains in suffering,
so too the embodied soul, enveloped by the fetal membrane, remains in pain. (21)
Just as falling into the ocean brings terrible suffering,
so too at the end does a man become distressed, his limbs drenched by the fluids of the womb.
Just as one placed in an iron cauldron is cooked somewhere by fire,
so too, cast into the womb-cauldron, he is cooked by the digestive fire.
Whatever suffering might arise from being pierced incessantly by needles the color of fire—that very thing would be a blessing in the womb. || 24 ||
There is no dwelling anywhere more painful than dwelling in the womb;
it is exceedingly terrible, filled with manifold suffering, and crowded with distress for the sake of the body. (25)
Thus, this suffering of the womb has indeed been fully described for living beings;
for all true creatures, whether moving or stationary, great suffering is recorded as existing within the womb. (26)
The suffering from being crushed by the mechanism of the womb is ten million times greater than that within the womb;
and as the embodied being is being born, intense fainting occurs. (27)
The body is covered by thirty million sheaths, which are pits of sleep and other such states;
it is endowed with gross and subtle forms, both visible and invisible. (28)
Through those same millions of channels, that impure perspiration which exists within flows outwards. (29)
Thus, this house of the body has arisen for the eternal Self, which is itself impermanent;
it is impure, having been constructed by the karmas of that [Self] which is pure.
In the month of gestation there is great suffering from being crushed by the mechanism of the womb;
in childhood there is suffering due to ignorance, and in youth there is suffering from the discipline of the teacher. (31)
Furthermore, in youth there is suffering from the disease of passion and envy; likewise, through activities such as agriculture, trade, service, and cattle-herding. (32)
In old age, one is tormented by decay and diseases;
at death there is great suffering, and even greater than that is the agony of longing. (33)
There is great fear of kings, fire, water, heirs, thieves, and enemies;
and there is suffering in the acquisition and protection of wealth, as well as in its loss and expenditure. (34)
Miserliness, envy, meagerness, fear of grass and disease, great [fear],
and engagement in what ought not to be done— suffering always increases when fuel is added.
In a kingdom, for rulers of the earth, there is the suffering of mutual rivalry and the suffering of mutual subjugation; furthermore, there is the suffering of internal and external upheaval. (36)
The transience of powers, their rise and likewise their fall,
their mutual greatness, and even their devouring of one another— 37.
Through mutual excesses and downfalls, there are the occurrences of the flooding of enjoyments;
they are cut and split by weapons and tormented by diseases. (38)
One who is not dispassionate does not abandon the body through suffering under any circumstances, even if his own limbs are pierced by weapons and his senses are impaired. (39)

One who is enamored by its nature and qualities would not be able to abandon it; for whom, then, could passion—which is itself the delighter and characterized by the bliss of sense objects—not exist? (40)
By that [suffering] to which animals, humans, and gods are joined, they go to their destruction;
neither medicines, nor the taking of wealth, nor mother, nor kinsmen [can protect them]. (41)
The high-souled ones are able to protect a man oppressed by time who has accomplished his penance, recitation, and the perfection of yoga. (42)
Having fallen under the power of timely death, it is digested by men who are weak,
as well as by great-souled ones who have attained perfection in yoga through excellent means such as austerity and recitation.
"Even timely death is digested by the wise, but not by lazy men;
'O father! O father! O beloved!'—thus do they cry out in extreme distress. (44)
Like a frog being devoured by a serpent, a person is tormented by death, even while embraced by kinsmen and surrounded by loved ones. (45)
Sighing long and hot breaths with a parched mouth,
he rolled repeatedly upon his bed, which reached to the four quarters. (46)
Overwhelmed, he is tossed here and there from limb to limb—from his arms to his hands, from his feet to his head;
from the bed to the ground, from the ground back to the bed, and again from the bed to the earth.
Naked, devoid of modesty, smeared with urine and excrement, he begs for water, his throat, lips, and palate parched. (48)
But when reflecting on wealth, one thinks: "To whom will these belong after I have died?
Thus, with his five limbs exhausted and dragged by the noose of Time, he suffers. (49)
While all are watching, he dies; his throat makes a rattling sound, and like a grass cricket, the life-force gradually departs from one body and enters another.
I, who take delight in this impure body, which is subject to momentary decay,
beset by various diseases, and adorned with the serpents of the sense-objects. (51)
They are liberated from intoxications and madnesses that steal away discipline and conduct, and from the torments born of desire and anger, by which they have been repeatedly afflicted. (52)

O Queen, alas, I am deeply distressed in this world that is excessively full of hair [or: excessively dense], agitated by the fear of old age and disease, and completely filled with anxiety and grief. (53)
How can I take delight in this body, which is bound with skin, a foul-smelling mire of fat and blood, and filled with feces, urine, and semen? (54)
Just as a reflection appears in mirrors, or as a form exists in a painting, so too is this body— though devoid of intrinsic reality— yet perceived as something delightful.
In the lineage of Mahāmāyā, which is turbulent with the whirlpools of the three qualities (guṇas),
crowded with crocodiles that are the [false] graspings at reality, and is an ocean whose waves are ignorance; (56)
Beholding this ocean, he became overwhelmed with fear; after sighing deeply for a very long time and lamenting, [he spoke]. (57)
Alas! The ignorance in this world is deeply submerged and devoid of scriptural authority;
its mind is distracted by the sovereignty of sons, home, and other such things.
You alone are my mother and you are my father; you indeed are my wife and my sons;
you are my wealth, you are my friends, you are my kinsmen, and you are truly my home.
This delusion of this world was ordained by someone in the past;
now, children, wife, family, and wealth appear to me like enemies. (60)
But when one performs that action— whether arising from speech, mind, or body— with one's own self,
one experiences its corresponding fruit alone in another birth. (61)
By whatever means, through this or that action, wealth is acquired;
by resorting to these for the sake of enjoyment, people are made miserable.
Those kinsmen who are dear to him do not become his companions at the abode of Dharmarāja; they do not follow those who depart.
Indeed, a single living being alone dies and is born alone;
alone he experiences the fruit of his good deeds, and likewise his evil deeds.
Having understood this, one who is undeluded, seeing that the world has entered the belly of Time (Kāla),
resorts to supreme dispassion and seeks the goal of the self.
By what means shall I easily cross, without delay, this ocean of impurity— a formation of such extremely fierce form? (66)
Generosity, sacrifice, austerity, self-restraint, dispassion, knowledge,
and right conduct are declared to be like a boat for crossing over this ocean of saṃsāra.
Whatever fruit has been acquired through actions such as giving and sacrifice, that too goes entirely to exhaustion through his enjoyment. (68)
(Through its enjoyment as well, that too goes to complete exhaustion.
From sacrifice comes the attainment of the fruit of heaven; from its exhaustion, there follows the [returning] state.
Because of one's karma and because of heaven, there is therefore a return once again.
Endowed with such qualities as these through deeds such as giving and knowledge, this destination has been clearly perceived; yet all of them are subject to decay. (70)
For one who has properly performed austerity, heaven alone is the supreme fruit; however,
wisdom— the imperishable renunciation of action— comes to an end.
Even though it has been renounced, [it is not so] due to lack of realization... || 72 ||
The other is the state of detachment, and likewise, the supreme is the state of knowledge.
A great difference has been declared even by the immortals who know the truth:
one who has resorted to the primary cause (pradhāna) falls again to a lower state;
yet through knowledge, there is no return, and that [knowledge] is what brings about liberation.
From the acts beginning with giving (*dāna*) and ending with detachment (*vairāgya*),
the ritual actions prescribed by the Vedas are led through four stages in succession.
Those desires, characterized by the application of methods such as renunciation, yield their desired fruits. || 77 ||
When acts such as giving,
sacrifice, and vows are offered before the deity,
that indeed is the ritual of renunciation (*sannyāsikī kriyā*). || 79 ||
Having ascended to yoga, whatever action [is performed]—
those four which have been specified consist of the nature of the three guṇas.
179) I shall further proclaim their fruits in due order:
whatever merit has been acquired [is counteracted] by violence... || 81 ||
The remaining mode of existence, consisting of the qualities (guṇas), remains alone and undisturbed. || 82 ||

Then, by the power of their remaining conduct, they all experience the fruits [of their actions] with a body corresponding exactly to that karma— whether in heaven or in hell, wherever and in whatever manner it may be. (84)
Regarding those performed actions whose fruits were not intended— namely, all Vedic ritual acts performed according to injunction— (p. 180) [these are as follows:]
Those who perform renunciation of actions already performed... [86]
Or when the unmanifest has been completely exhausted, it no longer exists through its destruction. || 87 ||
And when [the mind] is not yet exhausted of its qualities, how can these two eyes [be restrained]?
Yoga is indeed twofold: with attributes (saguṇa) and likewise without attributes (nirguṇa), according to the division of gross and subtle by Śiva, the Supreme Self. (89)
Having attained the qualityless yoga by means of that which possesses qualities, those seeking liberation [attain their goal]. || 90 ||
Furthermore, by means of their qualities and supreme tranquility, they indeed attain universal sovereignty;
having enjoyed those objects of experience characterized by supreme tranquility and consisting of pure qualities, they finally [attain liberation] there. (91)
And even though they do not desire it, they return once more to an inferior state;
for those perfected through the yoga of knowledge, suffering remains characterized by its exceeding intensity. (92)
What indeed could be more miserable than falling downward?
Therefore, one should practice that yoga which is preeminent and endowed with the application of knowledge. (93)
The yoga consisting of the qualities (guṇas) and characterized by bondage is not desired for the sake of liberation;
now I shall explain the definitive teaching on the yoga of knowledge (vidyāyoga). || 94 ||
O Goddess of gods, listen even though it is without support; I shall tell you:
that which is called the dust of the wind is known as the triple-atom (trisareṇu). || 95 ||
p.
182) One should know that a half-mora consists of four atoms (aṇu), and two atoms constitute one mora.
One should understand the atom to be the state of the mind, and the two atoms to be the place of speech. || 96 ||
Know that there is a triad of atoms (tryaṇuka) at the tip of the tongue; the wise know the Mātṛkā to have issued forth from it.
Short, long, and protracted—these are declared to be the three measures (mātrā).
Furthermore, the goddess who has transcended the leap (plutātītā) is proclaimed as the fourth part.
A blue jay (cāṣa) utters one mora, while a crow (vāyasa) utters two morae.
The peacock indeed has three measures; this is the conceptualization of measure. That which is proclaimed as the pause (virāma) is situated at the end of the sound of the bell. || 99 ||
Without that [breath], one should draw the imperishable sound (nāda) situated in the heart into the cavity of the throat by means of the very state residing in the heart. 100.
When that unmanifest [state] consisting of half a mora is meditated upon,
it is traditionally said that one should contemplate with the mind as long as it remains in the heart and has not yet been expressed by speech from the navel. (101)
"It is said that half of a half-mora is [the goal]; such is the certainty of the scripture. That which is called the Imperishable (akṣara) is established as half of a half-mora. (102)
The yoga of knowledge (vidyā-yoga) is to be understood as one thing, while the yoga of liberation (mukti-yoga) is otherwise;
this is declared to be the definitive determination of that yoga of the knower. 103.
This knowledge that [the gunas] are the cause of liberation is accepted;
this entire vision of the meaning of Sāṃkhya knowledge has this as its primary focus. (104)
Having understood this, O Goddess of gods, she spoke thus to the Teacher:
"O Blessed One, from this intense cycle of existence, which is crowded with the whirlpools of ignorance... (105)
Save me, who have followed you, O refuge for those who seek shelter!
Through your grace, may I attain all the supreme nectar of wisdom. (106)
I wish to know, in its entirety and exactly as it is, the destruction of worldly existence,
as well as the distinction between the Puruṣa and the Unmanifest, by means of the eye of knowledge.
"Having understood [this], you who enjoy the qualities of absolute liberation (kaivalya), please speak out of your grace.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā. The Lord said:
Henceforth, O Goddess, I shall describe the arising of the qualities of one who is eternally awakened,
and how his mind becomes established in the supreme state.
Having investigated and become skillful, possessing great intelligence regarding the three principles,
he seeks that which transcends the principles, being devoted to service toward the Guru. (2)
One who desires liberation through yoga must again restrain the *liṅga*; O Goddess, without the restraint of the *liṅga*, one does not attain success.
Just as the mind of embodied beings constantly moves toward the objects of the senses,
so too does it move toward that state which transcends the senses and is not of a single form.
The mind, which is not to be known as a protector, grasps forms from every direction;
and when the form is led away, it follows after it.
When existence has been exhausted and the solitary intrinsic nature remains, then, O Goddess, it ceases;
otherwise, it does not cease.
The mind turns away from forms; it cannot be described anywhere.
One should not say anything about that, for who would ask such a thing, O beautiful one? (7)
When that supreme Brahman is to be contemplated as being devoid of all volitional construction (saṅkalpa),
then the wise man should abandon both volitional construction and speech.
Through the relationship between disciple and teacher, having known that [reality], one does not turn back from it;
rather, right there, the intellect, wisdom, memory, and understanding find eternal delight.
He who indeed knows that which is inexpressible, free from doubt, devoid of vowels and consonants, auspicious, peaceful, supreme, and subtle— he is a knower of Śiva.

Those fools who speak of [the distinction between] all things, from the imperishable (akṣara) onwards, as being sequentially perishable (kṣara) rather than imperishable (akṣara), do not reach the further shore of Śaivism.
Free from the fifty syllables, devoid of the perishable and the imperishable,
and having abandoned the bindu and nāda along with the entire collection of mantras without exception. (12)
Where trembling is observed of the teeth, lips, palate, and tongue, how can there be immortality for that which is always subject to decay? (13)
As long as speech is uttered and as long as the eyes function, so long is that [reality] to be known as "with parts" (sakala); otherwise, it is "without parts" (niṣkala).
Whatever can be grasped by the eye, or even that which is heard from hearing—all this, including gods, asuras, and humans, is impermanent. (15)
How can there be liberation in syllables? How can there be a flower in the sky? How can there be oil in sand? How can there be a bow in a rabbit’s horn? (16)
"Thus, O Goddess, the characteristic of the awakened one has been fully explained. (16½)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
Śiva is to be known as fivefold: as Sakala (with parts), Niṣkala (without parts), Sakalaniṣkala (both with and without parts), Sūkṣma (subtle), and Bhinnakala (of distinct parts). || 1 ||
What is the nature of the deity there as both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala)? Please explain the third division, namely how it is both with and without parts (sakalaniṣkala).
Tell me the distinctions between the subtle and the divided; [O] Īśvara, [please explain]. (p.
I shall explain this to you: Śiva, who consists of five divisions.
By the mere knowledge of whom one shall not undergo rebirth again—that supreme God, the Great Lord Maheśvara, who pervades the sky and consists of the five mantras. || 4 ||
Pierced by the thirty-eight kalās, possessing the form of the light of the letter 'A',
he who is called the Sakala is indeed the Lord himself, the husband of Umā.
For the person, while always abiding in all material nature and in the Impeller,
would pervade the entire world and would pervade all embodied beings.
And because he is established everywhere, he is remembered as "Sakala" (the Whole);
he is the non-conceptual, equal state wherein one is joined with the mantra. || 7 ||
By all the syllables and words of the mantra, He is designated as "Sakala" (the Manifested),
for He resides within the gross and subtle elements of all embodied beings. (8)
Because he pervades both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, he is remembered as Sakala;
O gods, because of his all-pervasiveness, he is proclaimed as the Kalātattva.
Because he is the abode of all arts (kalās), he is therefore remembered as Sakala;
Sakala performs creation and bestows the perfection of mantra. || 10 ||
He destroys all obstacles and brings about liberation at the end;
for he is immeasurable, indescribable, incomparable, and devoid of form.
It is said that there, the subtle and partless [sound] is devoted to all reality;
yet for all embodied beings, it is limited by the reality of the body as a resonance (nināda).
That which has transcended the power of sound (nāda) is called the partless (niṣkala);
it is liberated from the manifest (sakala) and devoid of both the point (bindu) and sound (nāda). || 13 ||
The reality situated in the void is partless, devoid of both the expressible and the inexpressible;
it is liberated from both knowledge and ignorance—the partless, supreme state.
In the sky, which resembles crystal and destroys old age and death, effect a dissolution into the partless [Brahman] with the mind for the sake of attaining liberation. 15.
Consisting of both *bindu* and *nāda*, it is the object of the senses of sight and hearing;
here, the visible [aspect] is to be known as half-pure, being both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*). (16)
One should know that form to be both with parts and without parts;
it is the subtle element of sound, the syllable Oṃ, which is heard but not spoken.
And that which is to be known as both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*) is not seen by means of form;
however, when one has joined the *sakala*, then the *niṣkala* is joined. (18)
Then the wise should know Śiva as both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala);
he who resides within the body is to be known as with parts, while he who is devoid of a body is without parts. || 19 ||
He is to be reached through the yoga of action and other means; He is to be known as both with parts and without parts. He is the fourth, consisting of space, beyond sound, and beyond the senses.
The stainless form called Sadāśiva is here described as subtle;
because it is subtler than even an atom, it should be meditated upon as free from all affliction.
Extremely profound, beyond the subtle vital breath, and devoid of defining characteristics,
it is subtler than even the smallest atom and is situated in the center of the heart.
He causes the entire world to breathe forth; he is indeed proclaimed as the subtle one.
He always perceives that which resides in the void through the foremost syllables and words of mantra. (23)
For the purpose of illuminating the yoga of knowledge, that which is to be known is subtle vision;
this arises from the destruction of evil, from yoga, and likewise from the cultivation of meditation.
He beholds Śiva, who is subtle, merged in the center of the light of the heart, abiding within all, established in samādhi, and accessible to the internal organ. 25.
It is not seen by the eyes; it is meditated upon by yogis.
It possesses the forms of earth, water, fire, air, ether, the kingdom (of the self), the moon, and the sun.
That Śiva is the self of all dharmas, yet he may be differentiated into parts;
his form consists of the phonemes from *a* to *kṣa*, which are the essence of the mantra-parts (*mantrakalā*).
That which exists in manifold ways is called "differentiated" (sakala),
because the intellect is established through the syllables and words of mantra and through the meanings of those words. (28)
Śiva, whose aspects are differentiated by words denoting distinct meanings, is thus to be known as tenfold; furthermore, he is to be known as fivefold. (29)
Sevenfold, then four, eight, and again four;
Śiva with his limbs (Sāṅga), then the Gāyatrī, and five others beginning with Sadyojāta. (30)

Having understood that the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) and the World-Guardians (Lokapālas) are non-different from that one, all-encompassing Śiva, yet exist in this state of differentiation, one should, being well-concentrated, effect their union.
He shatters the mass of fetters; for that reason, he is remembered as Bhinnakala.
This supreme Śiva, consisting of five states, has been described to you, O Goddess. (32)
"Knowing this, one is released from the bonds and goes to the imperishable Śiva.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter of the *Niśvāsakārikā*. (p. 195)
The Goddess said:
O Śiva, it is precisely because of qualities such as omniscience that you are praised everywhere.
Therefore, O Blessed One, I desire to hear of them; you ought to speak of them.

O Goddess, sovereign of all knowledge, he is called "all-knowing" because he [knows] the individual soul (paśu), the fetters (pāśa), as well as the principles (tattva), and likewise their emergence and dissolution. || 2 ||
He is said to be one who is perfectly endowed with all sovereignty, who is the support of all yet himself has no support, who is omnipresent and complete, and who is utterly satisfied.

Because it is beginningless, its own nature is the self of all and has a firm range of perception; since it awakens [beings] by its own power, it is therefore proclaimed as "Awakening" (bodha). || 4 ||
He could create the entire world, the three realms with all that is moving and unmoving; because he is the Lord of Gods and is independent, he is called "Svatantra" (the Independent One).
Because he is eternal, free from old age, and all-knowing, and because he is unimpeded by yogic powers, Śaṅkara is therefore called Alupta (the Undecaying).
Someone perceives that supreme [reality] which is without beginning, middle, or end;
and because its power is unimpeded, it is therefore called infinite.
These limbs of Maheśa should be understood with diligent effort;
one is liberated from all sins and attains the state of Śiva, which is free from affliction.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"O Maheśvara, regarding that which was stated by you, namely, 'devoid of the six vowels'—"
Tell me that, O Lord of Gods, regarding when one becomes deficient in caste. || 1 ||
O Goddess, listen; I shall declare to you that supreme secret which you have asked about, which is difficult even for the gods to attain. (2)
O Goddess of the gods, this should be understood with diligence in five ways:
the distinction of the phonemes (varṇa) must be known, as well as the distinction of the principles (tattva) according to their true nature.
Furthermore, the divisions of his vital breaths (vāyu) belonging to that God of gods have been proclaimed;
likewise, the divisions of the states of the deities—these are, in brief, the five divisions. || 4 ||
O Goddess, when the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, is devoid of these distinctions, then Śiva is said to be free from the six phonemes.
The Goddess said: O Lord Śaṅkara, how is there a division of colors (castes) and a division of principles?
Furthermore, [explain] the division of the winds and the division of the deities and colors associated with them.
O Lord, when one is devoid of these, what is the nature of that true being?
Tell me this, O Lord of Gods, for I have a great doubt in this matter.
O fair-faced one, listen with a one-pointed mind, having become absorbed in that and identified with it, as I shall tell you these things exactly as they are.
(199) O fair-faced one, listen as I explain the distinction between the classes;
I shall tell you how they are concealed by the classes and how they are lost. 9.
When the letter *a* is elided, the syllable *oṃ* is deprived of Śiva;
therefore, O Goddess, it is joined with the fifth [vowel] which has been elided.
When the sixth is deficient by the fifth, it is proclaimed as such;
when the sixth is deficient, O Goddess, the letter *ma* is seen there.
O Goddess, when he is devoid of that, how could he be like the moon? For when he is bereft of him, Śiva is deprived of his six colors.
But that which is devoid of phonemes is the partless (niṣkala) aspect of the entire reality;
it is not [attained] by elision, O lady of beautiful hips, wherein the form of the curved plowshare (the letter *ha*) exists.
O Goddess, when [the reality] is deficient, I shall explain that very thing to you;
the seven principles and so forth have been fully described by me in this body. (14)
The Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) should be fashioned as devoid of the six principles;
for the five principles are situated above, and he himself is established beyond them.
O Goddess, when one is deprived of those and becomes devoid of the six syllables, listen now to this description of the further classification of the winds for him. || 16 ||
Listen now to the order in which they are situated:
Udāna is established in the upward direction, while Apāna is positioned below. || 17 ||
There, the prāṇa is situated in the middle; vyāna is in the sphere of connection;
samāna is there, pervading everywhere; and among them, O Dhanañjaya, [the udāna] is the winner of wealth.
(21) O Goddess, when the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, is devoid of all these [attributes], then Śiva is said to be free from the six syllables. || 19 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Śiva themselves—
when [the reality] is devoid of Śakti and Nāda, it is devoid of them and is thus partless (niṣkala).
White, red, yellow, black, resembling crystal, and beautiful—
when it is devoid of these colors, it becomes one that lacks the six colors.
When it is devoid of these phonemes and only a single *bindu* remains established,
then [one reaches] the end, which is supremely peaceful and devoid of the form of phonemes.
Therein neither vowel nor consonant exists, nor form, nor indeed meditative cultivation;
the mind is not found there, and thought is not found there. (23)
(202) Nothing exists there, nor is any worshipper perceived therein.
The Goddess said:
Today, O Lord, I know that my life is well-lived. || 24 ||
O Śaṅkara, tell me that which slightly agitates the mind—that which is devoid of consonants and vowels, and free from the form of letters. (25)
"O Lord, how is it known that what has been declared by you, O Master,
is the tradition (sampradāya) originating from the Supreme Guru, O Goddess? || 26 ||
And I shall not speak of that which is not the nectar from the mouth of the Guru;
for the Guru, who knows the true state of beings, speaks according to and by means of whatever disposition [the disciple possesses]. (27)
But that is not so, for there is nothing else; this must indeed be believed, O beautiful one.
And just as existence arises from non-existence, O beautiful one, so does existence manifest. (28)
"In this manner I shall speak to you so that you will attain cessation.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
The Goddess said:
"This knowledge has many facets; no certain conclusion can be reached.
Therefore, let that one word be reflected upon by which I may attain the highest good."
The Lord, however, teaches that knowledge is manifoldly divided as it is presented in the world.
The object of knowledge is that which is distinct from it; in cognition, the object of knowledge is established as something other [than the cognition itself]. || 2 ||
Śiva is both absolute and pure, as well as impure along with the imperishable syllables (akṣaras).
His naturally pure form arises effortlessly indeed. (3)
For the attainment of milk is not desired by the mere word "cow"; rather, there are distinctions such as honey, milk, water, nectar, and so forth. (4)
Even when spoken, no fruit arises from the mere contact of the lips;
however, those who know the Dharma declare that the Lord should be praised for the sake of liberation— this is what must be understood.

From consciousness, however, comes the attainment of qualities, just as the elements [attain their properties] from contact; just as the impurities of metals are removed by mercury alone when it has the power to penetrate through touch. (6)
p.
205) Through contact with fire, the state of being gold is established;
knowledge is declared to be like touch, while the object of knowledge is held to be like fire. || 7 ||
O Supreme Lord, the temporal bond of the bound souls (paśus) is lost;
through the penetration of the qualities of its own cause, it attains identity with that [cause]. (8)
Thus, all yogins attain an equality of consciousness;
for each of them, that sovereignty is the cause of their equal nature.
Everywhere they attain, in the ultimate sense, that which is beyond consciousness;
for through consciousness, the threefold bondage is shattered.

When the bonds of a living being have fallen away, it attains the state of the power of will (icchā-śakti). Through the pervasive quality of the power of will, the living being shall no longer be a partaker of suffering.
(206) He attains the state of being the cause of all things; of this there is no doubt.
The Goddess said:
How could there be a path for Śiva, who is perfectly complete? || 12 ||
But tell me truly, what is the nature of the path of Śiva?
Just as in the case of space, there is nowhere an upper, a middle, or even a lower part; [so it is with that path]. (13)
Thus, the all-pervading God does not exist within the paths of time;
having transcended the state of being a bound soul (paśu), He abides as the Lord (pati). || 14 ||
For that which is all-pervading, what movement can there be? It is only figuratively said that it "goes" when it attains loftiness and the state of Śiva.
Awakening is called "going"; how can there be going for that which is all-pervading?
The Goddess said:
O Śaṅkara, that god is said by me to be all-pervading.
How can this contradiction within one's own position be rendered beyond doubt, if [the deity] is present everywhere—in leaves, flowers, fruits, and water? (17)

How can worship be performed when it involves the cutting of one's own limbs, which is suffering, and [involves harm] everywhere toward both stationary and moving beings, as well as seeds and the like? (18)
How can the burning of one's own limb, which is suffering, be appropriate for burnt offerings (homa), if such [suffering] is not found in the case of leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth? (19)
In that case, it would lack pervasiveness; how then could it be all-pervading?
For those who recognize form, color, and so forth, there is no manifestation within the unmanifest. (20)
If one accepts what is spoken [as a gift] or food given out of a desire for enjoyment, the body indeed becomes manifest in form; it is clearly of a conditioned nature. || 21 ||
Whatever forms take on a physical body perish in due time;
the God is all-pervading, yet the worship of the physical form is praised. (22)
O God, the ritual for the worship of a *liṅga* does not please me;
when there is an obstruction, the sky is indeed indifferent and faces in all directions. (23)
That which was previously described as the unborn and imperishable space (ākāśa) cannot be obstructed by stone pillars, water, walls, or mountains.
In that same way, [they conceive] Īśvara as unmanifest, not independent, insentient, dependent on another, a non-agent, ignorant, and subject to the nature of procreation. (25)
That which is pervaded, non-pervasive, subject to agitation, graspable, and possessed of qualities is said to be characterized by transformation,
excellence, and manifestation, yet possessing the nature of the unmanifest. (26)
Its lack of omniscience is declared to be its very source;
this is taught to be the nature of the Void, namely its state of being without a Lord. (27)
But the Lord, having understood this, said: "O Goddess, you shall not fall into delusion again;
for one who pervades the supreme reality cannot be obstructed. (28)
Just as a reflected form enters into the midst of a mirror of water,
neither emerging nor being divided, so too does the Lord shine forth.
Pervasive and non-contradictory, it is not obstructed by anything; indeed,
that which stands both within and without is not dependent on anything whatsoever.
There is for me no inference, nor comparison, nor anything else that exists for me.
Inherently stainless and pure, with the ointment of impurity never having arisen, it is impossible to describe even a portion of its characteristics or qualities. (31)
Just as the moon situated in the sky is seen in water, so too the omnipresent God is not perceived because of His subtlety. || 32 ||
And that [Self] may be seen through yoga as if directly perceived, like the moon in water;
yet the moon waxes and wanes, being unstable, uneven, and flickering. || 33 ||
The moon, once arisen, undergoes transformation;
yet he who is free from illusion and devoid of change abides both externally and internally.
The one who has attained union, having transferred his reflection, remains in the ether and not in that water;
yet the Supreme Lord is seen even within one's own impure body. (35)
O Goddess of gods, through instruction the [Supreme] becomes manifest like the moon in water;
just as the Supreme Lord exists within the body yet is not seen, so too is He present in leaves, fruits, and the like. (36)
For by its very nature, the moon is seen there in the sky;
yet, O Mistress of the Gods, through instruction it becomes manifest as being present everywhere. (37)
Just as leaves, flowers, fruits, and the like are not seen because they are impure,
so too, O Goddess, you are utterly deluded, remaining fixed upon that which is ungraspable.
Just as the circles of rays are seen in a gem, in water, or in a mirror,
so too is the Supreme Lord seen within leaves and flowers. (39)

Because of its subtlety, it resides everywhere within leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth, as well as within seeds and the like; having seen it thus situated there, one should not entertain conceptual constructions regarding it.
Although [the effect] exists everywhere within leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth, as well as within seeds and the like, it is not perceived because of its subtlety. || 41 ||
When seeds are being burned, they are not consumed because of their subtlety;
likewise, the fire-element is seen within gems and glass in the sky. || 42 ||
Indeed, no Veda is seen here regarding the ripening of water, weapons, and so forth, nor concerning these leaves, fruits, and the like, or their production from seeds and such. (43)
Because of the extreme subtlety of the God of gods, neither cutting nor burning is perceived.
213) His hands and feet are everywhere; his eyes, heads, and faces are on all sides. 44.
Since reality is all-pervasive by its very nature and is omnipresent, it should not be conceptualized; it shines forth through non-investigation. 45.
But when direct perception is being experienced, a logical reason is not the cause therein;
it is that which appears as everything yet is without appearance, formless yet possessing all forms.
And since it does not abide in any single location, how could there be an invocation of it?
It is taught that [the Self] pervades its own body during the withdrawal of the phonemes. (47)
Moreover, by the sound of the Yoga-pīṭha as it existed previously, since restraint was recited within one’s own body, from where could its [present] memory have arisen? (48)
Since the term "presence" (*sānnidhya*) is recited within one's own body,
there is neither cause for [its] presence nor any contradiction. (49)
In this way, these forms and others of Śiva are proclaimed in the inferior teaching as being caused by the collection of ritual procedures. (50)
O Goddess of gods, the invocation and the dismissal are of the nature of ritual action;
this is not a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda), but is proclaimed as an injunction (vidhi).
Having resorted to the doctrine of ritual injunction (vidhivāda), the gods, led by Brahmā, attained incomparable sovereignty, gain, and eternal immortality. (52)
O Great-Souled One, the scripture named Śaiva bestows the state of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
for it neither possesses defects nor requires purification, as it grants the accomplishment of both goals.
The Goddess said:
"O Śiva, the fault is as it would be for a man on a street."
The function would be localized; it could not be all-pervading for the omnipresent Lord. || 54 ||
The Lord Śiva,
the supreme cause, is both characterized by the manifest and the unmanifest;
He is endowed with specific characteristics in the form of an image, and likewise in the yoga of recitation.
The mind, the intellect, and the ego—designated as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—are said to be its very locus; thus, the mind, intellect, and so forth are merely imagined constructs.
This is remembered as being situated in the Supreme, devoid of the intellect of volition, free from egoism, and liberated from the injunctions of praise and the like.
"But he, O Goddess, is omnipresent and described as both with and without marks.
The Goddess said:
If the God is omnipresent, abiding in all states of existence; || 58 ||
Therefore, O Maheśvara, one should not entertain conceptual constructions regarding location;
Śaiva knowledge has been proclaimed for the sake of accomplishing both goals. (59)
The Great Lord is all-pervading; what fault could there be in liberation?
The Blessed Lord is the sovereign within all moving beings, yet he is not worshipped within physical bodies alone.
The Lord Śiva should be worshipped either in a *liṅga* or elsewhere in an auspicious place;
this involves invocation, meditation, and the restraint of the mind's enjoyments. (61)
One should contemplate union with Śiva through the mind and the intellect;
one should worship the manifest (sakala) God and recite the mantra of the manifest-and-unmanifest (sakalaniṣkala). (62)
One should meditate upon that which consists of light, subtle, and distinct from the kalās;
one should satisfy [the deity] in the sky, shining with the purity of crystal, the destroyer of old age and death.
For the sake of attaining liberation through the mind, perform absorption into the partless [reality];
the practitioner becomes pure through ritual bathing, and through recitation, success is attained—of this there is no doubt. (64)

Through worship alone, [the deity] grants the fruit when present; through fire-offerings (homa), he grants the fruit; and by meditating on the omnipresent God, one attains the state of a master of yoga.
Through the vow (vrata), there shall be purification of the body; in initiation (dīkṣā), liberation is desired.
[The rites of] invocation (āvāhana), installation (sthāpana), presence (sānnidhya), and confinement (sannirodhana) [are performed]. 66.
The names of actions established in the ritual procedure have indeed been declared;
yet no one at all is obtained [as an agent], nor is anyone at all caused to enter [into action]. (67)
O Goddess of gods, it does not cease, nor is its presence brought about;
being all-pervasive by virtue of the nature of mantra, they contemplate Supreme Śiva. (68)
"Then it is said, 'The vehicle,' and 'Forgive me' is the dismissal.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
The Goddess said:
For the mind is constantly wavering; it moves with force like a flowing current.
O Lord of Gods, even one established in meditative absorption—how does he remain motionless? (1)
Īśvara (p.
219) [taught] the yoga of the renunciation of action, as well as the great yoga of the intellect.
Yoga is said to be fivefold, characterized by the possibility of return. || 2 ||
O lady of excellent complexion, for those beings who are subject to rebirth,
their minds are always constantly agitated and ever-attached to karma.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear about the yoga of action (karmayoga), renunciation (saṃnyāsa), and likewise the great yoga of the intellect (matiyoga); it behoves you to speak of these."
The Lord [perceives] that which consists of egoism, designated by the terms "yoga" and "action";
when that very thing has been thus completed and cast aside, it is called renunciation (sannyāsa). || 5 ||
Together with them, there is dispassion, union, and the conquest of primordial nature (prakṛti). Having transcended the eightfold nature, they abide as lords of the Puruṣas. (6)
Four yogas have been taught so that the Great Yoga may come to be;
they exist one above the other, serving to increase the yoga of the practitioner.
In that very same way, they dissolve into their own karmas, which are the attributes of yoga;
yet, having fully realized the reality of dualistic existence, they undergo creation once again.
The qualities such as *aṇimā* consist of the perception of forms and so forth;
for those who achieve perfection in yoga through suppression [of the senses], liberation does not exist.
Having attained the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and become great lords with mastery over their limbs,
they do not attain union (sāyujya) so long as there is no oneness.
But those who are intent on the syllable *oṃ* and remain fixed in exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*),
their supreme state does not exist, because they destroy the self and the senses. (11)
The syllable Om is the wind below the channel, while Udāna is established above;
for yogis who have doubts regarding this, there is a return after they have departed. (12)
O Goddess, when the cage of knots has been ceased through the union of going and coming, the Vidyā, whose essence is Yoga, is attained by one who realizes the state of Vidyā. 13.
In one who possesses knowledge, [the realization] arises depending on the interval between existences and the yugas;
however, because they are necessarily subject to penetration (āveśa), those [others] are cited as being pervaded (vyāpya).
Whatever things exist due to the absence of causes are not liberated, nor are they of that nature; there is no yogi who is practicing yoga, nor is there any closing of the eyes.
(222) Furthermore, gazing at the tip of the nose is not praised as Yoga.
The Goddess said:
In that which has a support, there is impermanence; even in that which is without support, there is emptiness.
There is a fault in both positions; what then do the yogins meditate upon? [They say:
"The Lord is like a child—knowing nothing and even foolish—and yet he was not laid down to sleep. (17)
Persons who do not know the supreme reality are like children;
when that [reality] is unknown, it is called "knowledge," but once it is known, it is considered the "object of knowledge" (jñeya). || 18 ||
And consciousness arises from the object of knowledge; consciousness has that very [object] as its nature.
(Devī, p. 223)
Just as the mind will remain motionless through union with that which is to be known. || 19 ||
Tell me this with certainty, for I have a great doubt regarding it;
I shall explain the Lord as the Mind, endowed with its fourfold divisions. (20)
That which has not been told to anyone else, I shall tell you today—
specifically regarding the *sāttvika*, the *rājasa*, and the *tāmasa* [natures].
I shall explain in brief, according to the sequence of the divisions of yoga,
that which is the fourth, the great yoga, incomparable and free from affliction.
I shall proclaim those movements of the mind that are stirred within the mind, by the mere knowledge of which one attains the state beyond the mind (unmanatva). || 23 ||
The instructed mind, the withdrawn mind, the distracted mind, and the moving-and-coming mind—these are said to be the fourfold types of mind; hear now this classification of it. (24)
There is no mind, nor anything to be thought, nor is a thinker perceived;
absorbed within himself and liberated from sense-objects, he has become one, like one in deep sleep.
Even while grasping sense objects, he attains the state of being the knower; yet he is not joined with them, for when he is known [in this way], he is called "disciplined" (saṃśiṣṭa). || 26 ||
From ignorance one goes to knowledge, and from knowledge one indeed goes to ignorance;
for him who wavers due to weakness, there is this coming and going.
Because one who is devoted to the objects of the senses is constantly deprived of knowledge throughout the three periods of time, he is said to be distracted. (28)
Among those, the *svalīna* is the highest; he has transcended the qualities (*guṇa*) and is free from affliction.
The *saṃśiṣṭa*, however, is to be known as the middling; he is remembered as being characterized by purity (*sāttvika*). (29)
The lowest, characterized by meager results and belonging to the *rājasa* nature, is subject to coming and going;
that which is *tāmasa* is distracted, and this fourth type is considered the most base.

It is taught that for embodied beings, the mind is generally composed of the qualities (guṇas), yet it will eventually become absorbed in that which is preeminently devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). || 31 ||
Having attained a state of oneness within tranquility, it is perceived by its own time alone; and because it is superior to deep sleep, there is no further qualification required here. (32)
It is not possible to describe that, nor can it be retained;
there is no other indicator for it, as long as it is not [realized] by itself through its own nature.
That happiness which is experienced by the self when both the mind and the vital breath are well-absorbed—
this, indeed, those who know yoga declare to be the supreme state of yoga. (34)
When the mind, having attained its mark, becomes absorbed in the supreme reality, then all cognition without exception comes to an end. || 35 ||
For one whose being is all-pervading, he abides both externally and internally;
even if his mind should move, having moved, where could it go? (36)
Knowledge is the awakening to the meaning of reality and the illumination of meditation on the self;
the object of knowledge is the equality of all things, and through meditation, the mind becomes free from objective referents.
Supportless, free from conceptual construction, devoid of all substrates, without qualities, and beyond any defining characteristic—this is proclaimed as Śivayoga. || 38 ||
He whose mind is situated within the inner chamber [of the heart] and is well-composed is considered [liberated];
for just as the wind, however swift it may be, does not go anywhere once it has left the sky. (39)
It should be known that even one with a distracted mind remains motionless when standing in poison;
yet he experiences all sense objects, for he is neither a consumer nor a smearer of them. (40)
He whose being is all-pervading, established in the state of the knowable, and uninterrupted, does not move when the body moves; he is immovable.
For that wise one who has conquered the source [of rebirth] and, having made his mind steady by practicing it, perceives all this as the object of knowledge—what will he do after going there? (42)
Just as a calf turns away from its mother's udder when the milk is exhausted, so too does the mind of men quickly turn away when passion is exhausted. || 43 ||
The fluctuation of the mind is required for the sake of the moving and unmoving body;
yet that renouncer will not be well-restrained in regard to the body. (44)
Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, dispassion, and knowledge—by means of these thirteen types, the instrument was rendered motionless. (45)
That which is other than the nature [of things] is unstable; or by what could that which is stable be moved?
It would never become motionless, whether it be unjoined or joined. (46)
The Goddess said:
"The five vital breaths beginning with prāṇa, the mind, the five deities, the subtle elements, as well as the intellect and the ego—this is the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka). || 47 ||
But being agitated by these and joined with the mind, O Goddess, the vital winds always move, deluded by pleasure and pain. (48)
The mind wavers because of delusion consisting of pleasure and pain;
he for whom pleasure and pain are equal, his mind is perfectly steady. (49)
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, closing the eyes and gazing at the tip of the nose—this is not truly yoga as it has been described by you. (50)
"O Mahādeva, tell me how yoga— which consists of both the supported (sāvalamba) and the unsupported (nirālamba)— is to be understood."
The Lord is neither the instrument of yoga here, nor is He the support or the object of focus.
The gaze is fixed on the tip of the nose, not closing the eyes, while the mind is directed toward the heart. || 52 ||
Having perceived even a slight manifestation of that supreme body,
the breath, as if completely filled, moves through a subtle aperture.
Just as it is not known where [the wind] has gone, so too is the yoga of the object of knowledge.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, the body filled with air appears like a leather bag. (54)
But what is to be done with that which is artificial?
O Lord, one must understand in every way the path of that which is artificial, for it is essentially external and fabricated. (55)
The knowable has no product, nor does it have temporal paths or conceptual construction.
O Lord, tell me that which is the truth regarding this doubt of mine. (56)
p.
231) Of that glorious, qualityless reality which is the Unnameable (anākhyam), Īśvara is [the presiding deity].
Having performed the grasping of the qualities, one should speak of the Supreme Lord.
One may describe Śiva as merely a slight appearance,
as well as the path of the ritual procedure, the paths of the stages, and the utterances and instruments.
