But it must be made to stand still, O lady of beautiful hips, by abandoning [all objects] without exception;
in this way, that mind—difficult to conquer and fickle—remains subdued. 59.
It would never move, and it would always remain in the state of being an object of knowledge;
like an undefeated wrestler, it would cause many others to bow down in pride.
The steadfast one remains as one who has conquered; so too is the mind of those who know what is to be known.
Indeed, there would be no goer, nor does any place to go exist. (61)
Free from coming and going, it remains like the space within a jar; for the space enclosed within a jar is merely carried here and there [when the jar is moved].
Just as a pot passes through but not the space within it, so indeed is Śiva like the sky;
the body, which stands enveloped by the layers of the elements, is like the core of a plantain tree.

Therefore, for one whose mind has reached the state of meditative cultivation regarding the realization of the formless Self, that [intellectual understanding] then becomes like an expenditure, as it abandons even the partial adherence to reality. (64)
He who has no longing even for the slightest liberation attains that liberation which is renowned as being embodied yet formless. 65.
Liberation is inconceivable and devoid of qualities; liberation is not accompanied by dissolution.
Therefore, there can be no path to liberation at any time. (66)
The absence of views everywhere—that is liberation for those who proclaim liberation;
it belongs to those by whom dispassion has repeatedly pervaded the self. (67)
Not even one among them can go there without justification;
likewise, others who are somehow devoid of passion are also extinguished.
In that same way, they too shall go to Nirvana first, just as water resting upon a rock is dried up by the rays of the sun. (69)
Thus, when the self is extinguished, it goes to a state beyond rebirth;
it does not enter the water, nor does it remain in the earth, nor does it stay in that very place.
And yet it was not drunk by anyone; thus it departed without a basis.
In this way, that detachment from the nature of the graspable which was spoken by the Guru for one's benefit [is established]. (71)
This state has traversed the path; it is that one eternal reality.
What hope indeed can there be for those who preach liberation, wherein all things have gone to destruction? (72)
Even this absolute detachment brings happiness to the mind;
yet, for the most part, no one will find contentment therein. (73)
He who is liberated is free from conceptual construction, while he who possesses conceptual construction is bound.
Just as the name and form of rivers cease upon reaching the ocean, [so do they cease for the liberated]. (74)
There they do not perceive any mutual distinction, nor does any other specific quality of the water arise there. (75)
In that regard, the rivers have reached their end, yet the single great ocean remains.
Likewise, the embodied being is like a river, and nirvāṇa is like the ocean. (76)
Free from possessiveness, those rivers resting upon the ocean remain;
indeed, they abide in immobility, for contentment arises within them.
He does not experience pleasure or pain; he grasps the auspicious qualities by relying on existence within non-existence, having rendered existence supportless. (78)
Having made the mind abide in the Self, one should not think of anything at all;
relying on the state of non-existence, even when absorbed in existence, one remains free from doubt.
He is to be understood as all-pervading; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
How could there be existence for that partless Great Soul, who is himself non-existence? (80)
For him for whom all states of being dissolve in the waking state as if in deep sleep, there is no instability of the mind; that is his state of Nirvana. (81)
His consciousness is sufficient; those three steps have not been transgressed by you.
The first should be known as imperishable, and the well-considered one is indeed without syllables.
Then, through the practice of *kuṃbhaka*, one should know Śiva, who is beyond both the perishable and the imperishable;
having abandoned everything within the range of the internal organ, one remains established in *samādhi*.
Then, that which is eternally perceived by yogis and worshipped by them is seen according to the tradition as it exists, as pointed out by the instruction of the Guru. 84.
He is both external and internal, subtle, beginningless, auspicious, and immutable.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, [tell me of] the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna) and likewise the path of the gods (devayāna). || 85 ||
O Lord, I wish to hear the definitive conclusion regarding the distinction between the two paths.
Those devoted to sacrificial rites and charitable works travel by the path of the ancestors to the celestial realm.
There they experience the fruits of whatever good deeds were performed here;
when those deeds are exhausted, they return and are born again upon the earth. (87)
When his store of merit is exhausted, he returns from that path just as a leaf falls and turns back;
the entire lunar path is his destination, and Mṛḍa is his charioteer.
This is to be known as the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna), the way of those who perform sacrifices;
it is like the moon, which wanes and waxes, unstable, uneven, and flickering. (89)
The destination of one who has set out upon the path of the ancestors is also like this:
on the path of the gods, the Sun is his chariot, and Suṣumnā is his charioteer. (90)
Having pierced that, the yogi proceeds by the southern path, never to return,
toward those virtuous ones who have become the self of all beings and who perceive reality.
For those yogis who have desisted from all desires and practice that path through repeated cultivation,
those yogis do not return again by way of the path of the gods.
Therefore, having abandoned everything, proceed by the southern path;
thus, O Goddess, they know the way of the ancestors (pitṛyāna) in brief.
There is no path leading to the gods; hear the reason why:
whatever path one travels by is merely something conceptually constructed.
In this regard, what kind of path is there for the unspeakable Creator?
239) Just as neither the path nor the yoga exists within any tantra. || 95 ||
This has been taught in the scriptures solely for the purpose of instructing disciples;
this statement regarding its measurement is exactly as it is in the case of the Devayāna path.
What kind of path leads to the realization of all-pervasiveness?
Where one goes, that [destination] does not exist, nor is there any path there at all.
Therein exists no movement of yoga; that state is beyond all characteristics.
Once attained, the movement does not return, even though it is far removed from the reach of ordinary yoga.
On the path of the gods there is no [return]; therefore, he does not return.
But as for any man who has gone by the path of the ancestors, [he returns]. || 99 ||
Even if he has traveled a very great distance, he turns back from there;
having gone by the path of the gods, he is liberated from all sins. (100)
And thus one should enjoy sovereignty, freed from the snares of hope;
likewise, the instruments, the designations, and the ego-sense as well. (101)
Since everything ceases [therein], how can anything be differentiated there?
Sovereignty, as described in the scriptures, is incomparable and belongs to one of little merit.
In the state of non-appearance, such sovereignty will never exist;
for even a lord is praised as one who is without hope when he has become free from desire.
By him who has renounced the entire world, the self alone is indeed to be enjoyed;
for the sake of the self, he engages in all activities, becoming the very embodiment of hope. (104)
For one who has renounced even their own self, for what reason would they have hope?
One is bound in saṃsāra only so long as one does not abandon hope. (105)
He by whom hope has been severed is liberated from all bonds—past, future, and likewise the present. (106)
Furthermore, the self’s possession of qualities such as being the limit of all stationary things and omniscience is artificial;
that which has arisen does not exist, and likewise, that which is unarisen certainly does not exist, especially in its specific form. || 107 ||
In this way, through a state of hopelessness, one will abandon great delusion;
because it is unarisen, there is no "unborn," and there is no "born" that is indestructible. (108)
And that fourfold knowledge is considered to be conditioned;
the great tree of worldly existence has desire as its root and is filled with sharp thorns. (109)
It is drenched by the water of passion and grows through the grasping for its fruit;
the wise man will not be conquered by that craving for sensual desire. (110)
He will uproot the entire cycle of existence, which is like a tree;
all the power of the previously mentioned factors is comparable to a flash of lightning. (111)
Whoever attends upon a sacrifice is attended upon by death;
therefore, [one should observe] the gap, the purifier, the secure, and the finger-measure.
May there be well-being, peace, and auspiciousness for him whose heart is devoid of luster;
from Pātāla to the ends of the seven worlds, all this is merely a source of terror.

Those practitioners of mantra who remember the *bhaganāśā* mantra with the *śūnya-mantra* have neither offered oblations nor given gifts, neither for the sake of the next world nor for this one. (114)
And herein no one is bound, nor is anyone liberated; neither that which is to be bound, nor the binding itself, nor likewise any other binder exists. (115)
The giver and the recipient, as well as that which is to be given;
the fire, the darbha grass, the mantras, the priest, and that which is to be offered—[all these must be present]. 116.
Where there is emptiness and the absence of appearances, how could these things exist:
the Agnihotra and other sacrifices, the Vedas, and likewise the sages? (117)
Asuras, ancestors, and gods—all these are indeed not ultimate realities.
All gods consist of mantra; the god is remembered as the collection of mantras. (118)
The rites for the gods and the ancestors, as well as all sacrifices, abide by means of mantras;
therein the mantras function, and therein that which is to be known exists in its state of perfect integrity.
Therefore, one should know that everything proclaimed in the mantras is not ultimate reality;
all phenomena are contradicted by the certainty of the ultimate truth. (120)
This knowledge is not for householders; rather, it belongs to those who have reached the final goal.
Nor is there no ritual action; sacrifices exist, and when performed, they bestow their fruits.
And because they have renounced even their own dear selves for her sake, Sundarī belongs to them;
she would not speak to anyone unless asked, nor when questioned improperly. (122)
But he who does not speak when questioned by improper means,
even though the true nature of yoga is known to that questioner, shall be reborn as one who cannot endure it and is unable to grasp it again.
One should speak to him who has said, "I shall not dwell in a house again"; one should first inform him of that which is to be known, for whom there is certainty regarding dispassion. 124.
This entire world is attached to children, wives, and family;
the renunciation of that [attachment] by one who has done so is the characteristic of dispassion. (125)
It should be spoken by one who has not reached the ultimate goal to a member of a social circle,
to a householder, to one who possesses desire, to one who is dispassionate, to one with a wicked mind, and to one whose senses are unconquered.
"O Goddess, it is known to me that you are my devotee, O beautiful one;
therefore, apart from a renunciant, you must not disclose this to anyone. (127)
She said:
"O Mahādeva, tell me according to the final conclusion: what fault is revealed for householders who, being envious, do not perceive equanimity? (128)
The path proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti is joined with dharma, kāma, and artha;
in the Siddhānta, however, there is only knowledge, devoid of dharma, kāma, and artha.
In that case, virtues and the like are lost, yet they alone appear;
their purpose is not accomplished, and the undertaking of it is useless. (130)
If one who is possessed by ignorance offers impure substances upon the altar without first performing the purification that removes impurity,
his medicinal herbs will never succeed, for he is a person whose mind is overwhelmed.
O Goddess, in that same way, a fault becomes manifest for householders;
tell me, "Is this not a fault?"—listen to the reason why. (132)
O fair-faced one, he who enjoys the excellent pleasures of this world and the next, yet occasionally performs a sacrifice—by him the sacrifice has been defiled. (133)

For one desiring to eat what is unfit for consumption, this [rite] would be useless; however, it is not appropriate for one who possesses longing, even when the ritual sacrifice is the authoritative standard. (134)
Through renunciation one attains perfection; it should be known that one who possesses desire does not succeed.
For a householder, renunciation will never occur. (135)
Having abandoned the cravings for both this world and the next, one will become a renunciant;
yet even as a householder, it is impossible not to abandon worldly things entirely. (136)
The state of being a householder can never be successfully established for one devoid of wealth;
therefore, the acquisition of wealth by every possible means is the necessary cause. (137)
When one stands through detachment, having abandoned craving without remainder, then one is no longer seized by householders with the five faults that are disregarded by them. (138)

The state of being a householder is a terrible fear; he will conquer it through [the destruction of] greed. He does not abandon the vow that dispels the darkness of the delusion and greed for worldly existence.
(248) Just as one should renounce everything, so has the Śruti declared: "All this, whatever moves within the world of beings, is to be pervaded by the Lord. (140)
"By means of that which has been renounced, you should enjoy; do not seize the wealth of anyone else. For what external thing remains even in this world for a householder? (141)
O beautiful one, liberation is not seen even in the house of that person who, being attached [to wealth], abandons compassion and seeks to destroy the multitude of living beings. (142)
Nor does even a householder fail to attain perfection by means of the yoga of renunciation, through the avoidance of desire and hatred, and by being free from deceit, envy, and the like. 143.
Those devoid of renunciation do not achieve success, for they mock both sides;
indeed, action is proclaimed to be of two kinds: engagement and withdrawal. (144)
For one who is devoid of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), nothing at all is accomplished.
Such a person is silent toward the world in every respect, equanimous, peaceful, and composed. (145)
One should perceive everything within the fourfold collection of beings as being under one's own control.
The Goddess said: "Nothing whatsoever exists for the sake of another's benefit, nor does any other quality arise. (146)
"O Lord of Gods, silence is therefore meaningless;
for the Lord acts as a benefactor toward others out of a desire for their welfare. (147)
For by that through which the self is extinguished, dispassion is grasped;
for this reason, suffering ceases from the body. (148)
For by that through which the self is extinguished, dispassion is attained;
for this reason, suffering ceases from the body. (149)
"Whatever suffering one inflicts upon others through whatever speech one intends," the Goddess said.
Will there be success in this yoga of detachment, or will there not?
"I desire to know this, O Blessed One; you should speak.
"Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret and its incomparable accomplishment, which is the Lord's. (151)
It is neither form nor color, nor is there any cultivation of it;
it is both with parts and without parts, and is devoid of instruments and substratum. || 152 ||
It is devoid of high-pitched accents, grammatical inflections, and the forms of phonemes;
it is the great yoga beyond the mind, the bestower of all accomplishments. || 153 ||
O fair-faced one, the lineage consists merely of the grace of the Guru;
having obtained that, as soon as it is received, a man attains perfection. (154)
This knowledge is a composite whole and never separate;
devoid of vowels and consonants, it is auspicious and bestows all accomplishments. 155.
Therefore, it is called "the knowable" because no delusion arises;
for this is the destroyer of delusion and the means of accomplishing all knowledge. (156)
It should be known as "all-knowing," which accomplishes all phonemes;
O Goddess, this is the great knowledge, the wisdom that is empty and imperishable. (157)
This is declared to be that which is to be known as liberated from the *bindu* and *mātrā*, and devoid of vowels and consonants; it is the destroyer of old age and death. (158)
It removes all diseases and likewise brings an end to all sins;
it is inconceivable, subtle, like space, all-pervading, and supreme. (159)
Having slightly opened the mouth, one should apply the tongue to the space [within];
in that place, one should perceive whatever slight touch may arise. || 160 ||
This supreme [practice] must be cultivated by yogīs for the sake of accomplishment;
O Goddess, one should explain this very same supreme method of yoga. (161)
"But having been requested, O Goddess, I shall speak the truth:
neither gods, nor asuras, nor yakṣas, nor nāgas, nor rākṣasas [are able to prevent it]. (162)
Neither Kinnaras nor Apsarases, nor Piśācas on the surface of the earth;
neither Vasus, nor Vidyās, nor the hosts of Vidyādharas [were there]. 163.
Neither the world-protectors, nor the constellations, nor indeed the moon and the sun;
neither wind nor water, nor trees, nor mountains [are able to protect]. (164)
Neither Meru, the king of mountains, nor likewise the [entire] world-realm;
neither Brahmā nor Viṣṇu, O Goddess, nor even I together with you [are equal to it]. 165.
All this is infinite; he should not think of even the slightest thing.
Thus the yogi should meditate upon the pervasive, empty, and imperishable. 166.
Neither Yama nor Death has any power over him, even if he is bitten by great serpents such as Ananta, Gulika, and others. (167)
Poison does not affect him who contemplates emptiness;
moreover, both the lower and the higher—all is established within this. 168.
(254) O Goddess, this meditation on emptiness has been duly taught by me to you;
it brings about the exhaustion of merit and demerit, and the destruction of karma, birth, and disease. (169)
One should not grant the existence of such knowledge to just anyone;
O Great Goddess, after having initiated them, it should be given only to one who has been thoroughly tested.
Moving here and there within the range of the body, [one thinks]:
"This is reality, this is reality; this is knowledge, and this is indeed omniscience. (171)
"Having understood this very movement within the channels (nāḍī), one is liberated.
Thus speak many who are proud of their mutual knowledge. (172)
Having thus ascertained this with certainty, one should not reveal the reality;
rather, one should say, "I am a celibate student," or again, "Oh, how peaceful! (173)
Having thus satisfied [the deity], one should remain silent and perform [the rite].
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret, that most excellent application of mudrās. (174)
By the mere realization of this, one shall attain the state of non-existence;
with the left hand, one should perform the unsurpassed binding of the mudrā.
This great [teaching], which removes all pride, belongs to all the wise;
for if some wise person should come to the house of another wise person... (176)
O Goddess, display a gesture by which my fatigue may be recognized;
for when one is thus known as a man of knowledge, one must indeed be questioned about knowledge once again. 177.
O Goddess, one should explain the deity corresponding to a particular mudrā in successive order; then, furthermore, the gurus of that person must be questioned in due sequence. 178.
Having understood the lineage of the gurus and the sequence of the scriptures,
one who is likewise proficient should then worship them, O Goddess, as Śiva himself, being approved by Śiva. (179)
O woman of excellent complexion, tell me the characteristics of that mudrā, by the mere knowledge of which one shall not undergo rebirth again. (180)
Brahmā resides in the little finger, Keśava in the ring finger; Rudra resides in the middle finger, and the unborn Lord in the forefinger. || 181 ||
It has been taught in brief that Sadāśiva resides in the thumb;
having joined the index finger and the thumb, one should move them upward and release them again. (182)
But when performed directly, O Goddess of Gods, it is proclaimed as being done once;
it is joined with the middle, ring, and little fingers. (183)
O Goddess, one should always perform the auspicious symbolic gestures (*mudrā*) such as *prasṛta* and others. By knowing this, one is liberated from the bondage of the fetters (*pāśa*). (184)
"More than a hundred million lineages shall be delivered from hell.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
Having realized the supreme, divine knowledge, the highest essence of yoga, the Goddess, with her palms joined in reverence, spoke these words. (1)
The Goddess said: "O Śaṅkara, [tell me] the yoga of the knowledge of reality, as well as Śakti and Nāda,
and the knowledge of the eightfold Bindu-deity."
(258) By your grace, O Lord of Gods, I have understood the knowledge of the true existence of Yoga, wherein [it is not found] in that Sūtra concerning the supreme true existence of the Pati. || 3 ||
All that has been told in this one [chapter] has been understood through your grace;
yet I wish to hear more, O Blessed One—please deign to speak.
O Maheśāna, O Lord, beginning from the primordial nature (prakṛti), explain the question regarding the channel (nāḍī) conjoined with the vital air (vāyu), which is most secret. (5)
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret, the excellent essence of Yoga, which is common to all compendiums; I shall declare it, for it yields great fruit.
Likewise, they say that withdrawal, meditation, breath control,
concentration, deliberation, and absorption— this is called the six-limbed yoga. (7)
Mind, consciousness, and likewise thought—these have been described by me as fivefold.
These have been declared by me to you as the instruments of yoga.
In this way, yoga arises for one who has well-performed the practice of *dhāraṇā*.
The Goddess said:
"Through meditation (*dhyāna*), retention (*dhāraṇā*), and reflection (*cintā*), as well as through the initial activities of commencing yoga," || 9 ||
O Blessed One, if [enlightenment] were accomplished by time alone, what would have been achieved by you, since it is attained without afflictions and free from self-inflicted suffering? (10)
O Lord of Gods, tell me that knowledge which bestows immediate fruit and prosperity,
such as it has been described in the Purāṇas, Sāṃkhya, and Yoga, O Lord.
p.
260) Even here, such [a teaching] has been proclaimed; what specific distinction is illustrated?
O Supreme Lord, the Vedas and other scriptures are joined with the practice of yoga-meditation (yogadhāraṇa). || 12 ||
O Blessed One, what have you done here without even possessing great knowledge—that which has been told is both inexpressible and indefinable? 13.
Therefore, O Lord, I have understood that [the world] is firmly held by life-force, as well as by primordial nature (prakṛti), the person (puruṣa), destiny (niyati), and time (kāla). || 14 ||
Tell me of the Lord of Māyā and Vidyeśa, and of His true yoga—how the Lord exists without instruments, devoid of meditation and concentration. (15)
Therefore, O Blessed One, I wish to hear this; you should deign to speak, O Lord.
I shall tell you the supreme, essential reality of yoga.
Knowing which, a person becomes successful at that very moment;
which bestows ultimate happiness and is adorned with the fruit of all things. (17)
This knowledge of the gods and the sages has been revealed, by which every person attains this immortal Brahman. || 18 ||
Then the world is liberated and the earth becomes empty;
all phenomena, including the performance of the Vedas, sacrifices, and austerities, dissolve away. || 19 ||
The Agnihotra sacrifices perish, as do the various established norms;
and the gods, being deprived of their meditations and austerities, fall from their divine status.
For this reason, O Goddess, I have kept [this] hidden;
the treatises on the meaning of the yoga-dharma are extensive and profound. (21)
Mutual contradictions are observed among them; no finality is found therein.
Thus the world, mounted upon the wheel of the bodiless [soul], indeed wanders on.
All yogis exist in mutual opposition;
yet, though you are wayward, you have questioned me, impelled by devotion.
I have been seized by a powerful obsession; I must certainly tell you:
neither Brahmā, nor Viṣṇu, nor indeed any other of the best of gods [can help]. (24)
O fair-faced one, no one other than you could have asked such a question;
therefore, listen to the true nature of things without doubt and in full detail.
In an instant, they bestow the attainment of the qualities of the marks, free from all exertion;
they grant success, liberation, contentment, and the increase of nourishment. (26)
Jñānadā, Prītidā, and likewise Āyurārogyadā;
Ghoṣiṇī, Piṅgalā, Vaidyutī, and Bindumālinī. (27)
Cāndrī, Manonugā, Sukṛtā, and likewise another, Saumyā, Nirañjanā, and Nirālambā are thus described. (28)
These channels have been described as adorned by Marut and the others;
previously, however, the wise one was [united] with the supreme Śiva. (29)
Having first performed everything without exception, one should subsequently commence meditation, becoming single-minded, with anger conquered and the senses subdued. (30)
In the twenty-fourth principle (tattva), there is a measure (mātrā) named Ghoṣiṇī;
in the twenty-fifth principle, the second is named Piṅgalā. (31)
The Vaidyutī [power] always resides, established by relying upon the twenty-sixth;
O Me, the Bindumālinī is to be known within the twenty-seventh principle.
In the twenty-eighth reality (tattva), the lunar measure (mātrā) abides;
in the twenty-ninth, the measure that follows the mind (manonugā) should abide.
Then, when my essence had reached thirty, they called that state "Sukṛtā";
having resorted to twenty-one, the gentle measures became established.
The stainless *mātrā* abides resting upon the thirty-second;
in the thirty-third it is without support, and no sign of it is found.
The thirty-three-fold [measurement] is nine finger-breadths hanging down from the person;
among these, the characteristics and so forth are to be observed by the wise. (36)
The Goddess said:
"How can the attainment of these principles, which indeed rest upon the nine measures (mātrās), be perceived immediately?"
In the common treatises on yoga, deer fall into traps set with snares of many forms; they perish through great exertion, as if caught in a snare. (38)
O God, O Maheśvara, tell me that which grants the bliss of immediate realization, even without the restraint of breath (vāyurodha) and devoid of meditation and concentration (dhyāna-dhāraṇa). 39.
O Goddess, listen attentively, for this is not to be heard by those who have not disciplined themselves.
Having attained which, they immediately obtain the state of Śiva, free from all exertion. || 40 ||
Devoted to their respective stages of life (āśrama) wherever they may be, and dwelling wherever they may be, they dissolve [into the Self] in a mere moment, as if into a target. || 41 ||
Likewise, when the ears are perfected by means of the two thumbs and the nose by the fingers,
then his sound, pervading everywhere, expands upward.
The fire within the bodies of embodied beings digests whatever has been eaten;
because of that function of his, they say his sound is uncreated (akṛtrima).
By hearing the twenty-four principles, one is liberated from sins;
therefore, in ancient times, the Self-born One himself created the seven notes beginning with Ṣaḍja.
By these [means], all this—along with the gods, asuras, and humans—is constantly [perceived];
for the seven musical notes (svaras) arose from him as he was perpetually practicing the resonance (dhvani). (45)
Then, within just one month, his *nala* becomes condensed into a single mass;
thereafter, having pierced through passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*), the light shines forth at the end.
Just as he perceives externally, so too does he perceive within;
after three months, he becomes independent, and the state of Śiva arises for him.
This first measure of yours, O Goddess Ghoṣiṇī, has been declared;
you should not show contempt for this knowledge within a hundred thousand [verses], even if it is known only by the mind. (48)
He who understands in this way is not defiled by sin;
even when eating among dog-cookers, he remains like a lotus leaf in water.
Thus, O Goddess, the first [form], Trātu-ghoṣiṇī, has been described to you. Hereafter, I shall proclaim that which is devoid of dissolution and illusion. (50)
Having immediately emerged from one's own body, one should hear the Piṅgalā [nāḍī] as soon as it is perceived;
standing outside in the sunlight, one should remain there for a short while, fully supported by devotion. || 51 ||
One should observe the smoke of one's own self as it emerges, having pierced the palate; and in whatever manner one fixes the mind upon this mark (lakṣa), [so shall one attain concentration]. 52.
In that very way, his great wick of smoke increases;
thus, by the practice for one month, the movement [of the breath] in the head becomes unobstructed.
At the end of the fourth state, one should perceive the dissolution of Piṅgalā alone;
having seen the path of the gods, one beholds the Self within the Self.
Having seen all the worlds and the non-worlds situated both outside and inside, as well as the luminaries following the path of smoke, he beheld that unfilled state. (55)
Liberated from all evils, one shall attain the state free from dualities;
thus has the mark of Piṅgalā been observed by you through the mind.
There he beholds himself as Śiva, both transcendent and immanent;
by this method, O God, he becomes completely enveloped in splendor.
Through the yoga of constant practice, one attains perfection in just six months;
he effortlessly accomplishes everything conceived by the mind.
Upon the fall of the body, one quickly attains the supreme state of Śiva;
this is proclaimed as the one hundred thousand-fold [practice] regarding my twenty-five principles. (59)
O beautiful one, this secret, which purifies the path to liberation, has been told; the twenty-fifth [chapter], consisting of one hundred thousand [verses], has been recounted to you. (60)

Now, O virtuous one, hear concerning the Vaidyutī [power] in the twenty-sixth principle (tattva), which is adorned by the path of play, consisting of the commencement of yoga and breath control (prāṇāyāma). (61)
But at night, at the time of going to bed, having entered the interior without [a lamp],
and in the darkness without lamps, he indeed closes his eyes.
Then, having seen those rays born from his eyes— flickering like lightning and resembling the shimmering circles on the edge of a water-wheel— the beholder perishes.
Having performed this practice repeatedly, one should take rest;
after remaining so for some time, one should practice those same [exercises] once again. (64)
To whatever extent the practitioner performs the practice at night,
to that same extent his splendor increases, like a drop of oil upon water. (65)
Just as one sees the sky obscured by others like sparks within gold,
so too the wise man undoubtedly perceives those very same houses.
Through the practice for five months, light shines at the end;
having seen the flame everywhere, the divine eye is set in motion. (67)
From that, it attains independence and enters the supreme Śiva.
This has been told to you: the hundred thousand [petals] established within the Suṣumṇā.
I have explained to you according to the proper method that which was hidden and concealed by me;
consequently, there is no doubt that one attains autonomy through the reality of Śiva. (69)
I shall describe to you the perception and the defining characteristic of that Bindumālinī who resides within my twenty-seven principles. (70)
Having become pure and having gone outside the village, he should take shelter in the shade of a tree;
then, slightly raising his face, he should gaze at the clear sky.
In that state, he perceives consciousness as having the brilliance of the sky;
[visions] resembling light and crystal fall down and rise up.
That form belongs to the gods through the *iḍā* and by means of their lightning;
for in whatever manner he fixed his aim upon that through yoga, [so it became]. (73)
In that very manner, all directions were as if filled by him on the outside;
yet, while he was under control in many forms, he remained both within and without.
Having seen that by himself, the yogi is then no longer stained by merits or sins;
he becomes fortunate and pleasing to behold for all beings in the three worlds. (75)
It arises here, of this there is no doubt; from that, one attains the name.
This, O gentle one, has been described to you as the measure known as Bindumālinī.
One is liberated from all diseases and, upon the fall of the body, shall go to Śiva; [this occurs] after twenty-seven hundred thousand repetitions of my mantra, performed without exertion. (77)
In my system of twenty-eight principles, there is a measure known as Cāndriṇī;
it is effortless, without the commencement of yoga, and devoid of the utterance of mantras. (78)
In whatever country one may reside and in whichever stage of life one may delight,
whether in the first, middle, or later period, one should practice the supreme *lakṣa* as the cause.
One should observe the atoms (paramāṇu) as white, red, yellow, and black respectively, as well as brilliant and resembling crystal. (80)
Raising the face slightly toward the stainless expanse of the sky,
the lord of practitioners attains perfection through the practice of each [stage] individually.
The Vāyavya mantras are black in color; the knower of yoga should always employ them for the destruction of what remains, as well as for driving away and for intoxication. 82.
And others [perform] such acts as striking, paralyzing, and so forth;
as well as nourishing, increasing, pacifying, and other rites in their proper sequence. (83)
The illustrious master of yoga performs these by means of practicing each one individually;
through this monthly application, he should cause these rites to be accomplished.
Through the yoga of meditation for six months, that which proceeds within the three worlds becomes directly manifest to him; he attains success and shall become Śiva. (85)
The fifth performs all actions;
for this fifth, which is proclaimed, indeed possesses five forms.
Having meditated upon the self in this manner, the yogi should perform all actions;
yet, in the midst of them, the yogi perceives [the mind] as agitated by waves. (87)
Curved like ripples and waves, with a luster equal to a streak of lightning, resembling a serpent in its coils, and possessing a brilliance like a rainbow. || 88 ||
But the more he fixed his consciousness upon that target,
the more he perceived an internal wave of agitation.
O Lord of Yogins, upon seeing this, the destruction of merit and sin occurs;
through the yoga of constant practice, one attains perfection—of this there is no doubt. (90)
Within twelve fortnights, free from hunger and thirst, one is born with a divine body and divine vision; of this there is no doubt.
Within a year, the lord of yogis, whose self is disciplined and who is perfectly concentrated,
attains the knowledge of hearing from afar and the power of observing with the mind.
The three worlds as they exist become directly perceptible to him; likewise, he possesses the power of invisibility, the power of attraction, and the ability to travel on foot [through the air]. (93)
And one should perform [rites] with the Vāyavya [mantras], as well as those concerning the sky-dwellers and so forth;
with the Āgneya [mantras], one should effect drying up, striking, and killings. (94)
One should effect immobilization and even muteness by means of the Pārthiva [mantra];
having performed the rites beginning with nourishment (āpyāyana), one should effect it by means of the Vāruṇa [mantra]. (95)
This fifth [method] should always be employed by the yogin in all undertakings;
these are proclaimed to be the one hundred and twenty-eight measures (mātrās) for the purpose of this practice. 96.
In the twenty-ninth principle, the measure that follows the mind should be observed with effort if one desires one's own success.
Having gone to a solitary, secluded place, one should close the divine eyes;
the self, possessing a golden luster, remains there, veiling the eyes.
Having focused his consciousness upon that, he enters the resonance,
which is white, red, yellow, and black, possessing a luster like a rainbow.
Having repeatedly observed the colors of those who pierce one another,
he should then again mark that [target] as being the size of a mustard seed. (100)
Within the shadow, however, O Goddess, there are seen various auspicious forms that are all-pervading;
for you, O Goddess, consist of all the gods, yet each of the gods is distinct.
The beautiful woman sees those forms as the shapes of drops;
by the union of those two, the yogi sees nothing else with his eyes, whether by day or by night. (102)
Within a month, one becomes free from excessive excrement and devoid of hunger and thirst;
the body becomes fragrant and divine, and there arises a state of constant contentment.
Through a continuous practice for two months, the divine eye arises;
merits and sins perish, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun. (104)
By means of constant practice, there is no doubt that in twenty-nine months, O fair-faced one, this [attainment] is equal [to the goal]. (105)
The Nāḍī is indeed well-established, known by various names, and the destroyer of great sins;
O Goddess, listen with one-pointed mind to its characteristics from me. 106.
It is without application or effort, devoid of measure and the bindu, free from the throat, palate, and lips, and divested of the utterance of mantras. || 107 ||
A man who is well-versed in that [state] is fit for immortality;
it is characterized by non-application, non-undertaking, and the absence of exertion.
O Goddess, listen to the effort by which one should fix the mind upon the all-pervading space that fills this entire universe. 109.
Whether situated here or there, whether pure or even impure,
one should fix the mind and the ear in concentration, free from external sounds. (110)
O Goddess, in a windless place or where there is only a slight breeze, the curtain, when struck like a bell,
shall hear [the sound] which brings about the destruction of merit and sin.
Having heard a sound similar to that of perfectly pure bell-metal (kāṃsya) which is devoid of bright luster, one becomes fit for immortality. || 112 ||
By that [consciousness], which is all-pervasive, this entire space is filled;
through its constant practice, the knower of consciousness perceives the earth. 113.
By this, for half a month, the lord of yogins is not afflicted by diseases;
he attains good fortune and, upon the fall of the body, shall go to Śiva.

That which consists of three syllables from the beginning, which has been proclaimed as being of three kinds—that indeed should be known as belonging to Śiva; because of its universality, it is the illuminator. (115)
O Goddess, the second *praṇava* is endowed with the form of a swan (*haṃsa*);
together with the *bindu*, it is proclaimed to have the form of Rudra. || 116 ||
Those beginning with "Akāma" proceed forth, characterized by pervasiveness;
this subtle one, whose activity is independent, is called the treasury of the syllable Om (Aṅkāra). || 117 ||
The letter *ha* joined with the letter *u*, endowed with the syllable *oṃ*, and accompanied by the *bindu*, O Goddess—this is proclaimed as the third. (118)
The origin of the syllable Oṃ is proclaimed to extend up to the path of Brahmā; Rudra, beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha and ending with Ananta, is said to be the syllable Oṃ.
Above that, one should know the third, which is remembered as the Praṇava.
The accomplishment (siddhi) characterized by peaceful knowledge is that which ends in death at the time of death.
But his unsurpassed movement has transcended the space of sound;
all this path is proclaimed to be threefold.
The *sakala* consists of the five elements (*pañcatattva*), while the *sakalaniṣkala* consists of three;
when it is devoid of utterance (*uccāra*), the *bindu* has attained the state of being partless (*niṣkalatā*). || 122 ||
By the will of Śiva, the practitioner is graced; he desires liberation.
This is renowned as the Saumya-nāḍī, which destroys even the greatest sins. (123)
O Goddess, that sound which is heard, characterized by the ringing of bells and so forth, transcending the primary musical notes— that is called the Rudra-omkāra.
Divine, performing all rites, and bestowing fruits such as *aṇimā* and the rest—one should know it to consist of thirty-one [syllables]; Śiva’s *oṃkāra*, however, is beyond that. (125)
The thirty-two [channels] are said to be devoid of the qualities of the subtle elements (tanmātra-guṇa);
the channel conjoined with the Pervasive One (Vyāpaka) is called Narañjanā. 126.
The auspicious syllable Om is known as the supreme, divine, and stainless;
through the yoga of constant practice, it bestows [its fruits] upon practitioners. 127.
Within half a month, one attains the eightfold qualities beginning with atomization (aṇimā), as well as the power of hearing from afar and the knowledge of what is spoken in all worlds. 128.
And he of great splendor beholds [himself] established everywhere; indeed, he is all-pervading, possesses the power to assume any form at will, and likewise possesses omniscience. 129.
The fall of the body leads one swiftly to the supreme state of Śiva.
At the end of the cessation of the sound of the bell, the syllable *oṃ* of Śiva is uttered. (130)
That crest-lock (śikhā) is described by its characteristic as the "Stainless" (vimalā);
it is said to be the very essence of time (kālatattva), and the channel (nāḍī) is called the "Spotless" (nirañjanā). 131.
O Varārohā, [I shall describe] the one named Vimalā, which is conjoined with the supreme syllable;
I shall explain the supportless [state], which bestows the fruit of the nine principles.
One should recollect the reality of the *bindu*, which is beyond syllables and beyond utterance;
thereafter, one should not contemplate even this supreme [state] as anything at all. (133)
O fair-faced one, that reality is known as the thirty-third, which is stainless;
it is declared to be the thirty-second, established in the supreme state beyond support. (134)
That which is beyond the thirty-three, which is to be designated as being devoid of name—knowing that, O Goddess, one attains success; this is what has been proclaimed as the goal. (135)
Thus has the one reality been proclaimed by Śiva in many ways;
it bestows both spiritual accomplishments and liberation—one should contemplate that which has been revealed. (136)
Having thus understood the entire essence of knowledge, conduct yourself as you please;
this auspicious nectar of knowledge must not be given to anyone.
All this has been fully explained as the utterly pure meditation on reality (tattvadhyāna). O Goddess, this which has been proclaimed is the supreme among all realities. 138.
Of these, that which is beyond description, free from affliction,
and the sustainer of all— He indeed is devoid of any support.
"O Goddess, such meditation as that has not been proclaimed for you.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
O Goddess, the Ācārya knows the Śiva-tantra, the knowledge of Śiva, and all that pertains to Śiva in its entirety; he is free from worldly motives. || 1 ||
Detached from worldly treatises and possessing exclusive passion for the knowledge of Śiva, one should speak an answer to them by whatever means [is necessary] regarding the Lord. (2)
"Therefore, O Maheśvara, I desire to hear this through your grace.
Īśvara said:
"If someone were to ask, 'Which word is recited as being subject to destruction? (3)
p.
287) From this point, one should speak further to him: "Listen to that, O fair-faced one!
Is the *pudgala* composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), or is it a quality of wind, or else a quality of space? (4)
Then, distinct from the phonemes and ending with the *nāda*, that which expresses the Lord in the form of the *bindu*—the *sphoṭa* consisting of words and sentences—having bowed down, withdraws. (5)
"The teacher declares that the *saṃhitā* of words comes first;
every sentence is based on words, and a word is traditionally held to be based on phonemes. (6)
All phonemes depend upon speech, and speech depends entirely upon the vital breath (prāṇa).
For the Lord Vāyu, the vital breath, is said to have space (ākāśa) as its support.
Resting upon the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), he is established within the sources of the elements;
likewise, the originator of the elements (bhūtādi) and Mahat are each supported by what follows them.
O Goddess, because he arises from the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*) and so forth, he is of the nature of reality (*sadātmaka*).
Even beyond him is the Supreme God, the cause of all causes. (9)
O God, that which is beyond him is undoubtedly the supreme Śiva;
this entire universe has him as its support, and he is considered the highest of the high.
Neither speech proceeds nor does the mind truly reach that place where this supreme deity, the cause of all causes, resides. (11)
In brief, that by which the deity is propitiated is "sound";
the deity is propitiated by sound, yet there is no deity apart from sound.
From the unmanifest arises sound; sound is its manifestor.
Furthermore, that which is threefold and then released is called subtle sound.
By that non-final word, [the reality] devoid of intellect and mind is perceived;
by that divine word, it is eternally seen as free from affliction.
But that which is the subtle sound alone, situated within the body in the body—
this is distinguished by all sounds, beyond comparison, and free from affliction.
The divine Śiva is remembered as subtler than the subtlest;
for those who [seek] the Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Īśvara, he is the essence of the mere hearing of the Vedas.
It is not grasped here by sound, nor by hand, nor by the eye;
it is that sound which exists without [ordinary] sound, resembling a sacrificial fire fed with beans.
Within the hearts of all embodied beings, the supreme Śiva exists as the pure sound known as Ghoṣa,
Ārava, Svana, Śabda, Sphoṭa, and Dhvani.
The humming sound, the utterance of "huṃ," and indeed the eighth [element], which is space itself—
the sound that arises from the conjunction of the ear and the thumb. (19)
That which is equal to the flame of a blazing fire is designated as *ghoṣa*;
however, that sound which is proclaimed and perceived as slightly soft is called *īṣanmanda*.
The sound of broken bell-metal is proclaimed to be harsh;
thereafter, the subtle resonance of a flute is like a rain shower in a windless place.
The fourth is the great sound, which is resonant, supremely subtle, and that state which is free from affliction; it pervades all sounds.
One's own word shall accomplish everything for the yogi, there is no doubt;
indeed, the fifth great sound brings benefit to all yogis. (23)
(291) For men, the *sphoṭa* alone is considered the medicine that brings delight to the mind;
one whose mind is absorbed within the word [perceives it] as merged in the supreme reality of sound (*śabdatattva*), situated inside the word. (24)
The Sphoṭa, which bestows the accomplishment of all goals, attains supreme perfection—that sound which proceeds entirely free from the resonance of the vocal organs. (25)
Eternal, beginningless, and unmanifest, sound is characterized by resonance;
it is like the gentle tone of a lute or the ringing of a peaceful bell. || 26 ||
The humming sound, like the noise of bees intoxicated by the fragrance of flowers, is known as the *jhaṅkāra*; it is the entire Supreme Goddess. (27)
It appeared like a mass of lightning, a dense cloud with a deep resonance, containing the collection of all the kalās, and as terrifying as the fall of a thunderbolt. || 28 ||
When the sounds have been dissolved, the sound remembered is that which is the abode of the dissolution of all other sounds.
That is Śiva, established in the principle of Śiva; he is the "Dhvaṃkṛta" (the Destroyer), remembered as the Praṇava. || 29 ||
O Goddess, eight sounds have been briefly described as supreme;
they should be practiced with effort if one desires one's own perfection.
"O God, I wish to hear in truth how the word 'goddess' (devī) conveys its meaning;
O Maheśvara, how do they exist as non-different and yet as different? (31)

And the Lord [establishes] the relationship between word and meaning; that relationship is not employed as being either of the nature of cause and effect, or of the nature of the signified and the signifier. (32)
Otherwise, this effort would lead to doubt for everyone;
[the reason] is considered to be inseparable from the nature [of the thing], not as something other than that nature. (33)
If the relationship of cause and effect were derived from the nature of the thing itself, then that term would indeed denote something other [than its conventional meaning] for everyone. (34)
Now, is sound the lamp and the preceding sound its wick?
Like consciousness, it is knowledge; that which is the excellence of sound is indeed the wick.
But the sound of Dharma shall bind [the senses], accomplishing peace, desire, and worldly prosperity. || 36 ||
Knowledge in the form of the Lord is enjoined following the word "paśu" (the bound soul).
For indeed, the meaning is established by the word, and the word is established by the meaning. (37)
Knowledge that has forgotten the meaning of words is ignorance, yet it is devoid of purpose.
Here, the Lord is the sovereign among those who possess power, for all things are bound by speech and sound. (38)
The Self-existent Ones have declared that sound is the manifestation of the apprehension of meaning;
whatever is the manifestation of a particular meaning within the fourfold collection of living beings.
That very word should be understood as having a purposeful meaning by which the intended effect is accomplished;
for in this world, speech proceeds that is devoid of such purpose. (40)
That which is known as an incorrect word (apaśabda) may be either entirely Prakrit or even [otherwise];
however, those words that convey meaning and were spoken by sages or deities are indeed valid. || 41 ||
The wise describe those who employ ungrammatical forms even in the sacred scriptures as such; what is the use of that [language], however soft and elegant it may be in Sanskrit? (42)
By hearing this discourse on ignorance and passion, which is the cause of the afflictions of saṃsāra, whatever merit arises brings about the complete destruction of sins and other evils. (43)
Even that speech, though lost, should be known as most excellent;
for the worldly life consisting of sons, wives, and so forth belongs only to men of deluded mind. (44)
For the learned, immersion in the scriptures is an obstacle to the practice of yoga; when the state of agency and the state of knowing move from mouth to mouth in body after body. (45)
Then the living being is liberated; otherwise, never. Some men say this, but it is entirely false.
"The Blessed One, the Supreme Self, resides within the body—within you, amidst flesh, worms, phlegm, blood, and urine. (47)
O Sage among gods, how is it that what is difficult even for you to obtain resides within this body?
For the entire world is seen even within every single house. (48)
The sole sun of the world is delighted by the *nāḍikā*;
thus, by means of the supreme subtle power (*sūkṣma-śakti*) abiding in the beyond, [he is so]. (49)
The net of delusion has been woven among the creatures in the world.
The Goddess said: "Which are the eight supreme and subtle sounds, and what are those phonemes? (50)
"O Lord of Gods, please graciously tell me of the deities therein.
The Lord said: "I shall describe these deities among all the principles (tattvas)."
O fair-limbed one, by the mere knowledge of which the practitioner attains accomplishment, there are no sins; those castes are indeed deities. (52)
O fair-faced one, those sounds and those principles are to be understood;
O beautiful one, they are joined by the gods, by the principles, and by my imperishable syllable (akṣara). 53.
Then, O Goddess, one attains perfection; upon the falling of the body, one is liberated.
And in that sound, O fair-faced one, all the deities beginning with Brahmā reside.
O beautiful one, the gods beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha have attained dissolution in that [state].
The gods are the supreme abode of sound, and from sound the phonemes (varṇas) arise.
From the phonemes and so forth arises the manifestation of mantra; from that, everything proceeds.
From sound this entire triple world, with its moving and non-moving beings, was born. (56)
Therefore, O Goddess, this rite of the Supreme Word must indeed be practiced by you.
Having become intent on meditation upon the Word, one who practices with a well-composed mind— (57)
For you, that accomplishment has been explained by means of an accomplishment that is itself soundless;
first, one should touch the sound that is natural and bestows accomplishment. (58)
The third, which is the supreme sound, is the human [mantra] that bestows accomplishment;
the third, which is the supreme sound, is that which invariably bestows accomplishment. || 59 ||

The fourth is the principle of sound (śabdatattva), and the principle of limited agency (kalātattva) is likewise in brief; by meditating upon the Lord of Gods with that [mantra], one shall partake in the fruit of all [practices]. (60)
The fifth, which is known as Sound (śabda), is the supreme and difficult-to-restrain Māyā;
the sixth, which is the principle of sound, is remembered by the name Vidyā. || 61 ||
But that Goddess Vāgīśvarī, born there, is not born again.
That which is the seventh, the supreme reality, shall be declared as Īśvara. (62)
In that regard, when one is absorbed in sound (śabda), one becomes equal to Īśvara;
that which is the eighth, the supreme sound, is beyond comparison and free from affliction.
There, when the yogin is absorbed, O Goddess, he reaches the ninth state, which is called Sādākhya; it is known as the supreme, consisting of all sounds.
Emerging from that sound, well-rounded both below and above—by means of that meditation, O Goddess of the Gods, one shall partake in the fruit of all [deeds]. (65)
O Maheśvarī, all sounds are established within that Bindu-deva;
therefore, he has been described as the Bindu consisting of the aggregate of sounds.
O Goddess, ten [kalpas] beyond that are devoid of verbal cognition;
therein alone, representation-only (vijñaptimātra) is established through a continuous succession. (67)
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the Niśvāsakārikā. 67 1/2.

The Goddess said: "O Maheśvarī, regarding all that you have spoken— that this entire universe is born from Sound— I have understood, through your grace, the collection of phonemes and their essential principles."
O Maheśvara, for every word there is the manifestation of other gods;
likewise, O Lord of Gods, there is the yoga and meditation of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas). || 2 ||
O Lord, by your grace, tell me today about the eightfold powers beginning with *aṇimā*.
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret concerning that which you have asked.
Therefore, I shall fully proclaim this great boon, which brings benefit to practitioners; it has not been revealed by me to anyone else.
O Goddess, neither by the sages nor by the deities has this ever been asked in any way;
they were satisfied with the mere sound [of my voice], but I myself was not questioned, O beautiful one.
I shall explain the creation for every word and the occurrence of injunctions and so forth, as well as the lords of knowledge (vidyeśas), beginning with Aṇimā, for the sake of Bhava.
That which is called the sound of resonance (ghoṣa-śabda), devoid of the utterance of phonemes (varṇa), is attained through the instrument (karaṇa); I shall now describe its creation.
Therefore, that primordial nature which has arisen is called *māyā* by you;
the mantra that denotes it there is proclaimed to be the vowel *ū*. (8)
Ananta is proclaimed as the first among the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) within that principle; and for yogins, it is remembered that the Paiśāca birth is not produced among the various wombs.
But that which is attained through the instrument [of practice] is proclaimed as the power of atomization (aṇimā), as well as sovereignty (aiśvarya) and contentment (tuṣṭi). || 10 ||
The knowledge of *tāra* has been fully explained; the supreme *śi* sound is traditionally remembered [as the next].
This creation is proclaimed to occur within the first principle, the *śabdatattva*.
The word *rāva* has been fully explained by you, and it was known to you previously;
indeed, that which is born from a person within it was described by me to you.
In that regard, this mantra, the letter *ya*, is proclaimed as the designator (*vācaka*);
it is declared to be the subtle Lord of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*), who is remembered by yogis who have performed their recollection. (13)
The Rākṣasa is said to be among the sources of birth (yoni), and sovereignty is remembered as its dissolution;
it is called the creation of water, but no son was proclaimed by the king.
This creation has been proclaimed in relation to the second reality, which is sound;
now I shall fully explain it in relation to the third—listen to me with a one-pointed mind. 15.
The Maya previously mentioned has arisen from its own name;
however, O lady of excellent hips, Śivottama is the designator of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas). 16.
The majesty of yogins has been proclaimed; the yakṣas are declared to be their source. Their sovereignty, greatness, and likewise their contentment are all in vain.
(305) That knowledge regarding Tārā has been declared to you as the third;
I shall now fully explain the fourth—listen to me as I speak. 18.
O lady of auspicious countenance, the subject of sound was previously explained by me at your request;
therefore, the time has now arisen which is difficult for all yogins to conquer. (19)
The letter *la* is proclaimed as the designator (*vācaka*) of this essence of sound (*śabdatattva*);
and within it, O [Queen], Vidyeśa Ekanetra has been described to you.
For yogins, he is called Brahmā; in the womb, he is called Gandharva;
and his attainment of sovereignty, O Goddess of Gods, has been described to you as the fourth.
O lady of beautiful countenance, contentment has been described by me as rain;
joy has been declared as knowledge, and this was told to you in the fourth [chapter]. (22)
(306) I shall now fully explain the fifth; listen, O long-eyed one!
Sphoṭa is the supreme sound, the highest, and the source of the principle of Māyā. || 23 ||
The word "self" deludes these people who engage in debate, chatter, and cavil;
not knowing the supreme reality, they are bewildered by verbal discourse. (24)
The syllable *m* is proclaimed as the designator of that reality of sound (*śabdatattva*).
O Goddess, Vidyeśa is declared to be your single vision;
therein, the Vaiṣṇava state is proclaimed as the fifth for yogis. (26)
The womb of Indra has been fully described; now hear of sovereignty (aiśvarya).
It is renowned as "the power of will" (prākāmya), and supreme contentment is said to be its characteristic. (27)
(307) Knowledge has been proclaimed by Śiva, the Supreme Self, as "the Joyful" (Pramudita). This fifth [stage] has been fully explained to you in its proper sequence and order. || 28 ||
I shall now fully declare the sixth [chapter] to you; listen as it is being told by me.
Previously, the Sound (dhvani) was described by me, in which the origin of the Vidyās occurs.
The syllable *kṣa* is proclaimed as the designator of that reality of sound (*śabdatattva*);
and the threefold form of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*) has been described in their proper sequence.
Kaumāra is declared for yogins; the gentle state is proclaimed to be within the womb;
and lordship over the qualities has been fully described, O beautiful goddess. (31)
Excellent joy is called satisfaction (tuṣṭi), and knowledge is proclaimed as delight (moda).
This, O Goddess, has been told to you—the unsurpassed sixth sound.
(308) I shall now fully explain the seventh [sound], which is extremely difficult to obtain. O Lord, its origin within this [system] is designated as *jhaṅkāra*. 33.
The speaker of that reality is the supreme mantra consisting of the syllable *ra*;
from Vidyeśa comes Śrīkaṇṭha, who is celebrated as the *aum* of the yogins. (34)
And the Lord of Progeny was indeed spoken of by you as being in the womb, O beautiful one;
furthermore, sovereignty over that [womb] is proclaimed to be the state of Śiva-hood. (35)
From Sunetra, Tuṣṭi is said to have arisen; knowledge is called Ramyaka.
Thus has this seventh, most excellent Śabda been fully described to you.
I shall now fully explain the eighth; listen with a one-pointed mind.
Because that reality is Sadāśiva, it is declared to you as Dhvaṃkṛta.
The letter *ha* is proclaimed as the designator (*vācaka*) of that reality (*tattva*).
Among the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*), Śikhaṇḍīśa is said to be the yogin Śrīkaṇṭha. (38)
Yonibrahman is designated as the eighth, so it is proclaimed;
there, O Goddess of gods, resides sovereignty that accomplishes all desires. (39)
Contentment is indeed the mark of that reality; of this there is no doubt.
Knowledge therein has been fully described by me as being ever-rejoicing. (40)
I have declared to you this eighth [topic]: sound is the supreme cause.
Through knowledge, a living being is liberated from the entire bondage of the fettered (paśu). || 41 ||
The ninth is Tuṣṭi; Bindudeva is proclaimed [as the deity].
O lady of excellent vows, the Bindu consists of four kalās and is Śāntyatīta.
(310) I shall explain to you that great [teaching], more secret than the secret, concerning how Śakti and the fourfold Kala may indeed exist in nine ways. 43.
O virtuous lady, I have described to you these sixty-four divisions;
I shall now explain their ritual worship correctly—listen to that from me.
On the previously mentioned plot of ground, free from hair, insects,
and bones, one should there draw an eight-petalled lotus with a pericarp.
One should worship the god Śiva, the supreme cause, in the pericarp;
Ananta has already been mentioned previously, as well as Padmaśakti.
One should likewise place the limbs, beginning with Dharma, in their proper sequence;
and the placement of mantras in the heart-lotus should be exactly as previously described.
On the eastern leaf, however, one should worship Prakṛti with the Āgneya mantra; on the southern [leaf], Akṛta with the Paiśāca mantra, and with the Nairṛta [mantra]. || 48 ||
One should place Aṇimā in the west, and Vāyavyā in the water;
then, being composed, one should place Tārājñāna in the north.
O Great Goddess, one should visualize Bindudeva in the northeast;
having placed Ghoṣa in the center, one should then perform this again.
O beautiful one, by means of the letter *u* itself— in its short, long, and protracted forms—
one should effect the three principles (*tritattva*) there, following the path of resonance in due order.

The principle of the Self (ātmatattva) is proclaimed to be short, while knowledge (vidyā) is said to be long; one should always perform the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) everywhere with the protracted vowel.
O Goddess of the gods, in this manner the arrangement of the three principles (tritattva) must be performed sequentially for all [mantras] within their own words consisting of three syllables. (53)
O beautiful one, those phonemes which begin with the letter *ī* and end with the letter *ā*, starting from the east, are declared to be deities.
He is indeed the proclaimer for all of them until everything is completed;
one should assign him to all the various terrestrial rites.
In this manner, one should offer fifty oblations, beginning from the east;
for the element of sound, one hundred should be offered, and for the three principles (tritattva), one should offer three hundred.
The final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) should be offered upon hearing a sound while the ladle is well-turned;
one who desires the goals of spiritual perfection and liberation should meditate on the God consisting of sound.
O Goddess, [the rite] is well-performed when it is devoid of the five Brahmās, likewise the limbs of Śiva, the world-protectors, the lords of the sciences, and the weapon-mantra. (58)
One should perform sacrifice in two ways; this is the yoga in brief:
the sacrifice of material substances when one possesses wealth, and meditation alone when one is destitute. (59)
The teacher, having severed all doubts, should liberate [the disciple] even by means of the various [methods].
In the second [stage], the partless reality (niṣkala-tattva) is proclaimed; "rāva" is said to be sound.
In the third [element], the reality of emptiness is proclaimed as the sound of one's own voice;
in this sequence and so forth, the reality within sound follows its respective order.
One should not act otherwise, O Goddess; there is no conceptualization of "it exists" or "it does not exist.
And as for the accomplishment of the Command, O Mistress of the Gods, one should not think of anything at all. 62.
Just as the accomplishment of the lines was proclaimed by Śiva in the *Nayasūtra*,
there is no doubt that the accomplishment of sound occurs through the practice performed every month. (63)
O virtuous one, there is no yoga equal to this in all the tantras;
there is no accomplishment equal to this found within the three worlds. (64)
O Goddess, there is no other means of realization equal to these;
something supreme must be known, for the knowledge of sound is the highest. || 65 ||
The non-conceptual fourth state is direct perception established everywhere;
it is the drop (bindu), the digit (kalā), the four-cornered digit, and the fourfold power (śakti).
This is declared to be the supreme sacrifice; one should place the Nāda with the pericarp (karṇikā).
The letter *U* is the Utkṣaṇī, while Śakti is the first digit (kalā).
The letter *e* is indeed proclaimed as the second, the subtle;
the third is indeed *amṛtā*, and the letter *i* is proclaimed [as that]. (68)
Amṛtāmṛtā is the fourth; the vowel *ī* has been described to you.
As for that which is the divine digit of the Bindu, it was previously illustrated by me. (69)
O fair-faced one, regarding the Nāda as well, I have also stated in the Binduyāga:
"First, one should place a digit (kalā) of the deity Bindu in the east. (70)
The second is indeed to the south, the third to the west, and the fourth to the north; these are proclaimed as the digits (kalās) of the Bindu.
One should place Utkarṣaṇī in the southeast, Susūkṣmā in the southwest,
and the digit named Amṛtā in the northwest.
One should place the fourfold group of Śaktis— Amṛtā and Mṛtā—
in the northeast; one should then install them, joined with Nāda-Śakti, within the pericarp.
O virtuous one, the true nature of the Self has been told to you;
indeed, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra abide as the three castes.
Īśvara and the power of Nāda are established in the upper portion;
all are pervaded by the Tattva, for all are indeed Tattvas—of this there is no doubt. (75)
Initiation may be of two kinds; that which consists of meditation and ritual substances is not auspicious.
Initiation performed with a hundred oblations for each [of the elements] leads to liberation.
The principles beginning with earth have been described by me previously;
they are to be understood in their proper sequence within Śakti, Nāda, and Bindu.
O Goddess, this supreme sacrifice is indeed difficult for those of unrefined soul to attain;
even the gods, O beautiful celestial lady, strive for this sacrifice. (78)
O Goddess, such a rite as this is not obtained by me unless I am pleased;
it must never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who is not a devotee. (79)
When she has been consecrated for one who is dear to the Guru and self-controlled, and who knows the procedures for all the paths, this rite should be bestowed in such a manner. (80)
It should be given to a disciple endowed with noble birth, good conduct, and virtue, who speaks kindly;
otherwise, it must not be given—this is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said: "Is it by the eye, or by speech, or by touch, or by the mind, or by water?"
Through the yoga of meditation, she performs *dhāraṇā* out of a desire to bestow grace. || 1 ||
O Lord, this very great secret has been told by you;
yet this lack of distinction among them was hidden within your heart.
Therefore, O Blessed One, I wish to hear this; you should deign to speak.
As the Lord, I shall explain each one of these to you in detail.
This must be understood by the teacher himself in brief at the time of initiation:
just as in the world the sun awakens the lotuses. || 4 ||
Thus, having purified the lotuses, Śiva, being gracious, awakens them;
though situated at a distance, he is present nearby—abiding in the body (piṇḍastha), yet free from the body (piṇḍavarjita). || 5 ||
Stained and yet stainless, he alone indeed abides as many;
eternally subtler than the subtlest, the all-pervading Lord is further away than the farthest.
When [the body] is in close proximity, the body is darkness; it is not pervasive, nor is it the sovereign, imperishable [Self].
The principles (tattvas) and the deities remain according to their respective divisions.
Sovereignty, the contentment of knowledge, and the other [perfections], along with the deities,
and the specific locations for each within one's own body, in their proper order.
Having understood all this in its particulars, there shall be the destruction of all bonds.
I shall now describe the lotus of the body and, in particular, the lotus of the void.
(320) It is endowed with eight petals representing the Vasus, eleven filaments for Rudra,
and the Ādityas are to be known as the pericarp; twelve are traditionally taught for the lotus.
O Goddess, I am the one who has been meditated upon by him whose state of being exists within the city composed of all the gods; as for those other people, they have merely been led astray.
The heart of all embodied beings resembles the flower of the plantain tree;
in its center is situated a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
The lotus of the heart is one *vitasti* in measure, and it is four *aṅgulas* [in width];
it is situated eight *aṅgulas* above the navel.
The lotus stalk has nine openings and is filled with desires on all sides;
it is equal in size to the joint of a thumb, while the pericarp indeed possesses filaments.
On the pericarp there should be the Sun, and in the center of that is the Moon;
in the center of the Moon is Fire, and in the center of the Fire is Maheśvara. (15)
Sadāśiva is [the authority] for Maheśa, and Śiva is even beyond him;
I shall now declare the measure established by Śiva for all of them.
One should make the solar orb slightly smaller than that, and the lunar orb likewise;
one should know the supreme circle of fire to be smaller than the lunar orb. (17)
Stainless, purified as if by fire, divine, and resembling the rising sun;
he is the Lord (Īśāna) who consists of pure being, blazing like a flaming mountain peak.
Beyond his [ten-faced form] is the supreme, divine Sadāśiva, great-souled and as pure as clear crystal; above even him is the Parāpara (the both-supreme-and-non-supreme).
White, perfectly pure, divine, ungraspable, and supremely auspicious—this is declared to be the stalk of the body; the wise know it to consist of the petals of Brahman. (20)
Viṣṇu resides in the pericarp; the knot is proclaimed to be Māyā.
On the southern petal of the unmanifest is Buddhi, and on the southwestern [petal] likewise.
To the west, ego-sense; to Vāyu, the subtle element of sound;
to the north, the subtle element [of touch]; and likewise to Īśānī, the sense of taste. || 22 ||
The grasper of form is in the front; the nose is situated on the fire-petal; at the tips of the petals are the great elements, while the filaments are the sense faculties.
The mind alone abides everywhere within the subtle elements and the senses;
that which is obstructive in the heart is of the nature of darkness (tamas) and takes the form of sleep.
Beneath the pericarp, however, his body is established;
at the end, the pericarp is consciousness, conjoined with all objective states. (25)
That Śiva is situated above the pericarp within all bodies;
the gods reside in the lotus stalk, while those below dwell upon the filaments.
Various hosts were on his leaf, and likewise Daityas were upon his body hairs;
the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, as well as Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas [were there]. (27)
The sisters and mothers stood at the base of the navel;
he who, having pierced with the needles of knowledge that lotus which consists of all the gods— || 28 ||
One perceives the stainless self directly from within the body;
for all this that is awake, the teacher is said to be the Lord. (29)
When he is satisfied, may all the lords of the worlds be satisfied;
for the preceptor who performs the initiation is the most excellent of gurus, having reached the further shore of the Śiva-tattva. (30)
Otherwise, he is not to be known as a guru, nor does initiation grant liberation.
The preceptor is remembered as the embodiment of the mantra, and Śiva is the one who is beyond the form of the mantra.
The mantras should be known as being of that nature, and Śiva should be known as being of that nature;
therefore, grace proceeds toward all living beings. 32.
This is the will of the Blessed One; however, one should contemplate it thus:
Śiva, residing within the body of the teacher, is the one who bestows grace upon living beings. (33)
It bestows various accomplishments and leads the bound soul to liberation;
it is that which is peaceful, the supreme reality, the cause, and the lord of causes. (34)
Having become established therein, one should reveal the principles of Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman,
as well as the supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, and Śiva, the supreme cause. (35)
Abiding therein, he reveals it as it truly is and as it exists.
The Goddess said: "But what is the reality of the three principles (tritattva), and how is it known from the Imperishable (akṣara)? (36)
Tell me how there is ignorance in the world regarding all sentient beings;
for whatever object exists as it truly is, by way of its qualities, defects, and essential nature. (37)
O Lord, all that—both the fruit and the merit—is known to you;
tell me, how then could anything remain unknown in this world for one who possesses omniscience? (38)
When the knowledge of reality, which is perfectly pure, is known to be situated in the middle, [then] the Lord [is realized]. (p. 326)
Then his omniscience is fully manifested through every means. || 39 ||
Anger, malice, envy, lust, delusion, greed for wealth, backbiting, falsehood, and dishonesty [are found] even among men who have passed their youth. (40)
Hypocrisy, cruelty, instability, and crooked thinking are the things to be overcome;
the world is shrouded by these very qualities, and for that reason, it does not find the Divine.
Having performed this ritual of the words, the preceptor, well-established and virtuous,
should initiate all living beings through this meditation, O lady of excellent conduct.
This is known as the method of meditation; now the mental [meditation] is being described.
One should apply this method even when all the senses are fixed on a single object. (43)
O fair-faced one, all the senses function by means of the measure of a single sense; indeed, all beings and the principles [of existence] are likewise unified in that one.
Activity in all undertakings is beginningless; of this there is no doubt.
It is grasped by the mind, O Goddess, and the bound soul (paśu) is joined with the mind. 45.
O beautiful one, the mind exists in all [beings] through the measure of the single sense-organ;
since it is grasped by the mind, it is therefore of the nature of the mind alone.
That entire abode [of the Self] is to be perceived within Maheśvara by means of the mind, that mind being joined with the intellect and all the applications of the instruments of perception. 47.
One should likewise place Ātmavidyā and Śiva, along with the conceptualization of creation and dissolution; having thus arranged the principles (tattvas), one should place Śiva upon the top.
Having thus meditated with the mind, out of a desire to favor those who perform [the rite],
this single mental procedure has been told in brief. (49)
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, the procedure for the mental grace of the presentation of the purificatory rites, in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
Īśvara said:
Having become Īśvara, he creates; and as Sadāśiva, he withdraws. Śiva, however, acts as the sustainer, while Śānti is the supreme state. (1)
The supreme reality of the Self is said to be the lotus petal;
knowledge is indeed its filament, and the power of withdrawal (saṃhāra) is its pericarp below.
In the pericarp is the principle of Śiva, the agent of the principles of persistence and manifestation;
they know this lotus of Kailāsa to be the source of these three principles and the rest. (3)
The two lips are the petals of the lotus; the teeth are known as the filaments;
the tongue is said to be the pericarp, and the body is called the stalk. || 4 ||
The deity who is the teacher of the world resides in the space within the mouth;
the tongue, with the uvula at its center, is the pedestal of Kailāsa.
Because he practices conduct himself,
shows others how to practice it, and gathers together the scriptures, he is therefore called an "ācārya" (teacher).
Though his body is soundless, he is the maker of sound; he is the bringer of an end to karma that has been performed.
He is the master weaver of the city of the triple world’s illusion—he who beholds him is the doer of all.
Having thus established the abode of the deities within the Lord of Gods, he,
out of a desire to bestow grace, makes the final [deity] the mouth by means of the final [mantra]. (8)
"O Goddess, O fair-faced one, I have thus described the favor of speech.
Thus ends the favor of speech. || 9 ||
The Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, that which is called Sūtra is a term denoting the path of light.
