O Blessed One, I desire to hear it; you should speak it.
They say that the Lord is the "Sūtra" because of his indication; the name Sūtra is a great state.
By him all this has been proclaimed, as bees [are gathered] in a string.
One should know that the unbroken space is all-pervasive, the undecaying state;
resembling a circle of light, one should manifest it within the small vessel [of the heart]. (12)
You ought to draw that which is situated in the center of the heart-lotus, peaceful in the midst of the moon, sun, and fire, supreme, subtle, and well-defined. 13.
The Goddess said:
"Since all the Gaṇas are established in the Nyāsa precisely because of that reality,
please graciously explain this marriage of their mantras."
The Lord said: All deities consist of mantra, and all mantras consist of Śiva.
One should worship in the sacrifice of Śiva with a mantra that consists of Śiva.
Without attaining the true nature of Śiva, even if they recite the Saṃhitā,
both the disciple and the teacher who perform initiation without understanding fall downwards. (16)
Therefore, one does not present oneself as a disciple to someone who shares the same residence;
nor does this favor toward both husbands proceed in such a manner. || 17 ||
The one Supreme Lord alone perceives; the relationship of disciple and teacher proceeds [only through His grace].
That physician who performs a treatment without himself having correctly understood it [is like one acting in ignorance]. (18)
The patient suffers pain, and even the physician may not achieve the result—even he who is skilled in theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom, and who has mastered every possible condition. (19)
He liberates [disciples] from sins, his own impurities having been shaken off by knowledge;
even if devoid of all auspicious marks, one who possesses knowledge is called a guru. (20)

The preceptor (deśika), who knows the procedure for initiation (dīkṣā) and the ritual rules, is the burner of the net of bonds; he is a devotee of Śiva, possessed of great devotion, and acts with a spirit of devotion. (21)
There is no difference between the two—the teacher and Śiva.
He alone is the *aṅkāra* and the *bindu*; he is the *nāda*, the partless (*niṣkala*) state of dissolution.
In him all sciences are present, and he indeed is the Supreme Śiva;
he is perfectly replete with all knowledge and is skilled in the meaning of all sciences.
Ananteśa and the other Śivas do not make any distinction whatsoever between the Teacher, the Mantra, and Śivajñānaśiva. (24)
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā, in the section concerning the lotus-face of the mouth that bestows grace through speech.
The Goddess said:
"O God, I wish to hear in truth about the infinite seat; what indeed would its end be, O Maheśvara? (1)
Those liberated from the ocean of worldly existence go to Śiva upon the dissolution of the body, [under the guidance of] the Lord.
That seat, which is the support for the principles (tattvas) and for space, arising from the power of will, is the seat known as Ananta. (3)
By me, everything from the primordial ether down to the earth was known there in its entirety;
[this is] the power of Śiva, the Supreme Self.
(335) Rich with the mud of the karma of illusion, in the great ocean of the year,
it has Sadāśiva as its support and is designated as the "eternal foundation" (nityādhāra). || 5 ||
And by means of Māyā, those thirty-two principles are established in the water;
the thirty-third is Avidyā... || 6 ||
O Lord, the thirty-fourth [chapter] concerns that which is situated in eight petals,
rich with the primordial root-mud, and born from the water of knowledge.
The worlds are situated upon the thorns of the arrangement of the stalks of the *prakriyā*; ten crores of mantras are established within the lotus of Śiva.
For this is the great essence of mantras, the supreme refuge of all deities;
indeed, the entire path and the lotus are dependent upon that which is called Śiva.
(336) Beyond the seat there is no further path, O fair-faced one;
because persons are infinite, the principles (tattvas) and so forth are likewise infinite. (10)
Because the *prakṛtis* are infinite, their powers (*śaktis*) are also infinite;
there is no finite enumeration of bound souls (*paśus*) or worlds (*bhuvanas*). (11)
The mantras possessing the power to bestow grace upon them are likewise infinite;
this cycle of existence is beginningless, for its end is not found.
Because it sustains all and because it is infinite, it is called "infinite" (ananta).
There is no measure for the lotus, for Śiva himself is infinite.
Because it is devoid of an end, it is infinite; therefore it is called "the Infinite.
By that Infinite, you, who are presided over by the Infinite, are made infinite. || 14 ||

Śiva, however, is to be known as infinite, immeasurable, and incomparable; he is celebrated in the *Svatantra* by means of the *kalās* as being beyond the cognitive reach of bound souls (*paśu*). (15)
Beyond that is the infinite, yet infinite Yoga-pīṭha for the Great Self; therein reside agency and lordship, eternal contentment, and perfect tranquility.
Because its power is unimpeded, this dharma taught by Śaṅkara is such that it is always true everywhere, and it possesses knowledge and omniscience at all times. (17)
And because it is the locus of all knowledge, this knowledge of the Lord is supreme;
he is detached from material states and is always free from desire.
There is lifelong celibacy and supreme detachment toward the Lord;
and there is that prosperity which consists of all the qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and others, yet remains unaffected by worldly influence.
The sovereignty of that supreme Śiva has never been tasted by others in this world;
neither His realm, nor His path, nor His form, nor even His speech can be grasped. (20)
There is neither sound nor even space, which is pure and situated everywhere;
the stainless, immaculate void is unobstructed on all sides. || 21 ||
It is devoid of qualities, beyond speech and mind, and free from planets and stars;
in some places it has the appearance of molten gold, and in others it resembles snow.
In some places it resembled a rainbow, in others it had a luster like stars;
in some places it was like the moon or its crescent, and in others it had the brilliance of emerald.
Stainless and free from defects is that splendor;
it is great radiance, pervasive, immeasurable, the lotus of all, and most brilliantly shining.
The sky is its stalk, the directions are its petals, and the space-points are its filaments;
it is sustained by the all-pervading and infinite powers of nectar. (25)
It was vast and uninterrupted, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
it was the pure light of the universe, a great splendor with infinite luster as its very nature.
Wondrous, subtle, both tranquil and untranquil, and incomparable—these infinite powers of Śiva are established as endowed with all attributes. (27)
Adorned eternally by these powers, He shines;
He is as radiant as a stainless thread embellished with pure ornaments. || 28 ||
But he [beheld] that lotus-petal, divine and wonderful to behold, exceedingly pure, tranquil yet radiant with light.
(340) It is like a mass of a thousand lightning flashes, crowded with many rays,
having the appearance of pure moonlight, and with throbbing filaments.
A mass of shimmering rays, variegated and upward-turned;
multicolored yet colorless, with trembling and beautiful filaments.
It was struck by the rays of the sun, possessing a luster like that of a vaidūrya gem,
resembling many beams of light, and having a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.

In some places it had the appearance of molten gold; in some places it resembled the dissolution of the world; in some places it was like a rainbow, and in some places its radiance was equal to the star Tārā.
Resembling crystal stone and possessing a luster like that of rubies,
it was in some places a dense mass of rays that overspread the vault of the sky.
In some places, with the grandeur of universal dissolution, possessing the brilliance of the rays at the end of an eon;
and in other places, as multitudes of colors and as forms completely liberated from physical bodies. (35)
Manifesting the splendor of his own power, pervading everywhere, resembling a bubble on the water, and possessing a radiance like the autumnal moon. (36)
It possesses the fragrance of fully blossomed rays, is swarming with the bees that are the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas),
has the continuum of the suṣumnā as its stalk, and ends in Śiva, who is like the fire of cosmic destruction.
Resembling a circle of lightning, it surrounded him on all sides;
it was a mass of a thousand rays, difficult to behold from any direction. (38)
The power of his action and knowledge is indeed constant;
having himself realized the limit of all phenomena, he acts according to his own will and mastery.

The power of will (*icchā-śakti*) is the supreme attribute (*dharma*) of Śiva, the Supreme Self. Endowed with that, He is called the "One whose nature is the Good Attribute" (*sudharmātmā*) by those who are truly virtuous. (40)
This property is said here to have a real cause when it resides in a permanent substratum;
a property does not attain established existence in the absence of a substratum. (41)
Desire, Impulsion, Oneness, Time, Destroyer of Time, as well as Non-existence, Existence, and Knowledge—these are proclaimed as the power of action (kriyā-śakti). || 42 ||
Mohanī, Rañjinī, Bodhā, Prabhāvā, Vibhunī, Rasā, Damanī, Dhāmanī, Bodhā, Mananī, Unmanī, and Śivā. (43)
Dhātrī, Jananī, Krodhā, Ālinī, Aparigrahā, Virajā, Vijayā, Saumyā, Māyā, Avidyā, and Rāgiṇī. || 44 ||
Unobstructed and unimpeded, ageless and unconquered;
unborn and contrary, she is the fashioner even of the subtle parts. || 45 ||
Bestower of strength and giver of power, subduer and giver of dharma;
she is the essential form, the form of all colors, and she who envelops with a net of nooses.
Pāśinī, Mohinī, Trāṇi, Nigrahā, Anugrahā, Mahī, Harṣiṇī, Bhāvā, Saumyā, and indeed Saumyadharmiṇī. || 47 ||
Existents proceed as having intrinsic nature; she is intense and peaceful, the bestower of accomplishment;
she is immeasurable and measurable, the means of valid cognition, and the conceptualizer.
She is the all-pervading one and the protector of all; she is fear and the remover of fear;
she is the creator and destroyer, consciousness, contentment, sleep, radiance, and hunger.
The burner, the sacred revelation, the intellect, wisdom, the future, and the discerning;
the one to be contemplated, the gentle, the constant, and the one who carries away the eternal. (50)
Anantā, Amṛtā, Īśvarī, Avyayā, as well as Rati, Prīti, and she who should be known as Viṣādajananī. || 51 ||
It is that which causes the stability and the decay of living beings, that which brings them forth, as well as that which possesses them, obstructs them, and likewise fashions their destinies.
Amṛtā, Anantaśakti, and likewise Parāśakti—all these powers are eternally stationed in the filaments (kesara). || 53 ||
The hosts of Śaktis, possessing the luster of pure gorocanā, should indeed be known as illuminating the ten directions as far as the pericarp and the pedestal. 54.
The bulb (kanda), shaped like a *paṭola* gourd and surrounded by powers (*śakti*s),
is the eternal Lord situated within the pericarp and constantly surrounded by powers. || 55 ||
Just as the rays of the sun are established as indivisible, so too all the hosts of powers are proclaimed to be like rays. || 56 ||
The Supreme Goddess always acts through her power within the heart-lotus;
all those powers that are satisfied by her splendor are proclaimed as "nirvṛta" (tranquil).
Having thus understood it to be of the nature of power (śakti), one is then liberated and liberates others;
like Indra, their blazing strength pervades all that is moving and unmoving.
And that is immovable, indescribable, infinite, without a core, without beginning, middle, or end, one, and beyond comprehension. (59)
It is free from conceptual proliferation, beyond the paths of time, transcendent of the senses, and free from ailment;
it is partless, stainless, the supreme conduct, loftily pervasive, and ultimate. (60)
Resembling gold and the sun, it illuminates all principles;
its function is luminosity, it should be known as pure, with the sky as its pericarp.
Thus, having pervaded the supreme deity from Ananta up to Diśiva—
thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter in the section on the Power of Ananta within the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, tell me of the form [to be worshipped] upon such an auspicious seat, surrounded by the Śaktis, and of the presiding lord of the seat.
(347) I have previously explained that Īśvara is the form [of the Lord] for Brahmā and the others, who were formerly possessed of intellects.
And likewise the sages, as well as others such as Durvāsas and so forth, and yet others.
The self (ātman) should be known as the form, inactive and lacking independence;
O beautiful goddess, its union with the mantra is performed. (3)
The mantra is said to be fivefold by which it becomes "sakala" (with parts);
joined with [other] mantras, it is "mantrātman" (the essence of mantra), and joined with phonemes, it is "sadātmaka" (of the nature of existence). || 4 ||
But when he is joined with the *kalās*, then he is said to be composed of *kalās*;
likewise, he is composed of the distinctions of the *padas* and the distinctions of the *tattvas*. (5)

The "Paśu" was previously described by me; that is proclaimed to be the [individual] form (mūrti). Because its instrument (karaṇa) consists of the eternal reality (sat), it is therefore called Sadāśiva. (6)
Because he is eternally constant and inconceivable, he is called Sadāśiva;
having attained that ever-peaceful state, he follows after that very state.
He is the perfect, auspicious, and peaceful Guru, worshipped by the thirty gods;
he is the support of all worlds, situated within the seat of the sky.
Situated in the midst of the filaments of power, adorned with the ornament of power, perfectly filled with all powers, and the illuminator of all powers. || 9 ||
Just as the sun, having dispelled the darkness of night by means of its own radiant rays,
remains in the sky, so too does the form abide within the supreme Śiva.
It shines forth entirely with its own radiance, as if arisen divided by those very rays;
it appears motionless yet blazing, eternal and yet non-eternal, and stainless. (11)
It is profoundly peaceful, stainless, pure, all-pervading, and utterly immaculate;
it eclipses the splendor of ten million suns and possesses a radiance that shines forth eternally.
Because of its pervasiveness, no measure of it is taught;
because it is beginningless, it has no origin; and because it is eternal, it has no end. (13)
Devoid of qualities, all-knowing, the agent, independent, facing in all directions, completely full, imperishable, tranquil, subtle, unborn, supreme, and bodiless. || 14 ||
The eternally awakened, pure self, the cause, possessed of immeasurable form;
infinite, indeed without end, eternally satisfied, and without support. || 15 ||
The immutable source, the Lord, the protectorless one of immeasurable splendor,
the beginningless, the unique, the one who is to be restrained, the conscious one who dwells in all hearts— Śiva. (16)
The doer of all, the knower of all, the lord of all, possessing all power, unborn and imperishable;
he is the one who causes all to act and the non-agent himself—by him all this is pervaded.
The ultimate of all, the supreme of all, devoid of all defects, transcending the state of all principles, unborn, the Lord, and imperishable. || 18 ||
It is perfectly eternal, perfectly complete, perfect nirvāṇa, and most beautiful; it is liberated from all obscurations, the one wonder, and the ancient. || 19 ||
All-pervading, omniscient, and situated above all; omnipresent and transcending the omnipresent, he is the source of all forms and the entirety of the impurity.
This very Rudra, the Great God, is the embodiment of mantras within all forms;
through the division of the supreme and the non-supreme, he is like the imperishable one whose form is the universe. (21)
He is of infinite form and infinite; he is the infinite and indeed the infinite itself.
He possesses infinite power, an infinite self, infinite senses, and infinite faces.
He transcends all abodes; that state is beyond the senses.
This entire world, guided by speech, is of the nature of that [Reality]. 23.
Reality beyond reality is indeed reality; that reality beyond reality is the ultimate truth.
It is considered inconceivable, all-pervasive, most subtle, and beyond the reach of vision.
Ananta is the union of all forms; he is proclaimed as the "possessor of parts" (sakala).
This Ananta has been described to you—he whose end is not known.
But because he does not know the supreme Ananta-vidhi regarding the Lord of Gods,
he performs the Śiva-sacrifice and does not liberate the bound soul (paśu). (26)
The grace [bestowed] by me through the eye and the application of the *bindu* has been described;
the touch resulting from the union with the Hand of Śiva is proclaimed to be everywhere present. (27)
Listen, O Goddess, as I describe how one should act with water;
this procedure is declared to be common to all the Saṃhitās. (28)
The five Brahmās and the limbs of Śiva, conjoined with Śiva himself—these are the deities of the nyāsa therein, which is proclaimed as the path. (29)
All these should be performed everywhere, especially over water;
they are not [performed] by means of a sacrifice, nor by one who knows the ritual rules, nor by one skilled in the path.
The supreme rite should be performed by means of the three principles and the deity-principle:
grasping, joining, lifting up, and the application thereof by one who knows that. (31)
He who knows the reality of all things— their conjunction, their dissolution, and even their final liberation— and who possesses all knowledge, is indeed fit for the sacrificial rite of Śiva.
He who understands primordial nature (prakṛti) together with its transformations (vikāra), being wise and knowing both the container and the contained, is indeed fit for the sacrifice of Śiva.
The high-minded Ācārya, together with the Sādhaka, is always worthy of worship;
he is the Guru of the lords of Sādhakas, while all others merely bear his name.
Thus, the preceptor who knows the rules and procedures, who has mastered the tantras, and who initiates all living beings—he is indeed the leader to the supreme state. (35)
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Arrangement of the Form," in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said: O Maheśvara, tell me of the worship of the Omniscient One and his ritual injunctions;
at what time, O Blessed One, should one offer the *arghya* to the Supreme Śiva?
O Lord of the Gods, tell me how one may perform worship so that one proceeds to that [state] together with others and oneself in a single place.
O Goddess, listen to the supreme secret worship that fulfills all desires; by performing this sacrifice, the sacrificer becomes the sovereign of all worlds. (3)
Likewise, O Goddess, the power Vāmā is proclaimed to be on the left limb;
she is to be known through the eye of knowledge as the sovereign of the ancestors. (4)
Furthermore, Jyeṣṭhā, the presiding deity of the gods, is in the right limb;
one should always know that Raudrī, the yoga-deity of yogins, is in the middle.
The Vāmā energy resides in the iḍā on the left side of all embodied beings;
furthermore, the Jyeṣṭhā energy is in the suṣumnā, while the Raudrī energy is supported by the piṅgalā.
These powers have been described as resting upon the three phonemes (varṇa), joined with the three channels (nāḍī), and associated with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa. || 7 ||
The Lord Rudra resides in Piṅgalā, Brahmā in Suṣumnā, and Upendra indeed in Iḍā; they are established in all ritual activities.
When the deity is situated in the left position, one should perform the ritual bath there;
however, the knower of mantras should perform the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) and recite [the mantra] for the sake of the cause in the right. (9)
One should always practice meditation established in the Middle Country;
having eradicated [obstacles] and caused [the teaching] to spread, one shall become present in all states in an instant. || 10 ||
Having formed a handful filled with flowers and placed it at the mouth, one should offer that full añjali with either mental or physical water. 11.
One should recite the mantra according to the path established by one's own tradition as long as the sound persists;
until the sound dissolves, this is declared here to be the "time of merit."
One should contemplate that which is free from conceptual construction, having become stainless within the state beyond reality;
one should abide in that very state and thus becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
Having thus caused [the breath] to pervade, one should enter again by means of inhalation (pūraka).
When the self is awakened, it becomes awakened; otherwise, it does not. (14)
One should bring about auspiciousness everywhere and likewise accomplish that which is above; having performed all rites with Śiva, the remover of inauspiciousness, one should worship him. 15.
The Goddess said:
O Maheśvara, I wish to hear about the knowledge of the Siddhānta, that which is to be known, and its defining characteristics; please deign to speak of them out of your grace. (16)
The Lord, for the sake of that knowledge, has remembered the Vedas and thousands of philosophical systems;
for this reason, O Goddess, it is called "that which is to be known" (jñeya). || 17 ||
For the sake of establishing both the object of knowledge and the means of knowledge, the scripture establishes a proof in the form of a positive injunction;
therefore, that is remembered as the *siddhānta* (established conclusion). (18)
It has been said that perception is the characteristic; the characteristic is remembered with respect to the object to be characterized.
Because of the thorough knowledge of the object to be characterized, the characteristic is thereby correctly remembered. (19)
Devoid of meditative absorption and mental retention, and abandoned at the commencement of yoga,
that consciousness which perceives it cannot be known at all.
The conceptualization previously mentioned does not exist as a conceptualization due to its prior ascertainment;
he who is not deluded regarding its existence is wise and possesses self-knowledge. || 21 ||
He who possesses effort is established as this omniscient one;
yet the embodied soul, deluded by Māyā, perceives him through the notion of existence. 22.
Just as there is nothing permanent, so have I explained it to you:
that is imperishable, that is the immortal, that is the truth, that is the eternal. (23)
Even one who dwells in such a state is all-knowing through yoga;
yet the master of illusion is bound by illusion and enveloped by the noose of hope.
"Released from the snares of hope, he attends upon the nectar.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Knowledge and the Knowable," in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
In which [parts] of this body, composed of the five elements, do which deities reside?
And in the feet, the knees, the shanks, and the pair of thighs, who are stationed? (1)
And on the *liṅga*, O Lord of the Gods of gods, the two buttocks (*sphijau*) are situated at the hips (*kaṭike*);
likewise, [the other parts] are located at the sides of the region of the navel and along the spinal column (*pṛṣṭhavaṃśe*). || 2 ||
O Lord of Gods, in the intestines, the marrow, the blood, the phlegm, and the bile;
in the pores of the skin, and where else are they said to be? [The hands and feet... 3.
And likewise on the chin, the two eyes, the forehead, and the head. || 4 ||
O Lord of Gods, where do the channels of speech reside within the ego? And who, O God, presides over the senses, and what fruit arises from their being known? (5)
"O Lord of the gods of gods, you should deign to tell this to me out of your grace.
Īśvara said: (p. 361)
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret which you have asked about.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, I shall explain it for your pleasure;
beginning with the quality of goodness (sattva), I will speak—listen attentively.
Sattva is said to be Pradhāna, and he is called Brahmā; Rajas is Viṣṇu and Tamas is Rudra; now hear of the intellect with its eight qualities.
Knowledge of dharma, dispassion, and likewise supreme sovereignty;
as well as non-dharma and ignorance—these indeed are to be understood. (9)

Lack of dispassion and lack of mastery belong respectively to the lords of yoga; the qualities such as dharma belong to the deities beginning with Brahmā, while those beginning with power belong to the deities beginning with Śakra.
Rudra resides in the ego (ahaṅkāra); sound is established in the void (śūnya).
Wind is declared to be in touch (sparśa), and fire is proclaimed to be in form (rūpa). (11)
Varuṇa is established in that subtle element (tanmātra), while Earth resides in smell;
Prajāpati is indeed in Earth, and Soma is established in the liquid.
The sun, however, is established in fire; the wind is established in touch;
and the supreme, secret Śiva-tattva is firmly established in space. || 13 ||
O Great Goddess, all the directions are established in the sense organ of hearing;
the Maruts are in the sense organ of touch, and the Fire-eater (Agni) resides in the two eyes.
O Goddess, Sarasvatī, the power of the earth, is always present in the organ of speech;
knowledge resides in the organ of smell, and Viṣṇu himself indeed dwells in the two feet.
That which is designated as the power of action (kriyā-śakti) comprises both Mitra and Vāyu;
Jyeṣṭhā and Prajāpati are in the liṅga, while Vāmā and Raudrī are in the speech. (16)
Jalendu is to be known in the mind; Savitrī resides in the heart;
Gaurī Vāgīśvarī is in the ear; and Vimalā is indeed on the forehead. (17)
Ananta resides in the group of sinews; the subtle one is established in the semen;
the god Śivottamottama is always situated in the collection of bones.
Ekanetra resides in the flesh, and likewise Ekarudra in another; Trimūrti is eternally situated in the blood, as well as in phlegm and bile.
Śrīkaṇṭha is ever present in the mass of body hair,
and Śikhaṇḍin, the supreme Rudra, is situated everywhere within the nails.
Maheśa resides in that body, and the Ṛṣis reside in the joints;
Caṇḍīśa is situated in the spinal column and in the sides. (21)
The Nāgas reside in the fingers, the ancestors reside in the arms, and Agni himself resides in the navel of all embodied beings. 22.
Likewise, the Vidyādharas and Yakṣas reside in the pores of the skin;
Indu and Devatya are in the two hands, and the Aśvins are in the knees and shanks.
The two gods renowned as Mitra and Varuṇa are stationed upon the pair of thighs;
others are stationed in the eyes, in the two nostrils, in the neck, and in the chin.
The seven houses, along with their presiding deities, and the divine circle of the lunar mansions—whom do they not follow as they abide? (25)
Thus, indeed, he who understands that the body is presided over by all the gods and is born from all [elements], his knowledge is not defiled by sin. (26)
O Goddess, he who practices this supreme nyāsa day after day attains prosperity, O Goddess, and becomes equal to the Lord.
There is neither sin nor merit, and no fear shall arise amidst fears;
one is liberated even from terrible sins committed throughout seven lifetimes. (28)
This new method has been taught by me; therefore, those who desire liberation among yogins should practice it with effort, for by it they shall abide in the nectar of immortality. (29)
"He who is the supreme deity of all, the all-pervading one, is established [therein].
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Ritual Disposition of the Bodies of All Deities," in the Jñānakāṇḍa of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, you have stated in the teaching of Śiva that the Self is the form;
that which was previously called the bound soul (paśu) is likewise to be known as the God. (1)
O Nameśvara, you have previously described both the conscious principle (cetanā) and the individual soul (jīva);
that [soul] is indeed like a beast, devoid of action, lacking independence, and facing downward.
How do the objects of knowledge, beginning with Name and so forth, gradually attain the state of Śiva?
O Blessed One, I wish to understand this; you ought to explain it.
The Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, to that supreme secret which you have asked about;
I shall explain it fully for your pleasure, O lady of beautiful countenance.
(367) I shall explain this procedure, which is common to all the *saṃhitās*, in brief and according to the sequence for each one; of this there is no doubt.
The mental worship is to be known as sixfold, while power (śakti) is remembered as ninefold; this is called the "infinite worship" (anantapūjā), endowed with emission (visarga).
Having thus worshipped Ananta, one should place liberation (mukti) right there;
joined with the syllables *hāṃ* and *hūṃ*, it is the eighth of the eightfold division.
O Goddess of gods, the arrangement of the forms is proclaimed in this tantra,
as well as how the grasping [of the disciple] occurs according to the application at the time of initiation.
In that manner, I shall explain to you how and by what means their grasping occurs,
as well as the conjunction with infinite forms described through these seed-syllables (bījas).
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) with such effort, one should then perform the ritual of complete identification (sakalīkaraṇa).
Both that which transcends mantra and the mantra itself have been previously explained by me. (10)
Having known that entire deity, both with parts (sakala) and likewise without parts (niṣkala),
[one should worship] in the head, the two faces, the heart, and the secret place, respectively.
O Goddess of the gods, one should place Sadyojāta upon the forms;
O Queen of the gods, for the knower of the rule (samaya), this sakalīkaraṇa is beneficial.
I shall describe his worship; listen as I speak of it.
Upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should place a Śiva-liṅga, performing purification by sprinkling and other rites.
O Goddess of the gods, one likewise offers the substance into the fire and to Śiva,
performing the entire rite in its entirety with the five Brahmans.
One should place Īśāna in the center; one should install Tatpuruṣa in the east, Aghora in the south, and likewise Vāmadeva in the north. (15)
One should always place Sadyojāta in the west on a well-prepared site;
whoever, being well-composed, performs worship according to this rite, [attains success]. || 16 ||
I have described to you the conjunction for attaining the Lord at the proper time;
through the union with the five Brahmans and by means of the Kalās, he is well-enveloped.
O son, I have explained to you that which is joined with the ancillaries of knowledge (vidyāṅga);
the invocation and other rites of the deity have been told to you as before. (18)
The instructor should explain that it is joined with the door and the enclosure;
having thus performed the ritual integration (sakalīkaraṇa), worship is to be performed at the time of twilight.
"O beautiful goddess, that which must be performed by the son has been told;
by this rite, O Goddess, the son shall become perfectly concentrated. (20)
He undoubtedly attains the state of proximity to the one called Sāda,
being endowed with those very limbs of Śiva previously mentioned.
Through the conjunction of the inhalation and retention of breath, by those skilled in the yoga of meditation,
one attains union with the Self of the Great Soul known as Sādākhya.

O beautiful goddess, one who is well-composed should worship [him] as endowed with the four veils by means of mantras through the application of the instruments; such a person is a bound soul (paśu). 23.
He would indeed become identical with the mantra, and that [individual] would be a bound soul (paśu); of this there is no doubt.
One who is without mantra is called a bound soul; he enters only into consciousness. (24)
(371) He who possesses consciousness is declared by the Tantras to be a fettered soul (paśu); he who knows nothing is declared a beast.
O Supreme Goddess, one who is always endowed with mantras is possessed of consciousness. 25.
Then one becomes fit for meditation on Śiva; there is no doubt about this.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, how is the body of a bound soul (paśu) understood to consist of mantra?
I desire to know this, O Blessed One; you should speak of it.
Listen to the prowess of that Lord whose body is bound by mantras. (27)
It shall raise up the Nāgas from Pātāla, cast down the Daityas and Rākṣasas, destroy all obstacles, and bestow peace and nourishment. || 28 ||
The leaders flee from one whose body is bound by mantras;
likewise, they rise up during invisibility and during movement on foot. (29)
In the case of the sword and the sandals, as well as in evacuation and worship,
in the pill, in traveling through the sky, and in the staff and the sacred grass ring (pavitraka).
The seat and the vehicle are accomplished by all mantras;
however, O Goddess, when the conscious self is absent, nothing at all is accomplished. (31)
O Goddess, being shrouded by ignorance, he is afflicted by the elemental spirits (bhūtas).
O lady of virtuous conduct, I have thus described to you his nature as mantra and his nature as consciousness.
And the secret has been told: there is a distinction between both [bindu and nāda]. When, through the union of bindu and nāda, the phoneme resounds, [that is the secret]. (33)
That [Śiva], which is the supreme cause, is declared to be of the nature of mantra;
when Śiva is rendered "with parts" (sakala), he is endowed with the portions of the five Brahmans. (34)
In that [arrangement], the Lord, the Supreme Ruler whose essence is mantra, shines forth;
for Śiva, the ultimate cause, resides within this array of phonemes (varṇavyūha). || 35 ||
Therefore, O Goddess, the Supreme Lord, whose essence is mantra, has been fully described;
he is known as the Praṇava, joined with fear, and is remembered as Vyomavyāpin (the Pervader of Space). || 36 ||
O fair-faced one, the Supreme Lord, whose nature is Dharma, is conjoined with the *pada-mantras*,
beginning from Ananteśa and ending with Śikhaṇḍin.
He alone, the Supreme Lord whose essence is mantra, is eternally established as the guardians of the world together with their weapons, and as the three worlds with all things moving and unmoving.
The god Śiva, the supreme cause, abides as the essence of mantra.
Thus, O virtuous goddess, the nature of mantra has been explained to you. (39)
This must be known by the teacher himself who follows the Śiva-tantras:
the Bindu, the Nāda, the Śakti, and that which transcends them and is even beyond. (40)
When, by virtue of the nature of consciousness, he is beyond the mantras; that Supreme Lord is indeed transcendent, beyond sound, form, taste, and the rest. || 41 ||
Having realized this thread, O Goddess, the teacher becomes the destroyer of bonds;
that which transcends Nāda, the supreme peace, is designated as Śakti.
Beyond that, O Goddess, is the one who has transcended mantra; he is called "Transcender of Mantra" (mantrātīta).
One should first utter the phonemes and then cause them to dissolve into sound.
Furthermore, sound absorbed in sound should lead one beyond sound;
that which is beyond it, O Goddess, is called the supreme, transcending all mantra. (44)
This definitive explanation of the *kārikā* has been told to you, O Goddess;
it was previously stated and explained for you, O lady of virtuous conduct. (45)
The Goddess said:
"O Maheśvara, you have explained in the primordial sūtra, O Lord, that after worshipping the manifest (sakala), one should thereafter worship the unmanifest (niṣkala)."
The animal is said to be "with parts" (sakala) and is proclaimed to be the embodied form (mūrti);
how, then, can the Supreme Lord, who is "without parts" (niṣkala), be worshipped within it? (47)
The partless [Śiva] transcends all divisions; he is beyond the reach of mantra and phonemes.
How, then, can the supreme Śiva abide within a body possessed of parts? (48)
The Lord, having first placed Maheśvara within his heart, should utter the mantra;
when he is dissolved into the supreme sound of the *kūṭa*, he is indeed called the partless (*niṣkala*). || 49 ||
O Goddess, when through recitation one attains the state free from conceptual construction;
O Maheśvarī, when that is known within the body through the yoga of all its parts.
Transcending the parts, he indeed is called "partless" (niṣkala);
for when it is devoid of utterance, it enters the state beyond conceptual construction (nirvikalpa). || 51 ||
That which is conceived by the mind and wherein there is conceptualization by the intellect—when it is free from both intellect and ego, that indeed is called the partless (niṣkala). || 52 ||
Whether one is a *samayin*, a *putraka*, a *sādhaka*, or even an *ācārya*, the entire ritual procedure must be performed by all; I have explained the specific distinctions. (53)
Thus ends the forty-second chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear the unsurpassed procedure for initiation."
Everything has been told in brief; tell it to me in detail.
Just as the connection with the seizing of the sacrificial animal occurs at the time of initiation,
so too should you explain how the sacrifice is performed within this initiation.
Īśvara said: (p.
378) Hereafter, I shall proclaim the unsurpassed ritual procedure for initiation.
Or rather, I shall declare the entirety of what is common to all the Tantras.
O Goddess, this mantra of yours has been proclaimed for the sake of purification during the sacrifice, wherein the five Brahmās, who are the limbs of Śiva, are united with Śiva himself.
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī are proclaimed as the three Śaktis;
they must be understood by the lord of teachers through their separation, casting, and conjunction.
The practitioner of mantras should join [the soul] with Vāmā and separate it with Jyeṣṭhā;
the elevation [of the soul] is said to be performed with Raudrī, and one should join it again elsewhere.
Having begun from the earth up to the stainless Tattva,
one who understands this ritual once becomes purified by means of the *vyūha-homa*.
O Goddess, the most excellent of teachers should offer each oblation one by one;
he should perform the rite in this very manner until everything is completed. (8)
One should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) at the end; this indeed is remembered as the prescribed rule.
One should perform the striking with the topknot (śikhā) using the mudrā joined with a flower.
The sacrificial animal (paśu) should be seized with the *saṃhāra-mudrā* by means of the sound *haṃ huṃ*;
then, one should sever its bonds (*pāśas*) through Śiva by means of the sequence of the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation.
The teacher should understand this very sequence;
then, upon the completion of all the paths, he should perform the severing of the crest-lock (śikhoccheda).

The mantra-practitioner should cut off the crest-lock; having cut it, he should again offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), severing the various fetters (pāśas) in each respective principle (tattva) according to the proper sequence.
The bonds, both subtle and gross, which exist like the coils of a conch shell—
those thousands of millions of bonds were indeed described by Śiva. (13)
"Having reached the mouth of Śiva, the bonds are burned; there is no doubt about this.
The Goddess said: "O Mahādeva, O Lord, it has been stated that the bonds are innumerable. (14)
And since they are exceedingly profound, how can they be consumed in the sacrifice to Śiva? [The Lord said:
"Ishvara, Prakṛti, Puruṣa, Niyati, and Kāla—[these are the elements]. (15)
Māyā, avidyā, Īśa, Sadāśiva, and likewise Śiva—these, O fair-faced one, are remembered as the root bonds; indeed, these are the nine bonds.
By these staff-mantras, O Goddess, these fifty crores of nooses have been burnt; the fifty *praṇavas* were previously proclaimed by me. (17)
"O Goddess, these fifty crores of bonds are purified by those pure [mantras], just as the path is purified by the thirty-eight kalās. (18)
By those pure [energies], these fifty crores of pure bonds are purified:
namely, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, and likewise the power of Vidyā.
When the resonance (dhvāna) is purified by these, the fifty crores [of syllables] become pure;
that which is the digit named Amṛtā is likewise both immortal and mortal.
And just as it is proclaimed, O Goddess, that she is both extremely subtle and subtle;
by these [means], one should purify the path through the previously observed ritual action.
By means of these pure [mantras], these fifty million bonds (pāśas) become pure;
they are to be purified through the application of words and mantras in the sacrifice of Śiva. (22)
By these, when purified, these fifty million bonds are purified;
and thus, O Goddess, the path is proclaimed to be sevenfold.
It should be understood with diligent effort by those who follow the Śiva-tantras:
the path of the worlds has been described by me according to the number of oblations. (24)
By means of those very digits (kalās), O Goddess, the entire path is to be known in its entirety;
when, through you, O Goddess, one becomes the most excellent of teachers (deśikottama), the path is realized. (25)
One hundred oblations should be offered for each [tattva]; this is remembered as the procedure for the purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi).
O Goddess, it is exactly the same for the nine principles; of this there is no doubt. (26)
In the same way here, within the principle of *kalā*, there is indeed a second triad;
by means of one hundred and fifty oblations, the path of the phonemes (*varṇādhvan*) is proclaimed. (27)
In the path of reality (tattvādhvan), the path of limited powers (kalādhvan), and likewise in the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan),
one should not perform here either the upward projection (ukṣepa) or the conjunction (yojana) by means of these [methods].
Likewise, on the path of the feet here, one hundred oblations must be offered;
in this way, O Supreme Goddess, the path is purified sevenfold.
Having understood this, the supreme preceptor should then perform the initiation.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, you have indicated the entire path, but not described it in detail. (30)
Therefore, I wish to hear this; speak it to me in detail,
O Lord.
In the initial sūtra, that which was spoken by way of a mere sūtra regarding the time periods; || 31 ||
I shall explain that very thing in detail; understand it from me.
I will proclaim the path of the body (dehādhvan); listen as I speak of it. 32.
The Lord Ananta, the Supreme Sovereign, resides upon the tip of the big toe;
he has four faces, possesses great splendor, and resembles the rising sun. (33)
One should visualize the infinite Lord of the World (Bhuvaneśāna) seated below the yogin, who is surrounded by the Vidyās and the Vidyēśvaras.

Oṃ, O Ananta, come, come; accept this oblation; Śiva gives it to you, svāhā! One should offer the oblation with "Oṃ, to Sadyojāta. In this sequence, one should perform the sacrifice consisting of eleven parts.
In authority, as well as in enjoyment or dissolution, it proceeds in due order.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should withdraw [the elements] in due order;
likewise for Kālāgnirudra and in the hells.
Oṃ, Kālāgnirudra, come; accept this oblation; Śiva gives it to you, svāhā!

Oṃ, obeisance to Avīci. Oṃ, obeisance to Raurava. Oṃ, obeisance to Mahāraurava. Oṃ, obeisance to Tāmisra. Oṃ, obeisance to Andhatāmisra. Oṃ, obeisance to Śīta. Oṃ, obeisance to Uṣṇa. Oṃ, obeisance to Sañjīva. Oṃ, obeisance to Sujīvana. Oṃ, obeisance to Padma. Oṃ...
Homage to Mahāpadma. (p. 386) Oṃ, homage to Kāpa the Thread. Oṃ, homage to Sūcīmukha. Oṃ, homage to Kṣuradhāra. Oṃ, homage to Parvata. Oṃ.

Salutation to Sitālavana. Oṃ, salutation to Raudra. Oṃ, salutation to Kumbhīpāka. Oṃ, salutation to Ambarīṣa. Oṃ, salutation to Aṅgārarāśi. Oṃ, salutation to Bhuvana. Oṃ, salutation to Tīkṣṇatuṇḍa. Oṃ, salutation to Vajratuṇḍa. Oṃ, salutation to Śakuni. Oṃ, salutation to Mīnodara. Oṃ, salutation to Kharodara. Oṃ, salutation to Sandaṃśa. Oṃ, salutation to Kākatuṇḍa. Oṃ, salutation to Vānarānana.
Salutation! Oṃ, salutation to Ugrīva. The Hymn of Eightfold Splendor (*Tejoṣṭaka*). Oṃ, salutation to Lokākṣādhyakṣa. Oṃ, salutation to Gaṇādhyakṣa. Oṃ, salutation to Tridaśa.
Oṃ, salutation to Tripurāntaka. Oṃ, salutation to Sarvarūpa. Oṃ, salutation to Śānta. Oṃ, salutation to Unmeṣa. Oṃ, salutation to Unmeṣa. (p. 387)
The eightfold fire-oblation (tejoṣṭaka) should be offered by the preceptors who are well-composed;
after this, the unsurpassed eighth yoga is fully described.
Oṃ, salutation to Kṛta.
In this very sequence, one should again offer the eight yogas.
Above these, however, the twelve Suśivas are traditionally taught. (38)

Oṃ Vāma, homage! Oṃ Bhīma, homage! Oṃ Ugra, homage! Oṃ Bhava, homage! Oṃ Śarva, homage! Oṃ Vidyādhipa, homage! Oṃ Ekavīra, homage! Oṃ Pracaṇḍa, homage! Oṃ Īśvara, homage! Oṃ Ojas, homage! Oṃ Ananta, homage! Oṃ Ekaśiva, homage!
These are proclaimed as the Suśivas; they are to be purified in the Śiva-sacrifice.
From this point upward, Vīrabhadra is the lord and master of the maṇḍala.
Oṃ, homage to the Lord of the Maṇḍala!
Beyond this, Mahādeva [manifested] as Vāmadeva and Bhavodbhava.

Oṃ Vāmadeva, obeisance! Oṃ Bhavodbhava, obeisance! Oṃ Ekapiṅgekṣaṇa, obeisance! Oṃ Īśāna, obeisance! Oṃ Aṅguṣṭhamātra, obeisance! These are remembered as the eight Mahādevas. Above these are two rows of gurus: Oṃ Śivānanta, obeisance! Ananta, obeisance! Oṃ Prabhu, obeisance! Oṃ Vāmana, obeisance! Oṃ Caṇḍa, obeisance! Oṃ Pratāpa, obeisance! Oṃ Vratārti, obeisance! Oṃ Śiva, obeisance! Oṃ...

Salutation to Kapālin. Oṃ, salutation to Bhīma. Salutation to Oṅkārāli. Oṃ, salutation to Piṅgala. Oṃ, salutation to Mahendra. Oṃ, salutation to Dinakṛt. Oṃ, salutation to Pratoda. Oṃ, salutation to Dakṣa. Oṃ, salutation to Kṣemīśa. Oṃ, salutation to Kabaleśa. Oṃ, salutation to Kaṭaṅkaṭa. (p. 389)

Homage! Oṃ, homage to Buhantāna. Homage to Omanādara. Oṃ, homage to Śveta. Oṃ, homage to Yajurveda. Oṃ, homage to Sāmaveda. Oṃ, homage to Ṛgveda. Oṃ, homage to Atharvaveda. Oṃ, homage to Ācārya. Oṃ, homage to Śiva. Oṃ, homage to Virūpākṣa. Oṃ, homage to Nārāyaṇa. Oṃ, homage to Vibucaṇḍodara. Oṃ, homage to Saṃvarta. Oṃ, homage to Yamamālī. Oṃ, homage to Gahaneśa. Oṃ, homage to Pīḍa.
Homage!
The *paṅkti* meter is desired as the broadness. Oṃ, homage to Śveta! Oṃ, homage to Dāru! Oṃ, homage to Lokākṣi!

Oṃ, salutation to Sūtra. Oṃ, salutation to Suhotra. Oṃ, salutation to Ekapāda. Oṃ, salutation to Grantheśvara. Oṃ, salutation to Gautama. Oṃ, salutation to Jaimini. Oṃ, salutation to Dadhivāha. Oṃ, salutation to Ṛṣabha. Oṃ, salutation to Gokarṇa. Oṃ, salutation to Guheśvara. Oṃ, salutation to Guhavāsin. Oṃ.
Salutation to Śikhaṇḍin. Oṃ, salutation to Jhaṭimālin. Oṃ, salutation to Ugra. Oṃ, salutation to Śikhin. Oṃ, salutation to Śūlī. Oṃ, salutation to Sugati.

Oṃ, salutation to Supāla. Oṃ, salutation to Aṭṭahāsa. Oṃ, salutation to Dāruka. Oṃ, salutation to Ṣāḍhī. Oṃ, salutation to Tridaṇḍī. Oṃ, salutation to Bhāva. Oṃ, salutation to Bhāvya. Oṃ, salutation to Lakulīśa. This is intended as the second row. Oṃ, salutation to Devāvaraṇa. Oṃ...
Homage to Dīrghabāhu! Homage to Aṃśumat!
Oṃ amṛte, obeisance! Oṃ bhṛte, obeisance! Oṃ sthāṇave, obeisance! Oṃ sadyojātāya, obeisance! Oṃ bhuvane, obeisance! Oṃ caṇḍe, obeisance!

Oṃ ṣaṇmukhāya, obeisance! Oṃ caturānanāya, obeisance! Oṃ cakrapāṇaye, obeisance! Oṃ kūrmākṣāya, obeisance! Oṃ ardhanārīśvarāya, obeisance! Oṃ meṣasaṃvartakāya, obeisance! Oṃ bhasmeśāya, obeisance! Oṃ kāmanāśanāya, obeisance! Oṃ kapālīśāya, obeisance! Oṃ...
"Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, obeisance! Oṃ Vaṣaṭkāra, obeisance! This third row has been described as that which is to be purified in the auspicious sacrifice.
Now, hereafter, regarding the emanation of the principles (tattvas), it must be understood by the preceptor."
Starting from the earth element and extending up to the Pradhāna, whatever principles (tattvas) exist within this interval must be purified by the wise. 41.
(392) Thus, O beautiful one, the principle of Prakṛti has been explained to you;
all those situated below it are to be purified in the sacrifice of Śiva. 42.
He remained stationed, completely surrounding him by means of his own limbs;
he was situated above Prakṛti, perceiving the creation of all beings. || 43 ||
The wise should purify the subtle elements, beginning with the atom (aṇiman) and ending with the great (tāra). || 43½ ||

Oṃ Ambhaṇamaḥ | Oṃ Salilaṇamaḥ | Oṃ Oghaṇamaḥ | Oṃ Vṛṣṭiṇamaḥ | Oṃ Tāraṇamaḥ | Oṃ Supāraṇamaḥ | Oṃ Sunetraṇamaḥ | Oṃ Sumāriṇamaḥ | Oṃ Uttamābhāṇamaḥ | These are the desired ones to be purified. Oṃ Tārāṇamaḥ | Oṃ Sutārāṇamaḥ | Oṃ Tārāyatanamaḥ.

Oṃ pramoda, homage! Oṃ pramudita, homage! Oṃ modamāna, homage! Oṃ radyaka, homage! Oṃ sadāpramudita, homage! Oṃ siddhi, homage! Oṃ tāra, homage! Oṃ suvāra, homage! Oṃ sunetra, homage! Oṃ sumāni, homage! Oṃ uttamābhā, homage!
The Tuṣṭis are to be purified: Oṃ Tārā, obeisance; Oṃ Sutārā, obeisance; Oṃ Supāra, obeisance; Oṃ Sunetra, obeisance; Oṃ Sumāri, obeisance; Oṃ Uttamābhā, obeisance.
The Tuṣṭis are to be purified by the preceptors who are well-composed. || 44 ||
Oṃ, homage to aṇimā! Oṃ, homage to laghimā! Oṃ, homage to prāpti! Oṃ, homage to prākāmya! Oṃ, homage to vaśitva! Oṃ, homage to īśitva! (p. 394)
Oṃ, obeisance to the power of fulfilling all desires.
The supernatural powers, such as *aṇimā* and the rest, are to be purified by those seeking liberation.
Beyond this, O Goddess, that which is situated is known as the eightfold knowledge of the channels (*nāḍī-vidyā-aṣṭaka*).
Oṃ oṃkāra, obeisance! Oṃ caṇḍī, obeisance! Oṃ gaurī, obeisance! Oṃ śāntikā, obeisance! Oṃ mālā, obeisance! Oṃ malī, obeisance!
Oṃ svāhā, obeisance! Oṃ svadhā, obeisance!
From Rāga to Vidyeśa, these [deities] should always be purified by the wise.
Beyond this is the group of eight forms (vigrahāṣṭaka), which abides in both restraint and grace.

Oṃ, homage to the effect! Oṃ, homage to the cause! Oṃ, homage to happiness! Oṃ, homage to suffering! Oṃ, homage to knowledge! Oṃ, homage to that which is to be accomplished! Oṃ, homage to the cause! (p. 395)
Thus they abide in restraint and grace. The principle of the Puruṣa (puruṣatattva) is that which is to be purified.
Hereafter I shall speak; listen attentively, O beloved, regarding the refinement that is desired within the principle of Prakṛti itself. || 47 ||
I shall explain that to you; listen as I speak it.
When one has reached the world of mortals, he should purify himself from the state of animal birth. (48)
First, the stationary beings are to be purified; then the reptiles are to be purified;
thereafter the bird-wombs are to be purified, and immediately after that, the wild animals.
O Mistress of the Gods, the sacrificial animals (paśus) are to be purified in due order and according to sequence;
cows and the like are declared to be the sacrificial animals, while lions and the like are remembered as the wild beasts (mṛgas). || 50 ||

The birds, such as the *bhāsa* and others, are declared [to be the first group]; the reptiles, such as the snakes and others, are the second; and the immovable beings, such as the *saptacchada* trees and others, O Mistress of the Gods, are proclaimed [as the third]. (51)
One should approach these humans according to the rules of purification;
first, the outcastes (antyajas) are to be purified, and after that, those of Śūdra birth.
Then, having led him into the womb of a prostitute, one should lead him again into the womb of a low-born woman;
from the low-born state, having joined him to the Brāhmaṇa castes, one should grant him authority in due order.
One should always renounce the authority over low-caste people, as well as the authority to impose bonds, imprisonment, execution, and the various methods of inflicting injury.

O beautiful goddess, in the state of a Śūdra, his duty is always proclaimed to be service to the devotees of Śiva and the exercise of self-control; such is the qualification prescribed for the state of a Śūdra. || 55 ||
Trade and the duty of agriculture are proclaimed as the occupations of the Vaiśya;
O woman of excellent complexion, the portion of the Kṣatriya’s duties is likewise established therein. (56)
War, gambling, physical exercise, conflict, and its fruit—these are declared to be the sequential domains of authority for Kṣatriyas. || 57 ||
O Goddess, beginning from the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) and ending with the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi), the qualification for the Brāhmaṇa has thus been declared to you.
O Goddess of the gods, at the beginning, due to the purificatory rites (saṃskāra), forty-eight [verses] are to be known; these must be thoroughly purified by the preceptor.
Having become a twice-born student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī), he should perform his duties in due order;
having performed the rite of union with a wife, he should sacrifice with sacrifices accompanied by sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
While it is being thus purified, one should apply those fifty [syllables];
as previously stated in the Sūtra, one should quickly perform all of that. (61)
O Goddess of the gods, by means of non-conceptualization, the wise and supreme teacher must always purify [the disciple] above the person by means of the teachers. 62.
The two types of seats are to be purified by the high-souled teacher;
in brief, both the bond of happiness and the bond of suffering are to be purified. (63)
Having practiced passion and beauty in conjunction with Time,
I shall hereafter fully declare the stainless path of knowledge.
Oṃ vāmadeva, homage! Oṃ bhuva, homage! Oṃ śarva, homage! Oṃ bhavodbhava, homage! Oṃ vajradeha, homage! Oṃ prabhu, homage! (p. 399)
Oṃ, obeisance to Dhātṛ. Oṃ, obeisance to Kramaśa. Oṃ, obeisance to Sugeśa. Obeisance to Vikrameśa.
These ten are declared to be the Śaṅkaras, who are eternally established through the principle of leading [the soul].
At the time of initiation, all of these must be purified by the wise.
Beyond that, having taken [the soul] from Śiva, it is established in the principle of Time (kāla-tattva).
In that very Time, those [entities] are to be understood as the objects to be purified by the wise.

Oṃ, salutation to the Pure One. Oṃ, salutation to the Awakened One. Oṃ, salutation to the Well-Awakened One. Oṃ, salutation to the Tranquil One. Oṃ, salutation to the Supreme Imperishable One. Oṃ, salutation to the Immutable One. Oṃ, salutation to the Auspicious One. Oṃ, salutation to the Eternal One. Oṃ, salutation to the Perishable One. (p. 400)
These ten are declared to be those who are to be purified by the wise;
beyond these, Hari, Hara, and the others are to be purified within the principle of passion (rāgatattva).
From this point forward, there shall be disciples such as Kalyāṇa and others, of great asceticism:

Oṃ Kalyāṇa, obeisance! Oṃ Piṅgala, obeisance! Oṃ Bhuva, obeisance! Oṃ Vīra, obeisance! Oṃ Pravara, obeisance! Oṃ Medhā, obeisance! Oṃ Amastita, obeisance! Oṃ Chedaka, obeisance! ... Oṃ Ka, obeisance! Oṃ Śāstrakāra, obeisance!
These ten should be known as gurus; one should purify them within the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva).
I shall now describe Kālaraudra and those Rudras who are established therein;
Vāma, Jyeṣṭha, and Rudra are likewise proclaimed there. (69)
Oṃ Vāma, homage! Oṃ Jyeṣṭha, homage! Oṃ Rudra, homage! Thus are the three mantras of Mahādeva.
And likewise, Gopati is above, with the knot situated at the heart.
Gopati was surrounded by many tens of millions of countless Rudras.
Oṃ, salutation to Gopati. Beyond this, the universe is established.
Oṃ, salutation to Trikala. Oṃ, salutation to Kṣemeśa. Oṃ, salutation to Brahmaṇa. Oṃ, salutation to Adhipati. Oṃ, salutation to Śiva.
These five are declared to be those who must be purified in the Śiva-sacrifice.
Above this, O Ananteśa, the bonds (pāśas) themselves are situated. || 71 ||
And those aforementioned evils, in the sequence beginning with *udamāha* and so forth:
*Oṃ mada namaḥ*. *Oṃ moha namaḥ*. *Oṃ śoṣa namaḥ*. *Oṃ vaicitya namaḥ*.
In this very sequence, they are to be purified in the Śiva-sacrifice.

Above this is the Family of Sages (*ṛṣikula*). Oṃ, homage to the Family of Sages (*ṛṣikula-namaḥ*). Above this is the Goddess Vāgīśvarī. Oṃ, homage to Vāgīśvarī (*vāgīśvarī-namaḥ*). Above this is the Oṃkāra; above that is the Sādhya-Oṃkāra. Oṃ, homage to the Sādhya-Oṃkāra (*sādhyoṅkāra-namaḥ*). Above this are the Sustainers (*dhātāraḥ*). Oṃ, homage to the Sustainers (*dhātāra-namaḥ*). Oṃ, homage to the Lord of Mind (*maneśa-namaḥ*). Oṃ, [homage to] those whose food is meditation (*dhyānāhāra*).
Salutation! Oṃ, salutation to Bhasmeśa. (p.
403) All these [deities] within the womb of Māyā are to be purified; thus do the wise know. Hereafter follow the authoritative texts: Oṃ, salutation to Pañcārtha. Oṃ, salutation to Śivaguhya.
Homage! Oṃ, homage to Rudrāṅkuśa! Oṃ, homage to Hṛdaya! Oṃ, homage to Lakṣaṇa! Oṃ, homage to Vyūha! Oṃ, homage to Mādaśi!
The eightfold means of valid cognition (pramāṇāṣṭaka) should be purified by the high-souled preceptor (deśika). 73.
Above them indeed, the preceptor should offer oblations to Māyā;
above that shall be Vidyā, the destroyer of the existence of all vidyās.
He is proclaimed to be divided into eightfold forms according to his own nature;
yet, he is said to be once again devoid of those ninefold divisions.

Oṃ, homage to Vāmā! Oṃ, homage to Jyeṣṭhā! Oṃ, homage to Raudrī! Oṃ, homage to Kālī! Oṃ, homage to Kalavikaraṇī! Oṃ, homage to Balavikaraṇī! Oṃ, homage to Balapramathinī! Oṃ, homage to Sarvabhūtadamanī! These are to be purified within the principle of Vidya (vidyā-tattva).
O Goddess, one should worship Īśvara, the Lord of Yoga, situated above; or likewise, Ananteśa and the others should be worshipped by those who are composed in meditation.

Oṃ, homage to Ananta! Oṃ, homage to Sūkṣma! Oṃ, homage to Śivottama! Oṃ, homage to Ekanetra! Oṃ, homage to Ekarudra! Oṃ, homage to Trimūrti! Oṃ, homage to Śrīkaṇṭha! Oṃ, homage to Śikhaṇḍin! These are to be purified within the principle of Īśvara. Beyond this follows the fourfold form.

p. 405) Oṃ Dharma, homage! Oṃ Jñāna, homage! Oṃ Vairāgya, homage! Oṃ Aiśvarya, homage! These are the four forms (*rūpacatuṣṭaya*). Oṃ Vāmā, homage! Oṃ Jyeṣṭhā, homage! Oṃ Raudrī, homage! These are the three powers (*śaktitraya*). Above these are two further powers: Oṃ Jñānaśakti, homage! Oṃ...
Salutation to Kriyāśakti. Above this—Tejīśa and Dhruveśa are proclaimed as the authorities (pramāṇatva).
Om, salutation to Tejīśa. Om, salutation to Dhruveśa.
For those who have reached the culmination on the path of the vital breaths, it is endowed with initiation and knowledge.
Nirvāṇa is said to be the supreme state for you, O lady of excellent vows.

Above that is the *praṇava*: *oṃ praṇavāya namaḥ*. Above that is the triad of worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra: *oṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*, *oṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*, *oṃ rudrāya namaḥ*, *oṃ pratodanāya namaḥ*, *oṃ manave namaḥ*. Beyond this, having transcended, is the single syllable (*ekākṣara*).
Oṃ ekākṣara, obeisance! Oṃ piṅga, obeisance! Oṃ haṃsa, obeisance! These are the three Saumyarudras. Above this is Dhruva.
Above this is the abode of the eleven Rudras. Oṃ brahma, obeisance! Oṃ arka, obeisance! Oṃ daṇḍin, obeisance! Oṃ muṇḍin, obeisance! Oṃ saurabheya!
Namaḥ! Oṃ mṛtyuhara, namaḥ! Oṃ praṇīta, namaḥ! (p. 407) Oṃ sukha, namaḥ! Oṃ vijṛmbhita, namaḥ! The eleven Rudras are to be purified.
At the time of initiation, however, they should be known as being firmly established in the throat.
I shall now declare the third, Dhruva: *Oṃ Dhruva, namaḥ*.
The retinue of Dhruva consists of seven thousand crores;
beyond that is the stainless deity (Nirañjana), whose number is not known. (79)

Oṃ, salutation to Nirañjana. Above this, Śakti is to be purified: Oṃ, salutation to Śakti. Above that are those eight Lords of the Worlds (Bhuvaneśvaras): Oṃ, salutation to Prīti; Oṃ, salutation to Pramādita; Oṃ, salutation to Pralamba. (p. 408)

Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu. Oṃ, salutation to Gahana. Oṃ, salutation to Vitata. These eight are the lords of the worlds (bhuvaneśas). Beyond these is the state of Bhava. That which is small is the pure fivefold action of Śiva. Oṃ, salutation to Prabhava. Oṃ, salutation to Raudra. Oṃ, salutation to Vimala. Oṃ, salutation to Śiva. Beyond that is another, named Aghana, which is impenetrable by all yogins. Salutation to Aghana.
Above that, Rudra is proclaimed as the syllable Om (Oṃkāra).
In front of the palate, the Lord Rudra is proclaimed as the syllable Oṃ.
Thus, Īśvara alone is the reality. Om Rudroṃkāra, obeisance!
Sadāśiva, through his eightfold division, is established between the eyebrows.
The seat is enriched with a hundred thousand petals, like the risen full moon;
upon that seat, the four powers of yoga are eternally established.
Oṃ, salutation to Nivṛtti. Oṃ, salutation to Pratiṣṭhā. Oṃ, salutation to Vidyā. Oṃ, salutation to Śānti.
Above this, there should be the Nāda, possessing a splendor like that of a lotus filament;
it is to be known as Puruṣa, abiding pervading everything. (83)
Pervaded by great beings whose splendor is equal to ten million suns,
he rules this cosmic egg, impelled by the power of Śiva.
Therefore, the Suṣumnā should be known as that which leads to the completion of the entire path;
it remains merged in the aperture of the Brahman-sound (nādabrahma), appearing like the fiber of a lotus stalk. (85)
The moon, which delights like a snowflake, should be meditated upon constantly by yogis;
above that, O Great Goddess, is the great [element] consisting of fire and sound.
The outflow of nectar from the moon, a treasury of the most excellent immortal luster,
briefly illuminates by means of the radiance of its own power-beams.
O beautiful one, all shine forth from that great flood of his splendor;
that power of the God of gods must be meditated upon by the preceptor.
Without interior or exterior, without support, and devoid of all temporal paths;
it is the culmination of the creative process, the great knowledge, incomparable and free from affliction.
Having thus purified the path, one should unite it with the supreme state;
having established the locus of the *vidyā*-tattva, one should unite it with the supreme state. (90)
Having meditated upon the process within one's own body, and especially within the body of a bound soul (paśu),
one should know that the worlds are situated one by one at every single barley-corn interval.
Prakṛti was previously described as established below the navel;
Puruṣa is situated in the middle of the heart, and Niyati is outside the feet.
At the bottom, however, is Kālakaṇṭha; he should be known by the eminent teacher, composed in mind, according to the sequence of Kalās and Vidyās at the time of initiation.
Māyā is situated above that, established at the location of the knot;
however, Vidyā is to be known by the teacher as being in the region of the throat. (94)
O beautiful one, Īśvara has been described by you as being in the middle of the palate;
Sadāśiva, however, is at the end of the head—this is the explanation of the reality, O vanquisher of enemies. (95)
O Goddess of the gods, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in sequence with the mantra Śāntyatīta;
it may also be given with the Navātman or with the Praṇava.
The final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for Śiva should be offered with the supreme syllable (paramākṣara).
At the conclusion of the entire path (adhvan), one should perform the cutting of the topknot (śikhācchedana).
O Goddess of the gods, one should consecrate the scissors with the *śikhā* mantra;
then, having grasped it with that very mudrā, the wise practitioner should perform the cutting. 98.
O Suvrata, the four fingers should indeed be cut off;
having prepared them with clarified butter, the wise one should offer them as a burnt oblation (homa). || 99 ||
Having offered that oblation, the preeminent guide should cause [the disciple] to perform a bath with ashes.
Then, having sipped water and purified his own body, the teacher— (p. 413) —[should proceed]. 100.

Having performed everything without exception, the wise one should cause [the victim] to fall by means of the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), having unified his own infinite self with the state of being the sacrificial animal (paśu). 101.
Then the mantra-practitioner should apply himself according to the ritual previously observed; perform the practice in such a manner as the path of the *kalās* has been described. (102)
But when [the time] is appropriate, O Goddess, I have previously declared the characteristics; as for those duties which belong to the practitioner in the Śivadharmas, [they are as follows]. 103.
The Goddess said: "O Lord, you previously described to me that form (mūrti) is of three kinds. By what means is its acquisition [attained]? This I wish to know. (104)
Īśvara is declared to be the fifteenth self; by means of that, one should pierce the one called Haṃsa.
One should grasp it together with the Bindu, which is indeed extended. || 105 ||
Having struck with the *śikhā* [mudrā], one should perform the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) by means of the *grāhya* mudrā,
with each hand turned downwards and well-circled.
The preceptor should take [it] with the "Hand of Śiva" joined with mantra; O Goddess of Gods, he should employ the left hand with the palm turned upward.
O Goddess, this release of the bound soul (paśu) from capture has been explained to you;
it must be performed by the preeminent teacher through the ritual action prescribed by the rules. || 108 ||
The Goddess said: O Maheśvara, [tell me] the yoga and the sacrifice consisting of thirty-eight kalās.
How is initiation established in them, and how should it be applied by the teachers? || 109 ||
"Or by what means is its grasping? This I wish to know.
O beloved, listen attentively as I shall explain the sacrifice of Kalā to the Lord."
I have not revealed this to anyone; I shall tell it to you, O lady of virtuous conduct.
O Goddess of the gods, whatever yoga among the arts I speak of, [you must keep it secret]. 111.
And likewise, O fair-faced one, I shall describe the union with a digit (kalā);
there are five digits of Maheśa and four of his face.
The five faces have been fully described by you, O virtuous one;
this, O virtuous one, has been told to you as the enclosure of the womb. (113)

By means of the sequence starting from the southeast and proceeding through the east and so forth, up to the north, one should place the Puruṣa in four ways: in the southeast, the northwest, and the southwest.
Having placed [the mantras] in the four directions and in the intermediate directions starting from the east,
one should place those eight digits (kalās) of Aghora, O Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa).
Now listen as I describe that which is the Vāmadeva-kalā;
the placement of the kalās must be performed starting from the east.
Two [kalās] in the east, two in the south, and likewise in the west;
then, O Goddess of the Gods, one should again place one kalā in the north.
In the four directions, Unmanī is declared to be the most excellent of the aforementioned phases (kalās).
Indeed, this is the supreme [phase] of Śiva; one should contemplate it within the body. (118)
One should place the eight *kalās* of Sadyojāta fourfold within the causal [state].
O Goddess of the gods, one should then assign the nine powers (*śaktis*) to the eight directions and to the *praṇava*.
One should place the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and detachment (vairāgya) in their proper order;
by that very means, O lady of excellent complexion, one should fashion the infinite lotus.
The wise preceptor should effect the union with the form by means of that very [mantra];
the intelligent one should perform the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) with the Brahma-omkāra.
The woman of excellent complexion should arrange the seat of Unmanī for him;
O Goddess of gods, one should place the Vidyā-tattva in the sleeping chamber.
O fair-faced one, these are indeed the fourfold portions of Īśāna;
his seat should be prepared by the teachers together with the Rudra-mantra and the syllable Oṃ. (123)
One should perform [the rite] with that which is called the Śiva-tattva, ending with the syllable Oṃ;
and the fifth kalā, which belongs to Īśāna, is Maheśvarī.
One should have an image made with five heads, Īśāna as the [upper] face, and four [other] faces; it has five faces and a seat— by this, there is no doubt regarding the end of death.
O Goddess, having performed the deposition of the forms (mūrtinyāsa) again with all the constituent parts (kalās) in due order,
and having rendered oneself complete (sakalīkṛtya), one should cause the Supreme Imperishable (Paramākṣara) to descend.
In this way, O Goddess, one becomes partless; of this there is no doubt.
One should then conceive of the Praṇava for him in five ways, according to the proper sequence.

The preceptor should place [the mantras] in the heart, at the head, and at the crest, according to the sequence of armor and weapons, ending with the kalās of Sadyojāta and Vāmadeva in every instance. (128)
Those who are established in the reality of the Self should perform [the rites] with the syllable Om;
likewise, they should offer fragrance, flowers, lamps, food, and the ritual oblation.
Rudra is [to be worshipped] with the syllable *oṃ* in that which is called Vidyā; O Śiva, [one should worship] the forms, colors, and digits.
Having thus performed the sacrifice according to the rule, one should then administer initiation.
One should conceive of Vāgīśvarī as being of the nature of the Sadyojāta digit. || 131 ||
One should join [the elements] with that very [mantra] there, and offer those [oblations] with that same [mantra];
one should offer as many oblations as there are paths known as the worlds.
One should employ [the disciple] in seizing, striking, and lifting up;
and indeed, having engaged him in the performance of special tasks at every moment. (133)
One should offer the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) at the end; this indeed is remembered as the prescribed rule.
[This should be done] for the Lord of Gods with either the Navātman mantra or the Śāntyatīta mantra.
The full oblations (pūrṇāhuti) should be offered in sequence with the supreme syllable (paramākṣara).
First, one should establish the Kalā, and then one should install Vāgīśvarī.
Alternatively, the path of the digits (kalādhvā) may be purified by the well-composed teachers, either by means of single units or by groups of digits. || 136 ||
Those arts which have been described as belonging to the *āsana* (posture) should not be employed with the *āsana*;
in that regard, O fair-complexioned lady, there is for the three [goddesses] only the single remembrance of the *praṇava*. (137)
O Goddess, when the principles beginning with earth are to be purified in their proper sequence by means of the *kalās*, I shall explain that to you; listen with a one-pointed mind. (138)
One should offer a hundred oblations for each principle (tattva), beginning with earth and proceeding in sequence;
O Goddess of Gods, one should offer a hundred oblations for each at the end of Prakṛti.
Having thus renounced what has been described, O Goddess, one should perform an oblation for each individual principle (tattva) with each of the parts (kalā) that have been proclaimed. 140.
Furthermore, I shall speak of a specific distinction regarding Vāmadeva; listen to that. Beginning with the Puruṣa, they are grasped together in brief. (141)
In each and every reality (tattva), however, two pairs of digits (kalās) are to be offered.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should offer a hundred oblations with a single digit. (142)
O beautiful goddess, this has been fully explained as the portion of Vāma;
the wise one should offer Māyā and Avidyā with the portions of Aghora.
However, with each individual oblation, one should offer the twenty-five principles:
Īśvara, Devīśa, as well as the principle Sadāśiva. (144)
A man should offer oblations at the proper time with a well-composed mind;
he should perform fifty oblations for each individual.
With twenty or twenty oblations, according to the portion of Īśāna,
the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) should be offered by the high-souled preceptor.
Now, O Goddess of gods, when there is a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) for every hundred [breaths], the full oblation is prescribed on the left by means of two [units]. (147)
Furthermore, the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) for Aghora is prescribed with one mora;
however, the final oblations for Śiva consist of four morae.
It should likewise be given by the lord of teachers to the man;
O woman of excellent complexion, one should offer oblations with the five parts of the Īśāna-kalā.
The final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) should be offered by the high-souled preceptor;
as for the ritual procedure for the joining (yojana), that which was previously described by me [should be performed]. (150)
O Goddess, this has been understood by you; what more shall I tell you?
O Goddess, this path of the parts (kalādhvan) has been fully explained to you without exception. 151.

O Goddess of the gods, the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) and the path of the energies (kalādhvan) have been briefly explained; however, they must be understood by the teacher (deśika) in two ways. (152)
O Goddess of the gods, this has been told; it must be understood by the preceptor.
Thus, upon the completion of the initiation, the teacher, being well-composed, [should proceed]. (153)
Having dismissed [the deity], O Goddess of Gods, one should worship Caṇḍeśvara there;
on the following day, O Goddess of Gods, one should worship the Lord Caṇḍeśvara.
O fair-faced one, the mantras endowed with five limbs were previously taught by me in the first sūtra at the excellent city of Ardhacandra. 155.
Having worshipped with just a single offering, the wise one,
having performed the libation in the maṇḍala, should offer oblations one hundred and eight times in sequence.
Thus, O Goddess, in this [section] concerning Caṇḍeśa for the great [rite],
on page 425,
line 145, no insertion of verses is observed other than the subject matter previously mentioned.
And in the second enclosure, one should again worship with the limbs of the Vidyā.
O fair-faced goddess, all the outer enclosures are to be known [in this manner].
This lotus-wheel of yours has thus been described to you, O Goddess. (159)
The first is that of Śivagarbha, the second is that of the Cakravartins;
O Great Goddess, in the third [direction], one should place the enclosures of Vāyu.
The fourth belongs to the Gaṇeśas, immediately following that in the southeast;
the sixth belongs to the Lokapālas, and the seventh is remembered as belonging to Mahendra. (161)
O Supreme Goddess, one should place the ten and the nine principles in their proper sequence; one should assign them outside the lines of the limbs of Vidyā.
One should arrange them in sequence according to the order starting from the east;
those which consist of eight or one foot each are declared to be hymns (stotra).
O Dear One, all [the oblations] should indeed be offered in sequence starting from the conception;
or else, having performed the ritual procedure beginning with the seat (āsana), one may start from that point. 164.
O beloved, one hundred oblations each should be offered in the eight external directions and in the eight directions starting from the womb; thus one is purified—of this there is no doubt. || 165 ||
The woman of excellent complexion should be given by Śiva as the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti);
the eighty-one positions have already been described previously. (166)
I shall describe the auspicious sacrifice; listen, O Goddess, in due order.
It should be performed on the previously mentioned ground, which is free from husks, hair, and bones. (167)
On a level stretch of ground, free from depressions and elevations,
in a region sloping toward the northeast, one should mark out the auspicious site with a cord.
The measurement of the field is proclaimed to be twenty-four cubits; having laid out the lines according to rule, one should divide it into nine parts. || 169 ||
Furthermore, one should mark out the middle [section] here itself by dividing it into nine parts;
among those divided into nine parts, one should omit half a part.
The lotus is thirty-two finger-breadths [in size], and the ritual procedure consists of thirty-two finger-breadths;
it is endowed with the fourfold method and adorned with eight doors. (171)
I have previously explained the measurement for the door; one should construct it according to that very measurement.
Just as it is with the center, so too must everything always be performed by the preceptors.
O Lord of Gods, they say that the space between the surrounding petals of the line-lotus should be sixteen finger-breadths; thus has the line-lotus been described.
There should be no doubt regarding the placement of the enclosures;
O Goddess of the Gods, listen as I explain the Śivāṅgas—understand them from me. 174.

Oṃ, salutation to the All-pervading One. Oṃ, salutation to Him whose form is space. Oṃ, salutation to the Infinite One. Oṃ, salutation to the Lord of Space. Oṃ, salutation to Him who is not dependent on space.
(p. 429) These are proclaimed as the limbs of Śiva. Oṃ, salutation to the Eternal One. Oṃ, salutation to the Everlasting One. Oṃ, salutation to Him who is established upon the Yoga-throne. Oṃ...
Salutation to the one eternally united [with Yoga]. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose nourishment is meditation. These are proclaimed as the limbs of knowledge (vidyāṅga).
But the Brahman of the word (padabrahman), O Goddess of gods, has been previously described as an limb.
It must be understood by the teacher himself at the time of initiation; of this there is no doubt. (175)

Oṃ, salutation to Unnata. Oṃ, salutation to Vyomavyāpin. Oṃ, salutation to Vyomarūpa. Oṃ, salutation to Sarvavyāpin. Oṃ, salutation to Śiva. Oṃ, salutation to Ananta. Oṃ, salutation to Anātha. Oṃ, salutation to Anāśrita. Oṃ, salutation to Dhruva. (p. 430)

First, one should perform this placement within the womb of Śiva (śivagarbha); thus it has been declared: Oṃ, obeisance to the Eternal One. Oṃ, obeisance to Him who is seated upon the Yoga-throne. Oṃ, to the Ever-yoked One. Oṃ, obeisance to Him whose sustenance is meditation. Oṃ, obeisance. Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva. Oṃ, obeisance to the Source of All. Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva.
Oṃ, salutation to Īśāna, the head; Oṃ, salutation to Tatpuruṣa, the face. This is indeed proclaimed as the second enclosure, that of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas). || 176 ||

Oṃ, obeisance to the heart of Aghora. Oṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva, the secret one. Oṃ, obeisance to the form of Sadyojāta. Oṃ, obeisance, obeisance. Oṃ, obeisance to the one more secret than the secret. Oṃ, obeisance to the protector. Oṃ, obeisance to the one who is the end of the endless. (p. 431)
Salutation to Onnidhana.
O Goddess, the third enclosure is proclaimed as belonging to Devādya and the others.
