Om, salutation to the Lord of all Vidyās. Om, salutation to the one whose form is light. Om, salutation to the boon-granting Supreme Lord. Om, salutation to Cetaṇa. Om, salutation to Acaitaṇa.
Homage! Oṃ, to Vyomin, Vyomin, homage! Oṃ, to Vyāpin, Vyāpin, homage! Oṃ, to Rūpin, Rūpin, homage! Oṃ, to Prathama, Prathama, homage!
Oṃ, to Tejas, Tejas, homage!
In the fourth [circle], however, the enclosure of the Gaṇeśas is proclaimed:
Oṃ jyotirjyotir namaḥ; omarūpa namaḥ; oṃ agni namaḥ. (p. 432)

Oṃ madhu namaḥ | Oṃ bhasma namaḥ | O manādi namaḥ | Onnānā namaḥ | Ondhudhūdhudhū namaḥ | Oṃ bhūrnamaḥ | This is indeed declared to be the Āgneya-āvaraṇa (the fire enclosure) for the Yogādyas. Oṃ bhuvarnamaḥ | Oṃ svarnamaḥ | O manidhana namaḥ | Onnidhanodbhava namaḥ | Oṃ śiva namaḥ | Oṃ sarva namaḥ | Oṃ paramātman namaḥ | Oṃ maheśvara namaḥ |
The sixth enclosure is indeed proclaimed to belong to the world-protectors.

Oṃ, homage to Mahādeva! Oṃ, homage to Sadbhāveśvara! Oṃ, homage to Mahātejas! Oṃ, homage to Yogādhipati! Oṃ, release, release, release, homage! Oṃ, first one, first one, homage! Oṃ, Śarva, Śarva, homage! Oṃ, Bhava, Bhava, homage! (p. 433)
Oṃ, homage to Bhavodbhava!
The seventh enclosure, that of Mahendra, is proclaimed as belonging to Tārā and the others. (178)

Oṃ, salutations to the one who bestows happiness upon all beings! Oṃ, salutations to the one who brings about the presence of all! Oṃ, salutations to the one who is beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra! Oṃ, salutations to the one who is both worshipped and unworshipped! Oṃ, salutations to the one who is both consecrated and unconsecrated! Oṃ, salutations to the one who was present from the beginning and remains present from the beginning! Oṃ, salutations to the witness, the witness! Oṃ, *turu turu*!
Namaḥ! Oṃ pataṅga pataṅga namaḥ! Oṃ piṅga piṅga namaḥ! The eighth, the enclosure of the weapons of the world-protectors (lokapāla), has been fully described. || 178½ ||
Oṃ śabdaśabda, homage! Oṃ sūkṣma sūkṣma, homage! Oṃ śiva, homage! (p. 434) Oṃ śarva, homage! Oṃ sarva, homage! Oṃ oṃ namo namaḥ! Oṃ oṃ śivāya namo namaḥ! Oṃ oṃ namaḥ!
This is indeed proclaimed as the ninth enclosure, consisting of Ambhā and the others. || 179 ||
In the tenth [section], one should place the nine principles (tattvas) in their proper order:
*oṃ ūn namaḥ*, *oṃ yan namaḥ*, *oṃ ln namaḥ*, *oṃ an namaḥ*, *oṃ kṣan namaḥ*, *oṃ ran namaḥ*, *oṃ han namaḥ*, and *oṃ prasannamūrtaye namaḥ*. One should place the ninth [syllable] in the center.
One should place the limbs of knowledge (vidyāṅga) according to their lines; these are proclaimed as belonging to Īśvara. || 180 ||

Oṃ, to the Self of all, the Supreme, the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign of Yoga, the Source of Yoga, the Giver of Hands, the Immediate Giver, the Origin of Existence, O Vāmadeva, the mantra that pacifies all undertakings, O Sadāśiva, gracious one, salutations, salutations!
The heart of the body of the universal self:

*Oṃ suśiva namaḥ*. *Oṃ suśiva* is the head of the deity. *Oṃ śivahṛdaya jvālinī namaḥ*. Jvālinī is the crest-lock (*śikhā*), the great splendor whose essence is Śiva, the omniscient, imperishable Lord.
One should recite the most formidable, auspicious, and tawny-hued armor-mantra.
Come, O Piṅgala, you of great roar, by the command of Śiva! Bind, bind the heart! Blaze up, blaze up! Reel about, O Kakṛṣṭakṣman!
O Vajradhara, Vajrapāśa, Vajraśakti, and Candrā, having entered my body and my heart— (p.

*Stambhaya* (paralyze) all evil ones! *Huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. That armor named Piṅgala is: *Oṃ-kāra-bandhaṃ huṃ phaṭ ka va hṛdayam*. *Oṃ prasphura prasphura ghora ghoratara tanurūpa caṭa caṭa pracaṭa pracaṭa kaha kaha vaṃ vaṃ ghātaya ghātaya huṃ phaṭ*—this is the Aghorāstra. *Oṃ oṃ aghoraśivāya huṃ phaṭ*—this is the Aghorāstra-hṛdaya. *Oṃ vyomavyāpine vyomarūpāya sarvavyāpine*.

Salutations to Śiva, the infinite, the protectorless, the independent, the fixed, the eternal, who is established upon the seat of yoga, the perpetual yogi whose nourishment is meditation. *Oṃ*, salutations to Śiva, the source of all; salutations again and again to Śiva, whose head is Īśāna, whose face is Tatpuruṣa, whose heart is Aghora, whose secret part is Vāmadeva, and whose form is Sadyojāta. *Oṃ*, salutations, salutations!

To the one more secret than the secret, the protector, the imperishable, the presiding authority over all yoga, the sovereign lord of all ignorance, whose form is light, who is devoted to the Supreme Lord, who is both insentient and sentient, O Pervader, O Pervader, O Formless One, O Formed One, the first among the first, the brilliance of brilliance, the light of light, O Formless One, O Non-fire, O Smokeless One.

Non-ash, beginningless, manifold, manifold, *dhū dhū dhū dhū*, *oṃ bhūḥ*, *oṃ bhuvaḥ*, *oṃ suvaḥ*. O you who are without end yet the end, the source of the end, Śiva, the Supreme Soul of all, Maheśvara, Mahādeva, Lord of true being, Great Splendor, Sovereign of Yoga, release, release! First, first! Śarva, Śarva! Bhava, Bhava! Source of existence! Bestower of happiness upon all beings! Maker of the presence of all! Supreme over Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra!

p. 438) Anarcita-anarcita, para-apara, asaṃskṛta-saṃskṛta, pūrvasthita-pūrvasthita, sākṣi-sākṣi, turu-turu, pataṅga-pataṅga, piṅga-piṅga, jñāna-jñāna, śabda-śabda, sūkṣma-sūkṣma, Śiva, Sarva, Sarvada! Onnamo namaḥ! Oṃ namaḥ! Oṃ Śivāya namaḥ!

Homage! O Supreme Mahānātha, the venerable Śiva! Om, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; homage indeed to Sadyojāta! In existence and beyond existence, favor me; homage to Bhavodbhava! Homage to Sadyojāta, homage to Vāmadeva, homage to Jyeṣṭha, homage to Rudra, homage to Kāla, homage to Kalavikaraṇa, homage to Balavikaraṇa, homage to Balapramathana, homage to Sarvabhūtadamana, homage to Manonmana!

Oṃ. To those who are non-terrible, and to those who are terrible, and to those more terrible than the most terrible, to all of them, everywhere, who possess the forms of Rudra—salutations to you! Aghora. Oṃ. We know that Tatpuruṣa; we meditate upon Mahādeva; may that Rudra inspire us. Tatpuruṣa. Oṃ.

The Lord of all beings, the Sovereign of all beings, the Overlord of Brahman, the Overlord of the Veda—may that Śiva, Sadāśiva, be mine. The Ruler. Oṃ, may we know that Great Lord; may we meditate upon Him whose speech is pure; may that Śiva inspire us. All this has Śiva as its essence; from Śiva alone does it proceed. (181)
For Śiva, for the one who contains Śiva within, may the All-Śiva impel [this].
440) Oṃ Āṃ Īṃ Ūṃ, obeisance to the one who pervades the sky; Oṃ Oṃ, obeisance to the Tranquil One; Oṃ, obeisance to the Self of the *praṇava*; Oṃ Huṃ, obeisance to Śiva; Oṃ.
Oṃ huṃ namaḥ | Oṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ juṃ namaḥ | This worship of the letters within the *asthi* (bone) is declared for the sake of Śiva, the Supreme Self. || 182 ||

Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations! Oṃ, salutations indeed to Sadyojāta! Oṃ, salutations to Bhava! Oṃ, salutations to Abhava! Oṃ, salutations to Anādibhava! Oṃ, favor me, salutations! Oṃ, salutations to Bhava! Oṃ, salutations to Udbhava!
Homage, Oṃ, to Vāmadeva; homage, homage! Oṃ, to Jyeṣṭha; homage, homage! Oṃ, to Rudra; homage, homage! Oṃ, to Kāla; homage, homage! Oṃ, to Kala; homage! (p. 441)

Oṃ, salutations again and again to the One Without Form (Vikaraṇa). Oṃ, salutations to Power (Bala). Oṃ, salutations again and again to the One Without Form. Oṃ, salutations to Power. Oṃ, salutations again and again to the Agitator (Pramathana). Oṃ, salutations again and again to the Subduer of All Beings (Sarvabhūtadamana). Oṃ, salutations to the Thinking Mind (Manana). Oṃ, salutations again and again to the Transcendent Mind (Unmana). Oṃ, salutations to those who are not terrible (Aghora). Oṃ, and salutations to those who are terrible (Ghora). Oṃ, salutations to the Terrible One (Ghora). Oṃ, salutations to those who are more terrible than the terrible (Ghoratara). Oṃ, salutations to all sides (Sarvataḥ). Oṃ, salutations to all the Śarvas.

Salutation to you, O Rudra; salutation! Oṃ, salutation to the forms. Oṃ, we know that Puruṣa; salutation! Oṃ, we meditate upon Mahādeva; salutation! Oṃ, may that Rudra inspire us; salutation! Oṃ, Īśāna of all sciences; salutation! Oṃ, Īśvara of all beings; salutation! Oṃ, the overlord of Brahman, the overlord of the sacred word, the Brahman; salutation! Oṃ, may Śiva be mine; salutation! Oṃ, Sadāśiva; salutation!
One should apply each word one by one and offer each word one by one.
One should arrange the nine principles upon each individual pedestal;
by means of each individual pedestal, one performs the initiation that leads to liberation.
O Goddess, one should offer a hundred oblations for each leaf of every single word;
having performed the satiation of the mandala, one should offer the elevenfold oblation.
The full oblations (pūrṇāhuti) should be offered in their proper sequence and order;
having offered one at the "beyond-the-foot" (atipada) stage and having purified the sacrificial path (adhvara).
Furthermore, O Goddess, listen again as I tell you in brief:
by the presence of the invocation, each individual word is purified. (187)
O Goddess, one should fashion nine footprints on each pedestal;
by ten oblations for each, there is no doubt that the purification of the pedestal is accomplished. (188)
Thus is the initiation completed by means of the wheel of words (padacakra) in the well-arranged [system].
One should perform this procedure, which is common to all the Saṃhitās. || 189 ||
O Goddess, this unsurpassed *padayāga* has been fully explained;
it is common to all *saṃhitās* and is celebrated in all *tantras*. (190)
Having worshipped the Lord of the Sovereign Kings of Knowledge (Vidyārājādhirāja), one shall attain liberation.
Furthermore, I shall proclaim another most secret essence of mantras. 191.
By the mere knowledge of which one shall attain supreme accomplishment—
that three-eyed, ten-armed deity was previously described by me. (192)
Therefore, I shall explain that; listen with a one-pointed mind.
[He is] seated in the lotus posture, illuminating all directions.
One should contemplate the five-faced god situated upon the pericarp;
stationed there, he resides in the center of the Śakti, resembling the rising sun. (194)
In some places it resembles Indra (sapphire), in others it is like emerald;
in some places it is a mass of liquid mercury, and in its radiance it is equal to ten million suns.
The deity stands illuminating [all], resembling the thumb of the vital breath;
likewise, Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti are present.
The three mandalas:
the ten-armed deity Śiva, who is the essence of nectar, is for the sake of pacification.
They illuminate the seat of that god on all sides. || 197 ||
Having the form of the flame of a crest-lamp, she pierces the palate and emerges;
at the end of that, O Goddess, what lies beyond is proclaimed as Śakti.
That [process] should be understood as the end of the ritual procedure; having pierced that, one should join [the soul] to the Supreme.
Having severed [the bonds] and established the bound soul (paśu) within oneself, it should then be joined to the Excellent Abode.
Having known that reality, one should apply it for only the duration of a blink of an eyebrow;
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, this is declared to be the Self.
Thus, whoever perceives the Self is liberated, without a doubt;
and having seen the Lotus in the supreme Śiva, one shall liberate others as well, without a doubt. (201)
But without seeing it, one does not attain success, nor does the leader reach the supreme state;
therefore, it must always be meditated upon by yogis with the utmost effort.
Having placed the Self within the pericarp of the heart, the knower of yoga meditates;
thus, yogis perceive their entire location as it truly exists in its own place.
O Goddess, one sees for a hundred yojanas; there is no doubt in this.
O Maheśvarī, I shall describe it according to the arrangement for each leaf. 204.
The eastern petal and likewise the one in the northeast half of the southeast;
by means of the union of these two half-petals, he perceives the eastern region. (205)
By means of half of Īśāna’s [petal] and that of Vāyu, well-rounded, and by means of the northern petal, one beholds the northern path. (206)
O beautiful one, the single western petal should be adorned by the half of the northwest;
thereafter, the lord of yogis should look toward the southwestern direction.
O Goddess of gods, by means of the southern half of the southwestern quarter,
and by means of the southern half of the southeastern quarter, one beholds the entire southern region.
But with four petals well-rounded on the side, it is called *tāpanī* in the second [chapter]; they know that as the instruction for each region. (209)
Thus, those who know the reality should understand it regarding all principles:
having made the self hollow and having placed the regions in the middle. (210)
Having made oneself of infinite form, one sees [all things] and not otherwise;
all rivers, oceans, and streams are encompassed within it. (211)
The yogi established in yoga perceives this; of this there is no doubt.
That true nature which was previously known to you has now been fully explained.
One should direct that gaze toward everything; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having made Meru its pericarp, one then beholds the three worlds. (213)
One should relate the entire account; there is no need for deliberation here.
O Goddess, this supreme essence of yoga has been declared by me. 214.
One who is disciplined in yoga perceives [the truth] in three months, without a doubt;
one disciplined in yoga for six months perceives everything, and not otherwise.
With his self disciplined for a year, he beholds both the divine and the non-divine;
he attains equality with the gods and traverses the worlds in due order. (216)
The practitioner who, being well-composed, meditates thus and performs the recitation, shall achieve success without obstacle; of this there is no doubt, O Lord of Practitioners.
O Supreme Goddess, the yogi who is joined with this method quickly attains perfection; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. (218)
On the eastern petal is Vijaya; in the southeast is Śatrunāśana;
on the southern petal is Śāntida; and in the southwest is Māraṇa. || 219 ||

One should seek prosperity in the western direction (Vāruṇī), or for the sake of destruction in the northern direction (Vāyavī); those desiring wealth should go to the north, and one desiring knowledge should go to the northeast (Īśānī). || 220 ||

O Goddess of the gods, those who seek victory over death should constantly meditate [on the breath] as rising upwards, resembling cow's milk; thus they are not afflicted by the sufferings of death. (221)
O Goddess, she leads the best of men downward and the lowest of men upward;
knowing this, O lady of beautiful hips, she leads them—of this there is no doubt. (222)
The Goddess said:
"O Mistress of the Gods, you have described the upward [flame] of that [fire], which is incomparable.
O Blessed One, I wish to hear about it; you should deign to speak. (223)
How is it that by that form his crest bestows the fruit?
And how, O Lord, does it lead downward the one of evil karma? || 224 ||
O Lord, how do yogins perceive [this] directly within the body?
Please, out of your grace, explain the procedure for the practice of mudrā-yoga. (225)
O Goddess, listen, O Īśvara; I shall proclaim the unsurpassed classification of the *śikhā*.
By the mere knowledge of which, practitioners achieve success on this earth. || 226 ||
In the Gāruḍa and Bhūtatanttras,
as well as in the supreme and divine Śaiva-jñāna, the ritual of the crest (śikhākarma) is likewise described as beautiful.
Resembling white cow’s milk and similar to a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon, the tuft of hair (śikhā) should always be meditated upon by yogins for the sake of conquering death. 228.
By the falling of torrents of rain, they fill [the world] on all sides;
they instruct the entire world and destroy poisons and planetary afflictions. 229.
It brings constant satisfaction and consists of the very meditation on the mantra;
and if one perceives that the streams do not flow with distinct divisions, [one attains success]. (230)
In an instant one should effect nourishment; there is no need for deliberation here.
When the yogi has performed the meditation on the red-colored crest, he becomes [successful]. (231)
In that manner I shall explain it to you; listen with a one-pointed mind.
[I shall teach] subjugation, possession, killing, and likewise withering.
Because it effects the removal of poison, brings about nirvāṇa, and renders [the seed] seedless; because it likewise causes the non-flaring of fire, induces a swoon, and is purifying. (233)
This has been declared to you by the one who wears red garments; now listen, O virtuous lady, as I speak concerning the one who wears yellow garments. (234)
Through meditation, one attains success that bestows wealth, grain, and fruit;
one can paralyze the entire earth and the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile. (235)
O virtuous one, listen as I shall explain the black-colored crest-mantra:
it effects eradication, incites enmity, and likewise brings about liberation. (236)
There is no doubt that it causes the transmission of poison and induces muteness;
there is no doubt that it paralyzes all principles (tattvas) and the objects of the senses. || 237 ||
O Dear One, everything is accomplished for him who knows the application of the *śikhā*;
however, no rite devoid of the *śikhā* is ever successful for practitioners. (238)
The Vāyavyā [line] is black in color, while the Āgneyī is red, O virtuous one;
the Mahendrī is to be known as yellow, and the Vāruṇī is said to be white. (239)
Black, red, white, yellow, and crystal-like in appearance—
these are always taught by those who know the ritual of the crest for the sake of accomplishing all activities. (240)
O Goddess of virtuous conduct, this Śikhāyoga has been told to you;
it is the common accomplishment of all tantras, of this there is no doubt. (241)
O Goddess, he who desires success while devoid of the *śikhā* [topknot] strikes at the sky with his fist and drinks a mirage. 242.
O Goddess, he who knows this fivefold nature attains success.
I shall now describe the restraint of initiation; listen with a one-pointed mind. (243)
O Goddess, one should perform this [rite] against one who is foolish, deceitful, cruel, and who walks the path of injustice; but never against anyone else. 244.
Having drawn [the disciple] away from the supreme reality by means of his own [individual] reality, the teacher leads him,
with five oblations for each of the five [elements], to wherever he desires. (245)
Then, having established it and covered it over with earth, the preceptor of excellent conduct remains there; for that teacher who attempts to leap over it is of a wicked nature.
In whatever place one applies [the practice], one experiences suffering there. O Goddess, listen as I explain how the obstruction of accomplishment occurs. 247.
Having placed a balance on the wind-wheel for the sake of accomplishing its perfection,
it was then completely covered by Māhendra, who had assumed the form of the earth.
Thus stabilized, O Goddess, he remains; of this there is no doubt.
Listen now to how this becomes manifest even to yogins. 249.
I shall now fully explain, O Goddess, in brief, at what time and by what means yoga is to be practiced by practitioners; listen. (250)
When one-third of a ghaṭikā has passed, O woman of excellent complexion, she should practice for as long as it takes to sit three times. 251.
With a well-joyful mind, intent upon that [mark], one should close the eyes with the city-gaze;
O fair-faced one, one then beholds her trembling in its center.
One sees that very same similar target; there is no doubt in this matter.
In the first stage, yogis always see it as having a dark blue hue like bronze.
Red, yellow, and white—each with an equal radiance corresponding to its color—one should fix the gaze upon one hundred thousand [of these], while that hundred thousand looks on. || 254 ||
"O Goddess, behold that supreme and great form shaped like a chariot wheel.
Having seen it, the yogi shall directly enter Śiva even while remaining in a different location. (255)
Without doubt, O Goddess of gods, he shall attain the state called Sādākhya;
he alone perceives the Self as the target and beholds it with certainty. (256)
But through practice toward the Lord of Gods, one attains equality equal to His; thus do I describe to you the sign of attainment for the supreme yogin. (257)
But when dead, the fire-god draws a lotus and honey-mixture;
O Dear One, he trembles in distress and carries out the command of the yogin.
It shines like a blue lotus; O Goddess, at whatever time the crest-lock of the yogin comes under control, he lives through great affliction. (259)
O Goddess of the Gods, one should predict success in whichever direction the crest-flame (śikhā) moves;
it is perceived without doubt, O Mistress of the Gods—of this there is no uncertainty. (260)
When one perceives within the heart that unsurpassed union with the crest (śikhā),
joined with the swan of vital breath (vāyu) and endowed with the sixth vowel, || 261 ||
By means of the final seed-syllable of the Nāda, one beholds [the reality] endowed with Bindu and Nāda; there is no doubt in this matter. || 262 ||
Then, O fair-faced one, when the heart-center is seen by the yogin within the interior of the radiant wing, [he attains success]. (263)

Then indeed, the yogis should place the *lakṣa* upon the region of the ear, having abandoned the color of the wind [the letter *ya*], and endowed it with the *ū*, the *bindu*, and the crest [the letter *m*]. (264)
When the yogi, well-composed, reaches the station of the head,
he is liberated from all sounds and joined with the syllable *ra*. (265)
When the state of the head, which is the seat of the crown,
is fully attained, then that which is released from the *bindu* is proclaimed as the *śikhā*.
The supreme Śakti transcends the crest (śikhā), and the supreme Śiva transcends Śakti;
these are declared as the state of Vāyavya and likewise that of Āgneya. (267)
The Māhendra and the Vāruṇa are likewise, without a doubt;
the fifth is proclaimed as the support for all yoga. || 268 ||
The consciousness of the true nature of *citi* is the supreme Śiva whose essence is consciousness;
for that singular knowledge emerges spontaneously, even from among the gods and asuras. (269)
The second [aspect], its true nature, is difficult to discern even for the gods.
O virtuous one, this knowledge has been proclaimed in every way throughout all the tantras. (270)
Having known [this] by means of the half-portion of all the gates, one is released from bondage;
for it is from this, O Goddess, that the division of day and night proceeds. (271)
O beautiful goddess, that was previously explained to you regarding the lineage;
the teacher knows him who is situated in the center, resting upon the lotus. (272)
Beyond this, O Goddess, is that which is supreme and beyond the lineage of gurus;
having set aside these three, that is proclaimed as the ultimate. (273)
In the Cāradeva [mandala], which is not auspicious, it is known to be thirty-six finger-breadths;
therein, the emission of the void (śūnyoccāra) is proclaimed through the division of parts.
The practice is remembered as being exactly as described in the *Navasūtra*;
by that, O Goddess of Gods, success is attained—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (275)
O Goddess, listen as I shall speak of another most secret [practice] according to the truth;
O Goddess, one may behold this supreme application at that very moment.
O Goddess, having performed the divine [rite] on the left and right [sides], the king of yogis should behold the four digits blazing like a lamp.
When the beginning is joined with the end in both [the eyes], it is auspicious;
however, when that which is touched in the middle region is seen in both, it is likewise auspicious. (278)
When one does not perceive the "third eye" (Aṃbaka) during the uprooting of the light, listen to the fruit of the yoga of meditation for all yogas indeed. || 279 ||
One gains intelligence, beauty, and likewise health; one grasps even that which is spoken but once.
Whatever there may be, whether divine or non-divine, one sees it all, and not otherwise. (280)
Within three months, they shall become knowers of all verbal compositions;
likewise, they shall possess the power of rising up [from the ground] and of invisibility through the application of ointments and collyrium.
Success through pills and other means shall be attained within six months;
O Goddess, this supreme nectar of practice has been fully explained. (282)
O Goddess of gods, O auspicious one, truth is seen directly as equal;
yet those who know other tantras are those who deliberate upon what is logical and illogical. || 283 ||
In this way, having obtained knowledge, those ascetics cast themselves down;
O Goddess, they do not [truly] know this knowledge, the supreme reality of knowledge. (284)
(462) Serve this conviction, for it belongs to both yourself and others; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, this Haṃsa-yoga has been described according to the full extent of the ritual procedure. 285.
Therefore, O Goddess of noble conduct, for one who understands the knowledge and realization of the process (prakriyā),
there is the vision of the three deities therein.
By that [method], it shall be seen directly according to the prescribed rule, and not otherwise.
O beautiful goddess, I shall explain the sacrifice once again. (287)
The seat [is offered] with the five Brahmakalās, with the one joined by the nine Śaktis, with the Praṇava alone, and likewise with the limbs of the Vidyā.
The Supreme Lord is to be worshipped by means of Varuṇa alone;
He should be worshipped in the lotus of the heart and upon the sacrificial ground by one who desires spiritual perfection.
And the yogin attains accomplishment if he practices for six months;
O Goddess of Gods, on the very first day, a direct realization shall arise. (290)
O Goddess, from that very churning, success (siddhi) always arises;
from sacrifice, success is born, and through knowledge, one attains absolute liberation (kaivalya). || 291 ||
Through meditation and the practice of recitation (japa), he bestows perfection; of this there is no doubt.
One should place Īśāna above, and Tatpuruṣa is traditionally taught for the east.
Aghora is indeed in the south, Vāmadeva likewise in the north,
and Sadyojāta, O Goddess of Gods, is situated in the west.
One should place the heart in the southeast and the head in the northeast;
O Goddess, one should likewise place the crest-lock in the southwest and the armor in the northwest. (294)
The wise one should place [the offerings] in the region where blood flows;
thus, being well-composed, she should worship with a single *avaruṇa* mantra. (295)
Having performed the libation for the mandala, one should offer the elevenfold oblation;
O Goddess of the gods, one should then offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra of Śiva in due order.
Sacrifice is declared to be performed upon the sacrificial mound and within the mandala;
now listen, O Goddess, as I describe the sacrifice performed within the heart-lotus. || 297 ||
One should contemplate reality from the letter *e*; the letter *ai* is to be pointed out as such.
Furthermore, the four bases of dharma (*dharmapāda*) are to be understood as straight and red. (298)
O Goddess of gods, one should not install the Śaktis with the syllable Oṃ;
rather, one should first fashion the Mūrti (the Form), by means of which everything is accomplished without exception. (299)
Having invoked the supreme Śiva with the tenth *praṇava*,
the wise one should cause the triple reality (*tritatva*) to be established through the application of the *nyāsa* of the *praṇava*. (300)
One should assign the letter Ā in the east, the letter Ī in the south,
the letter Ū in the west, and the seed-syllable of space (HŪṂ) in the north.
O Goddess of the gods, one should assign the seed-syllable *maṃ* to the northeast;
the seed-syllable *vyāṃ* to the region of the wind (northwest), and the seed-syllable *bīṃ* to the southwest.
O Goddess of the gods, one should place the seed-syllable in the southeast;
it is proclaimed that the placement [of the mantra] at the time of meditation is performed with that very same syllable. || 303 ||
Listen again, O Goddess of gods; I shall tell you everything:
the stationary and the moving, as well as those born from eggs and those born from sweat. (304)
Seeing those of evil nature who are harmful toward him— whether they be gods, dānavas, animals, or fanged beings of cruel deeds— the wise man should reflect upon them. (305)
O Goddess, this has been declared by me through my vision; one should contemplate all those [deities] of a yogin who is a wicked being, just as was my initiation in the past.
Having established oneself in both the real and the unreal, one should contemplate the imperishable Śiva;
for when thus contemplated, O auspicious one, they attain pacification.
Thus, among all those sinful mosquitoes, those evil-minded ones did not harm that yogin; having seen Śiva, they attained equanimity. || 308 ||
Reflecting thus constantly, wander at your ease, having become one with the auspicious [Śiva], devoted to the yoga of meditation. (309)
Wherever the mind may go for the yogi who is meditating,
that very thing is the supreme Brahman, established in its entirety through every mode of being. (310)
Regarding auspicious and inauspicious actions, and regarding desirable and undesirable rebirths,
as well as among all stationary beings, the wise man remains established everywhere.
That which the mind goes toward—both the inconceivable and the conceivable—that alone is to be known as the Supreme Brahman by those who desire their own welfare. || 312 ||
Having become equal-minded toward all things through their true nature,
and thus having attained equanimity, he enters the imperishable Śiva.
Thus, O Goddess, O beautiful one, the "Equal Flavor" (samarasa) has been proclaimed to you;
it is common to all the compendiums and was spoken by the Lord who is honored by all.
Having thus become one of equal flavor, the well-concentrated yogins attain accomplishment;
there is no doubt in this matter, they are liberated—of this there is no uncertainty. (315)
Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare the supreme secret in brief, by the mere knowledge of which one is liberated from the bondage of birth. (316)
O Goddess, I shall now explain that most auspicious supreme binding of the mudrā:
having placed the two hands palms-upward, one should form the braid-binding (veṇībandha). || 317 ||
But by means of the letter Ā, it is not the letter Na, yet endowed with the letter Aṅ;
joined with the letter Vya and endowed with the form of the sky (Vyoma). || 318 ||
Having extended both index fingers, it is proclaimed as the Netra-mudrā; when the two thumbs are joined, it is known as the Śikhā-mudrā, which severs the bonds of men. (319)
Having made these two [hands] equal, it is proclaimed as the *śiras-mudrā*.
The *hṛdaya-vidyā* is distinguished [by this], and likewise the *piṇḍita* is the *kavaca*. (320)
They say that the *Śāstra* consists of thirty-five syllables;
this, O Goddess, beautiful one, is renowned as being devoted to Yoga. 321.
All this is beyond description; one should reveal everything through speech.
O Goddess, the study [of the scriptures] is declared to be according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas. (322)
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the supreme consecration (adhivāsana)."
And the sacrificial pap (caru), O Mahādeva, as well as the tooth-stick (dantadhāvana). || 1 ||
"O Blessed One, please tell me the procedure for the awakening through mantras.

Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret, the most excellent preliminary consecration (adhivāsana). || 2 ||
I shall tell you in its entirety all that is common to every [astrological] compendium:
the auspicious lunar days, constellations, weekdays, and omens.
Having obtained sites that are celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial, and having thoroughly examined them,
one should first examine the terrestrial site according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures.
Or on the Himavat mountain and the Vindhya, or likewise on Pāriyātra and Ambuda; on Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, or on the delightful heap of holy rocks.
In the Ganges and other such foremost rivers, as well as in Antarvedī;
or likewise in a cremation ground, in a house, or even in a temple. (6)
And one should act likewise in a garden, in a cluster of lotuses, or on a riverbank;
in such auspicious places as these, or wherever else one finds delight.
It is fourfold, beginning with white, red, yellow, and black;
for Brāhmaṇas the ground is white, but for the other three [castes] it is red.
The earth of a Vaiśya is said to be yellow, and that of a Śūdra is black;
for a Brāhmaṇa it has a sweet taste, while for a Kṣatriya it is astringent.
For the Vaiśya, however, the earth is said to possess six tastes; for the Śūdra, it is recorded as having a pungent taste.
Today, the earth has the scent of fragrance for the twice-born Brāhmaṇa, while for the Kṣatriya, it has the scent of blood.
The ground of a Śūdra should have the smell of excrement and the smell of alkaline salt;
one should cause it to be dug up to the depth of a knee and then fill it back in. (11)
One should perform the formal acquisition of the ground on such a site of the earth.
Having performed the sacrifice, O Goddess of the lords of gods, one should offer oblations eight hundred times in sequence;
there, the high-souled preceptor must present the bali offering.
"O Goddess, thus has the consecration of the ground been described to you;
on the following day, O Queen of Gods, one should begin the preliminary rite (adhivāsana)."
The practitioner, having accumulated the necessary provisions, should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) there,
provided with perfumes and flowers, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and unbroken grains (akṣata).
Having worshipped with the *garbha* mantras, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) right there;
having offered oblations to this God of gods and to the mantras in their proper sequence, (verse 16).
O fair-faced one, one hundred oblations are to be offered to the deity;
having offered a tenth part of the mantras, one should then present the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having reached the path, one should worship all of them there;
one should worship all the principles (tattvas) according to the prescribed sequence of perfumes and flowers. || 18 ||
Having thus worshipped the principles (tattvas), perform the ritual immolation of the victim;
having immolated it with all the mantras, one should deposit the principles in their proper sequence.
One should bind [the soul] with the fetters of the tattvas, according to the sequence of each respective tattva;
having bound the fetters with knots, one should cause it to dwell there in union.

Having performed the *karaṇī* and *kartarī* [mudrās], and having prepared the various kinds of ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*), one should visualize all of them as being completely integrated and united with the deity. (21)

Having thus performed the ritual according to the rules, one should bring the Jātavedas fire into a copper vessel or an earthenware bowl, proceeding in due order through the various stations of the fire.
O Goddess of the gods, perform the sprinkling with the Gāyatrī mantra according to its true essence;
having worshipped it with the five Brahmans, one should then cast it into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The one skilled in purification should place a seat there;
he should purify the pit with the Astra-mantra, and having drawn lines upon it and sprinkled it with water, he should clear it out.
Having done this, O Goddess of Gods, one should prepare a seat;
there, one should establish Vāgīśī, the great sovereign who is in her menses.
Then, O Goddess, O beautiful one, having recited each mantra three times,
the fire of Śiva is kindled by means of the eleventh mantra. (26)
O Dear One, for the purpose of purification through ritual refinement,
one who knows the mantras of the fire-oblation should subsequently offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) into the Śiva-fire that has been generated.
O Goddess, one should cook the *caru* according to the ritual procedure prescribed by the rules;
having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for all the tantras, one should then place the three principles (*tritattva*) therein.
One should wrap the ear with a thread and cause it to be smeared with milk;
[one should also offer] balls made of *linīvāra*, *śyāmāka*, barley, and wheat. (29)
It should be prepared with honey and medicinal herbs, and likewise with *kaṅgu* grain;
the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) must always be made until the vessel is full.
Furthermore, whatever ritual action is proclaimed, such as moving and rotating,
is performed with the five Brahmans and also with the eleventh.
The preceptor should again perform [the rite] joined with this procedure,
having offered the *saṃpāta* oblation once with each of all the mantras.
O Goddess of the gods, one should cause the weapon-substance to be placed in the fire with the *svāhā* offering;
having thus offered according to the rite, one should then divide it into three parts.
Having offered the sacrifice, the woman of excellent complexion should set aside two or three portions for the deity;
she should then set aside a third portion for the practitioners according to the prescribed ritual.
One should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the ritual procedure prescribed by rule:
cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with kuśa grass.
Having brought these, O beautiful one, the *pañcagavya* should be prepared:
cow dung with the *Sadyojāta* mantra, and cow urine with the *Guhyaka* (Vāmadeva) mantra. (36)
One should take the clarified butter with the Aghora mantra, and one should take the curd with the Vaktreṇa mantra;
one should take the milk with the Īśāna mantra, and the water from kuśa grass with the Gāyatrī mantra.
Having consecrated it, O lady of excellent hips, one should recite all the mantras once;
whatever food or drink is to be given should be offered with the Vaktra-mantra.
Even the tooth-stick used here should be auspicious, provided with milk and leaves, free from notches, devoid of sharp points, and measured at twelve finger-breadths. (39)
One should give that which has been consecrated with the Vaktra-mantra to his guru.
Having placed the clarified butter on the fire, take it down and perform the purification (utpavana).

Then, having performed the *nīrājana* rite, one should perform the sprinkling of the faces (*vaktrābhidhāraṇa*). The wise practitioner should perform the sprinkling of the faces with the *sadyojāta* mantra using the left [hand]. (41)
One should perform the expiation with the Astra-mantra; its extraction is traditionally taught as being performed through the principle of reality (tattva).
When this has been done, O Goddess of the Gods, the fire of Śiva is generated.
Thereafter, those who are well-composed should perform the ritual arrangement of the lotus;
there, one should distribute the seats in sequence, beginning with Ananta.
One should invoke the Lord of Gods according to the ritual previously observed;
the wise man should always install Brahmā in the eastern direction.
They say that Rudra is in the south and Viṣṇu in the west;
one should always install Śivā, the Supreme Goddess, in the north for the sake of Śiva.

One should worship the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas), the World-Protectors (lokapālas), and the weapons in their proper order, seated upon their seats, using the Pāvamāna hymn according to the sequence. (46)
Now listen, O Goddess, to the procedure that must first be performed in due order:
one should fashion jars made of gold and silver, filled with jewels.
They should be made of copper or else one should have them made of clay;
they should be smeared with sandalwood paste and decorated with sprouts of unseasoned radish.
Having prepared the seat, one should place the jar called Śiva;
the principle of the self (ātmatattva) in the lower part, and the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) in the middle.
One should place the third principle, Śivatattva, above;
there, the one of great intelligence, having beheld all things with his vision, [should proceed]. (50)
All that becomes like a crest; no deliberation need be made in this matter.
480) When the *vardhanī* vessel is filled with water, [one should offer] with all the mantras once each. || 51 ||
Then, O Goddess, the preceptor should mutter the Astra-mantra, whirl [the vessel],
and offer an unbroken stream of water outside.
Accompanied by the *kalaśa* and the *ardha*, the preceptor, whose very self is Śiva, should go in front of the *vardhanī* while muttering the *astra-mantra*.
One should rotate [the vessel] within the square and then place it back in that very same spot;
having scattered the syllables, the wise one should worship with that [offering].
Having sprinkled them again with the five products of the cow and with scented water, one should then rotate the jar; this indeed is remembered as the prescribed procedure.
One should then whirl the full water-pot; thereafter follows the consecration of the deity (devādhivāsana).
Then one should go to the fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa), and after that, the libation into the mandala (maṇḍalatarpaṇa). || 56 ||

The consecration of the directions and likewise the sounding of the notes should follow immediately after; the cleaning of the teeth should take place on one's lap—this indeed is the prescribed rule. || 57 ||
One who knows the ritual procedure should fashion [the images] from gold, silver, copper, and likewise from ruby, as well as from sapphire and great sapphire.
If even these are not available, the wise man should fashion [the image] with pigments,
using very beautiful colors resembling rice and wheat for the reflection.
One should draw the divine maṇḍala with perfectly straight and beautiful lines;
the wise practitioner should execute those [details] as described in the Northern Sūtra.
By means of that classification of the sūtra, one should draw the auspicious maṇḍala;
there, O Goddess of Gods, one should perform worship according to the ritual previously observed. (61)
Having thus performed worship according to the rule, he should then carry out the initiation;

O Goddess of the Gods, the practitioner, having recited his chosen mantra one hundred and eight times, should perform the consecration, as has already been described.

Then the preceptor, whose doubts have been severed, should consecrate the disciples with twenty, nine, or ten water-pots. (66)
Beginning with the Earth and ending with Māyā as the final jar; beginning with the Nirmāṇa-jar and ending with Aiśvarya as the final one. (67)
Having enclosed this [mantra] within the *saṃpuṭa* formation, one should perform the consecration in the evening;
indeed, one should consecrate with fifty jars using the mantra known as the *vidyā*.
O Goddess of the Gods, beginning from the earth up to the stainless ultimate reality (tattva), one should consecrate the preceptor in due order.
The teachers who understand the meaning of the five sūtras have reached the further shore of reality;
when one is consecrated by them, that guru becomes equal to Śiva.
O Goddess, one who has reached the further shore of the Śiva-tattva should feed [the guests] by virtue of this vision.
Beginning from the earth, those pitchers which have been proclaimed [should be offered]. (71)
The arrangement of the ritual layout (vyūhanyāsa) must be performed; indeed, one should place the nine [deities] of the three principles (tritatva).
With nine water-pots (kalaśa), one should likewise install the nine principles (nava-tattva).
Having repeated those seven mantras over each individual flask by the wise,
or else, he should cause the consecration to be performed with a single flask.
Endowed with all the principles (tattvas), mantras, and oceans,
one should perform this rite here using a single water-pot alone.
The pedestal should be four cubits in size and adorned on all sides;
its height, however, should be made exactly one cubit by those who are well-composed.
The site of the altar was beautifully adorned with four archways, graced by banners and flags, and further embellished by canopies resembling water-bubbles. (76)
It was adorned with variegated flowers and beautified by mango sprouts, as well as with svastikas, lotuses, and *saṃdhārthaka* designs. || 77 ||

O lady of auspicious countenance, the *pūrva* [mantras] should be offered right there into the jars, accompanied by the sounding of conchs and kettledrums, as well as the sounds of musical instruments. (78)
At that time, one should cause the sounds of the Vedas and the cries of victory to be raised, accompanied by auspicious ceremonies, festive rites, and the music of stringed instruments. || 79 ||
Then the preceptor should consecrate the disciple, O Goddess of the Gods, beginning from the east and proceeding in due order until the end of Māyā, as it has been proclaimed. (80)
Then the preceptor should bring the consecrated one together with Śiva;
having held a parasol over him, his feet should be provided with sandals. (81)
Having established [the deity] upon that fashioned divine seat, the wise one,
having worshipped with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and other rites, should worship it even more abundantly.
From this day forward, O wise one, you must act as the teacher of the Śiva-tantra and constantly bestow grace upon those dwelling in the four stages of life (āśramas). 83.
One should perform the exposition and worship, as well as the instruction of the teacher and disciple;
one should perform a small amount of recitation during the day and offer a small amount of oblations into the fire. (84)
One should always perform even a brief meditation; this is your perpetual sacrificial session (satra).
Likewise, one should prepare the *karaṇī*, the *kartarī*, the *saṃhitā*, as well as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles. (85)
"Having worshipped [the deity] with the *arghya* and other offerings, one should practice the authority (*adhikāra*).
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
The Goddess said:

tell me now how they are illuminated among those mantras."
In all the tantras, the commands of Śiva are heard as "Oṃ" and "Namaḥ.
O Blessed One, please explain why these two command and authorize; it behoves you to speak.
O Goddess, listen, for I shall tell you in its entirety the supreme secret, the most excellent essence of mantra, which has not been declared to anyone. 3.
O virtuous lady, that which was declared by me as "all-pervading" should be understood as the half-moon within this tantra; of this there is no doubt. (4)
And one part of that very [syllable] is designated as "cessation" (nirodha);
joined with that, the syllable Oṃ is proclaimed to be situated above. || 5 ||
That which is indeed a portion of the sound (nāda), known as "the upward-moving," is proclaimed to be the letter *na* when it has become circular.
O Goddess of the gods, I shall describe those four parts of Śakti exactly as they exist; listen to me as I speak according to the truth.
Amṛtā, however, is situated at the head; she has arisen from me as the sun, extremely subtle, extending horizontally and reaching halfway toward the south.
The subtle power (kalā), however, which is named Sūkṣmā, extends upward and downward;
it is copper-colored at its tip, the fourth [power], and is well-joined with Bindu and Nāda. (9)
O beautiful one, O lady of excellent countenance, he has explained to you how Śiva, having pervaded all the social classes (varṇas), stands stationed at their side.
Emerging as if from lines, it impels [the sound] on all sides;
by that, the words are divided and severed, as are the junctions of the syllables.
Neither the gods, including Indra, nor the sages, nor other yogis dwelling on earth, were able to leap over her. || 12 ||
By him this entire world, both moving and unmoving, is pervaded;
by him all the collection of mantras is made known in its entirety.
Mantras are accomplished when their beginning and end are suppressed; it is not otherwise.
The principle of Śiva is supremely pure, abiding both externally and internally. (14)
The central principle has emerged from the Bindu below and above;
by that, those mantras and powers are impelled, without a doubt. (15)
Whatever is desired by the mind is accomplished here; there is no doubt about this.
Having placed the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning, one should employ the word of salutation (*namaskāra*).
O beautiful one, this conjunction of mantras has been explained to you:
namely, the utterances of Svāhā, Vaṣaṭ, and Suvauṣaṭ.
O Goddess, the syllable *phaṭ* accompanied by the syllable *huṃ*—this should be understood with effort as the union of power (*śakti*). || 18 ||
The ritual acts of worship and recitation are joined with *namaḥ*;
491) they are joined with *svāhā* in fire-offerings (*homa*) and in rites of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*). || 19 ||
One should employ the *vauṣaṭ* syllable when performing rites of pacification (*śāntika*);
and for the sake of nourishment (*puṣṭi*), one should always perform [the rite] joined with the syllables *sa* and *o*.
The second [syllable] is joined with that [first], conjoined with the letters *a* and *u*,
and through the application of the mantra of the letter *ṣa*, together with the letter *ha*.
For the sake of nourishing all mantras, whether for oneself or for another,
one should perform the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) accompanied by the syllable *vaṣaṭ*.
One should employ "namo namaḥ" for the purpose of fueling all the mantras;
indeed, when the entire collection of mantras is devoid of the *praṇava*. (23)

O beautiful one, by beginning with the syllable *huṃ* and ending with *svāhā*, one should summon [the deity] through recitation and so forth; one who is always pure through the vows and recitation [attains this]. (24)
By means of the initial application of the syllable *huṃ* and joining it with the syllable *phaṭ*, one causes even spirits dwelling in divine realms to be expelled. (25)
That same [mantra], joined with *mā* and ending with *phaṭ phaṭ*, is the second;
one should employ this procedure for killing (*māraṇa*), while all the remaining [mantras] are joined with *namaḥ*. || 26 ||
Thus it has been declared to you that they grant success in all undertakings;
this purity applies at the time of the fire-oblation (homa), as well as always during the practice of recitation (japa).

Having understood this through which [the goal] must be accomplished by the teachers at the time of initiation, [the disciple] should always be intent on eating only one meal, or even devoted to fasting. (28)
One should always eat only at night, or constantly subsist on alms-food,
or even perform the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances during the time of recitation. (29)
By following this very sequence, one should accomplish the deity of the mantra;
otherwise, the practitioners do not achieve success and instead wither away like trees.
I shall explain to you how a practitioner may accomplish all rites through the fire-oblation; listen to me with a one-pointed mind. (31)

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa according to the procedure previously observed, the knower of mantras—versed in the reality of the three locations and times and devoted to Śiva and Śakti—[should proceed]. || 32 ||
Then the practitioner, being self-restrained, should offer oblations while remaining disciplined in his recitation;
he should maintain the connection between each syllable and the *akṣata* grains, neither too fast nor too slow.
Clearly joined with a consonant, it may be short or long as required;
when joined with a *visarga* or combined with its own [vowel], it is called *pluta*—thus have I declared. (34)
Having understood this, the wise person should perform recitation and fire-offerings;
and having prepared a beautiful seat for the consecration with *śrīparṇī* wood, he should proceed. (35)
Likewise, O Goddess, there may be a seat of kusha grass or a seat of cow dung; with these principal seats, which are spacious and well-prepared, one should sit. (36)
Standing, the mantra-practitioner should always perform the fire-oblation (homa) and never be restless;
having risen from his seat, the preceptor should perform the oblation upon the ground.
Great and intense pain arises; there is no doubt about this.
When the practitioner is afflicted by such pain, he never attains the hundred thousand [recitations]. (38)
When the Adhipa is Kaṭigranthi, there is indeed consumption (aśoṣa), fever (āmaya), and a great stiffness of the waist;
likewise, there is a most terrible rigidity of the chest and disease in the sides. (39)
Such sufferings as these arise; of this there is no doubt.
When a disease occurs, the physician should act accordingly. (40)
Likewise, I shall explain it at the end; listen briefly, O virtuous one!
The commencement of yoga should never be undertaken without [proper] discourse.
Neither when afflicted by hunger nor when afflicted by thirst, nor indeed in the midst of a crowd of people, but remaining in that divine shelter protected from the wind, one should practice. 42.
But another who acts otherwise never attains the target;
that, O beautiful one, is said by you to be the yoga of conceptual construction (vikalpa).
O Goddess of the Gods, listen as I explain in brief how the initiation master must perform the fire oblation at the time of initiation. (44)
For even among the great, the remainder is born afflicted by hunger;
when tormented by thirst, a fault arises that causes a most terrible agitation of the walls.
From the agitation of bile (pitta), disease will undoubtedly arise for the guide;
there will be trembling, and bile, as well as boils and the like, originating from fire. (46)
O Goddess, from the agitation of bile (pitta), a most terrible illusory disease arises;
it occurs for one afflicted by hunger and thirst, O virtuous lady, along with the desire for meat. 47.
One who is fit for the application of perfected mantras becomes the most excellent of teachers;
yet, one who is preoccupied with the nine mantra-words may be distracted by hunger. (48)
Therefore, the best of teachers should eat in a well-prepared place;
having partaken of an offering-food (haviṣya) meal saturated with ghee and milk. (49)
Having consumed milk-rice (pāyasa), he should then commence the initiation;
it should be concluded with the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), but one should not perform the ritual dismissal (utsarga).
If the fire's heat does not burn [the offering], one should cause it to fall by means of the *prasṛta* [gesture].
When the practitioner is being burned, he should perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). || 51 ||
But for one whose mouth is burning, the mantras turn away from him; they do not accomplish his rites. Therefore, one should avoid such a person.
O beautiful one, when the eyes are being burnt, the gods become angry;
therefore, O goddess, a fault arises from that, so one should avoid it. || 53 ||
When the *rome*s are being burned, the sages always become angry;
when these [other things] are being burned, they do so out of respect for the sake of expiation. (54)
O Goddess of the gods, having bowed with a composed mind and uttered this single verse, and having meditated upon the reality, one shall be purified of all doubts regarding expiations. (55)
The preceptors should offer the ladle full with the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation;
the preceptor, having placed his two big toes together, [should do so] with the hand extended.
The wise one should cause [the ladle] to fall with both hands turned upward;
O Goddess, in this way the vessel is not scorched, nor is the oblation spilled.
But when the vessel is burnt, one should perform an expiatory oblation (prāyaścitta) according to the previously mentioned procedure; it becomes pure, of this there is no doubt. || 58 ||
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said: O God of gods, in former times the earth was entrusted by you to a portion in heaven;
O God, that deposit was maintained according to the rules of the sacred observance.
O Goddess of the Gods, how are the principles (tattvas) to be known within one's own body by the high-souled teacher? O Blessed One, you should explain this.
O Goddess, listen, for I shall speak the supreme secret, the unsurpassed knowledge of all, by the mere realization of which one is liberated; of this there is no doubt. (3)
First, O Goddess of the lords of gods, one should contemplate the Mātṛkā;
one should join the seed-syllable on the right and place the womb-syllable on the left.
(500) Endowed with the *praṇava* at the beginning and ending with the word *namaskāra*,
the mantra should indeed be performed by the preceptor for each and every class of letters.
Following that, the ninth [syllable] is the prior arrangement of the *mātṛkā*;
having again uttered the ninth, one should cause it to transcend sound.
Having thus performed the placement, O Goddess of gods, one should once again distinguish them; the letter *A* is to be known as that which one should place below the navel.
One should place the syllable *ya*, belonging to the one called Puruṣa, in the heart-lotus;
thereafter, O Goddess, one should place Niyati upon the petals.
Thus, O Goddess of the Gods, Māyā, Vidyā, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
the Śivatattva indeed stands above them all.
Having thus deposited the principles (tattvas) according to the sequence beginning with Sakala,
and having carefully deposited the Bindu, Nāda, and Śakti in the same manner, (verse 10).
O Goddess, listen next to the placement of the deities (devatānyāsa) originating from the heart; one should first contemplate the arrangement of the solar disc (sūryamaṇḍala). 11.
The second is the placement (nyāsa) of Aindava, and the third is the placement of Vahni;
likewise, there are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara.
Sadāśiva, Śiva, and [Īśvara], as well as [Śakti], in their respective order;
likewise Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti. (13)
One should then install Nāda-śakti and Śiva in their proper order;
the first is the digit (kalā) named Sūkṣmā, and the second is Su-sūkṣmā.
Amṛtā, Mṛtā, and the third, Bījāmṛta; beyond that, O Queen of the Gods, one should always install these five [syllables] according to the manner of the Śaktis. (15)
O Great Goddess, the placement of the wheels (cakranyāsa) has thus been described previously;
it is already known to you, O Goddess—what else shall I tell you? (16)
And that which was told to me here with both the eye and fear—that has been understood by you, O Goddess; is there any truth beyond this? (17)
I shall now proclaim the ritual placement upon the hands (kara-nyāsa); listen with a one-pointed mind.
One should first perform the ninefold placement, dividing each [syllable] individually; of this there is no doubt. (18)
Having again uttered the mantra, one should place [the thumb] with the tip of the right thumb;
the entire [mantra] is on the right thumb, and the remainder should be performed as before.
O Goddess, once the *kara-nyāsa* has been performed, one should contemplate Śiva right there; having first deposited the three principles (*tritatva*), one should subsequently deposit Śiva. (20)
When this has been done, O Goddess, the Hand of Śiva is then remembered;
by that, all this work—the worship as well as the sprinkling—is accomplished.
One should perform both the grasping and the joining with the hand of Śiva;
first, the placement of the hands is prescribed, but not the [placement] of oneself. || 22 ||
O Goddess, having indeed placed the second syllable of Mātṛkā, the Navātmā as the third, and that which is distinct from it as the fourth. || 23 ||
The fifth is proclaimed according to the sequence beginning with Sakala;
O Goddess, the thirteenth is supreme and established as the remedy for all diseases.
Having first performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) in this manner, the knower of yoga should meditate upon the reality (*tattva*).
If there is the presence of the thirteenfold self for the knower of reality, [then success follows]. (25)
O fair-faced one, he indeed bestows grace even upon one who is powerless;
he performs initiation by his word and by his glance—of this there is no doubt. (26)
O Goddess, this great nyāsa should be practiced with diligent effort;
by its mere sight or by its recitation, a living being becomes pure—of this there is no doubt. (27)
There is no doubt regarding mental [action], nor is there any doubt regarding touch;
O Goddess of gods, once the nyāsa has been performed, one is capable in all rites.
O Goddess, this great and meritorious Nyāsa has been proclaimed by me;
even he who understands it alone is liberated, without a doubt. (29)
Having thus first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), the teacher, with all doubts severed, is not stained by merit or sin; he is the liberator even of his own teacher. (30)
Thus, O Goddess of gods, this ritual placement (nyāsa) should not be given to just anyone;
it must be given to a wise preceptor who has been duly consecrated.
Otherwise, by speaking [falsely] to wicked mortals, one would become a partaker of a single word;
therefore, the general characteristics of all *saṃhitās* must be understood by the teacher.
O Great Goddess, when this has been performed, whoever they may be who have committed evil deeds, they are liberated by the sight of that Ācārya; of this there is no doubt. (33)
By this, one has indeed accomplished [the goal]; behold, or listen even to you: merely by the sight of his form and by the hearing of the mantras. (34)
(506) "O lady of beautiful hips, it is certain by the mere sight [of you], certain by the leading [of you] forward,
and indeed by the word 'Agni' and the word 'noose'. (35)
O Goddess, even the lowest of men is liberated from sins by hearing the sound [of the Guru];
O Goddess, [he is likewise freed] by beholding the body of the high-souled teacher.
One shall go as far as the world of Brahmā; of this there is no doubt.
Listen, O Goddess, as I speak: merely by hearing the mantras [this occurs]. (37)
Upon hearing the mantra, O Goddess, the sinful soul attains union with Rudra;
by beholding the smoke, one attains union with Viṣṇu. || 38 ||
O goddess of beautiful hips, listen as I speak with the word "Agni":
it refers to that manifestation which occurs within the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva) for one who performs evil deeds. (39)
There is no doubt through the mind, and there is no uncertainty through touch. This great fruit of the greatness of Śiva has been told to you, O Goddess. (40)
Knowing this, O Goddess of gods, perform the initiation as you desire;
by this, mortals who were bound like animals become liberated from their fetters. (41)
Being stainless and free from the fever of affliction, they attain union with Śiva;
therefore, O fair-faced one, I shall explain the classification of mantras.

Oṃ aṃ ūn namaḥ | Oṃ yaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ laṃ namaḥ | Oṃ maṃ namaḥ | Oṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ raṃ namaḥ | Oṃ haṃ namaḥ | Oṃ hṛṃ namaḥ | Oṃ āṃ namaḥ | [He] consists of the nine [vowels]. Oṃ kaṃ khaṃ gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ namaḥ | Oṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ namaḥ ||

Oṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ namaḥ | Oṃ paṃ phaṃ baṃ bhaṃ maṃ namaḥ | One should place [these] upon the fingers of the hand. Oṃ ya ra la va namaḥ | [One should place this] in the middle of the hand. Oṃ śa ṣa sa ha namaḥ | Oṃ [one should place this] at the wrist. Oṃ kṣaṃ namaḥ | [This is for] the joining of the palms (saṃpuṭīkaraṇa).
The placement on the left hand: Oṃ a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ | Namaḥ. One should place one syllable at each joint.
Oṃ aṃ namaḥ, in the middle of the hand.
O Goddess of the gods, one should place the supreme syllable at the wrist;
beginning with the thumb, one should then place the five Brahmans.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the limbs of Śiva, beginning with the middle finger, in their proper order;
[each limb] is joined with the syllable *rudra* and *oṃ*, and accompanied by the syllable *phaṭ*. (44)
One should perform the purification of the hands as well as the anointing of the body;
having purified the ground of the temple, one should carry out all of this with this [mudrā]. || 45 ||
O Goddess, this has been declared for the sake of some purification; indeed, by means of all this, whatever is necessary for purification must be performed.

Oṃ, salutation to Earth. Oṃ, salutation to Water. Oṃ, salutation to Fire. Oṃ, salutation to Wind. Oṃ, salutation to Space. Oṃ, salutation to Ego-consciousness. Oṃ, salutation to Intellect. Oṃ, salutation to Primordial Matter. Oṃ, salutation to the Spirit. Oṃ, salutation to Necessity. Oṃ, salutation to Time.
Homage! Oṃ rāgāya, homage! Oṃ vidyāyai, homage! Oṃ kālāya, homage! [p.
510] Homage to Vidyā! Homage to Īśvara! Homage to Sadāśiva! Homage to Śiva! One should perform the placement starting from the feet. Oṃ to the heart.
Namaḥ | Oṃ gīr namaḥ | Oṃ hun namaḥ | Oṃ śiva namaḥ | Oṃ laṃ namaḥ | Oṃ raṃ namaḥ | Oṃ juṃ namaḥ. One should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the heart, the throat, and the face.
O lady of excellent vows, this placement of the portions of power (śakti-kalā) has been described to you.
One should place the fifth as Śakti; one should then place the digit (kalā) of Śiva-Śakti.
But the remainder, O fair-faced one, should be performed as a mental placement (nyāsa). When the high-souled preceptor bestows the Hand of Śiva, [the disciple should perform it mentally]. (48)
One should perform the sacrifice and the ritual placement (nyāsa) in their entirety with the left hand.
O virtuous lady, listen as I explain the procedure for the Mātṛkā-homa at the time of the oblation. (49)
Having bound a single cord or even four, O woman of excellent complexion, the guide, having first performed the consecration with fire, [should proceed]. (50)
There, in that well-prepared [fire], the supreme preceptor should offer oblations one by one in direct order, and then again in reverse order.
One who desires success in the forward order should perform the path even in the reverse order;
indeed, the instructor must offer the oblation both in the forward and reverse orders.
Thus, O Goddess, this most difficult-to-attain ritual placement (nyāsa) has been told to you;
and the arrangement of the mantras as well, O beautiful one, has been explained to you. (53)
The Goddess said:
O Lord, what is declared to be the sacrifice preceded by the primordial [principle]?
I wish to understand this, O Blessed One; you should deign to explain it.
O Goddess, listen; I shall explain that which you have asked.
O Goddess of beautiful countenance, I will fully declare it to you.
O best of goddesses, those who are composed in mind should first perform the Gaṇa sacrifice;
it should be performed with one hand and endowed with five limbs.
With his mind fixed on the meditation of Śiva, he should perform the placement of the five-fold Śiva;
he should place an eight-petaled lotus, complete with filaments and a pericarp.
One should place the god Gaṇeśa, worshipped by the world, upon the pericarp (karṇikā). Having placed the heart-mantra in the southeast, one should place the head-mantra in the northeast. (58)
O Goddess, one should place the *śikhā* in the southwest and the *tvac* in the northwest;
one should place the *astra* in the four directions—this indeed is the prescribed ritual.

Oṃ hṛn namaḥ | Oṃ hin namaḥ | Oṃ hun namaḥ | Oṃ haiṃ namaḥ | Oṃ han namaḥ | Oṃ jahi namaḥ | Oṃ hanala namaḥ | Oṃ jahi namaḥ | Oṃ an namaḥ. These are for the heart, head, crest-lock, armor, and weapon, respectively.
Oṃ hrauṃ, homage! Oṃ Gaṇapati! In this manner, one should always worship [the deity] in the pericarp of the Blessed One’s lotus.
The invocation should be performed with the heart-mantra, and the dismissal likewise. (60)
Sprinkling and pouring over with water should indeed be performed with the five [mantras], there is no doubt;
one should purify the ground with the Astra-mantra—this is remembered as the prescribed rule. (61)
One should perform the rite of cremation with all of these;
having performed the libation in the mandala, one should offer the bali-oblation in the ten directions.
One should cause an offering to be given everywhere to the ninefold deity;
by that, the entire multitude of spirits attains satisfaction without exception. (63)
O Goddess of good vows, who does not rejoice at the festival of the lords?
Therefore, all beings always rejoice because of Śiva’s offering of oblations. 64.
And two kinds of offerings (bali) should be presented by the high-souled preceptor: milk-rice, rice mixed with sesame, turmeric-colored food, and rice with jaggery. 65.
One should likewise prepare yellow and black offerings mixed with meat;
O Goddess, this sixfold bali has been described by me to you. (66)
It should be bestowed by a preeminent teacher who desires his own spiritual welfare.
Thus has the sacrifice of Gaṇapati been fully described by me to you. (67)
O Goddess of the gods, one should always perform sacrifices so that they may be free from obstacles; first comes the sacrifice to Gaṇeśa, and second, the acquisition of the ground.
The third is the Adhivāsa, while the fourth is known as the Maṇḍala; the fifth is declared to be for the sake of the great-souled Caṇḍeśa. 69.
The worship of the Guru is remembered as the sixth; thus they have been proclaimed to you. He who, being well-composed, performs this sixfold sacrifice to the Ācārya— || 70 ||
He is liberated from all fetters and goes to the auspicious state that is free from affliction. || 70½ ||
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter of the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
The Goddess said: "Regarding that ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the elements beginning with earth, which was described by you in due order—"
The arrangement of the utterance of the mantras and their respective locations in successive order. || 1 ||
"O Goddess, those [beings] have been known by me according to their respective positions;
yet I wish to hear more, for I have a doubt, O Maheśvarī. (2)
Without form there is no ritual deposit (nyāsa), nor does accomplishment proceed;
those devoid of form do not achieve success, whether they be gods, lords of daityas, or rākṣasas.
Lacking beauty and being exceedingly cruel, these leaders create obstacles; they are overcome by spirits, and serpents enter their dwellings. (4)
The rites of expulsion and possession, killing, and striking;
as well as pacifying, nourishing, and the acts of immortalization. || 5 ||
Subjugation and the fulfillment of commands do not succeed for one who is devoid of beauty;
therefore, O Mahādeva, tell me the form of the mantras.
O Lord of Gods, tell me specifically the nature and form of the principles (tattvas), the deities, and the digits (kalās) that constitute the fruit of the ritual placement (nyāsa).
O Blessed One, you ought to explain this task in its entirety;
[you are] the Lord.
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom, since I have been exhorted by you! (8)
I have not been questioned by anyone—not even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the gods, or the asuras.
This question is highly meritorious and bestows the ground of all fruits without exception.
Among these, the production of even one [image] and its consecration (nyāsa) are extremely difficult to attain;
therefore, becoming intent on breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform it endowed with the characteristics of form.
O Goddess, being composed, one should place the collection of seed-syllables on the right side—
[the syllable] resembling the seven-rayed sun and as pure as clear crystal.
It has the luster of a well-heated iron ball, yet it is free from attachment;
it is as stainless as the rays of the moon, pure, and possesses a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning.
O Goddess, one should contemplate the seed-syllable, which destroys all sins, as it illuminates everything on all sides with thousands of garlands of rays. (13)
O Goddess, by the mere act of meditation, sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are purified;
indeed, yoga arises within the space of a month.
Such is the arrangement of the seed-syllables; now hear concerning the wombs (yoni), which shine forth on all sides like the fierce-rayed sun. 15.
One should contemplate the yoni-cakra as flowing with divine nectar that destroys old age and disease, resembling the moon and its crescents. 16.
In the center, the ninefold deity, resembling molten gold, should be constantly meditated upon by yogis as illuminating all directions. || 17 ||
Or else, in the seed-source, one should contemplate the rays of the God and Goddess,
their radiance like the beams at the end of an eon, all unified into one. (18)
But in the seed-syllable, O Goddess, the Lord himself resides manifesting [himself];
O lady of excellent hips, one should know that Navātman is Sadāśiva. (19)
The rays of these three—the seed, the womb, and the self—should be contemplated by the wise as having condensed into a single drop (bindu) located at the position of the head. 20.
Above that is a divine crest, a sound most difficult to attain;
beyond that stands the Śakti, illuminating all around.
Īśvara is to be known as the Bindu, and Sadāśiva is to be known as the Nāda;
but you alone, O Goddess of the gods, are proclaimed to be Śakti.

"O Goddess, listen here to what is proclaimed as the *mātṛkā* consisting of 'priority' (*paratva*) and 'posteriority' (*aparatva*). I shall now tell you about the principles (*tattvas*) in their combined state. (23)
The syllable *ukāra* should be known as Prakṛti, endowed with three forms;
it should always be meditated upon by yogis as black, red, and white. (24)
The location previously described by me must be understood by the guide;
he should contemplate the syllable *ya*, the principle of Puruṣa, as having the form of Śiva. || 25 ||
Or even if it appears as if instantly extinguished within the surrounding rim of the lotus, by becoming intent upon this meditation, one shall attain the perfection of yoga. || 26 ||
The letter *va* should be known as Niyati; one should contemplate its color as either white or black, impelled by a red thread. (27)
O fair-faced one, meditating in such a manner at the time of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one attains success; there is no doubt about this. O Goddess, I tell you the truth. (28)
One desiring purity should meditate upon the syllable *la*, which has a smoky-colored base, possesses the form of desire, and illuminates its own place. (29)

Having meditated upon [the deity] whose form resembles a dark blue cloud, most terrifying through the principle of illusion (māyātattva), illuminating his own abode, there is no doubt that perfection (siddhi) will be attained. || 30 ||
At the time of the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should indeed contemplate the Vidyā as richly colored red;
for the practitioner who is well-composed will achieve success without hesitation. || 31 ||
Those great forms previously mentioned are accomplished by that [syllable] without a doubt;
indeed, the syllable *ra* is declared to be the Lord (*īśvara*) and is of variegated form (*citrarūpa*). || 32 ||

One should contemplate the placement [of the mantra] in this way: illuminating the Great Reality (mahātattva), it is situated at the crown of the head; indeed, one attains success through non-mentation alone. (33)

Above Īśvara, one should constantly meditate upon Sadāśiva, the God of gods, who possesses the radiance of rays at the end of an eon, as the syllable *Haṃ*. This is to be perpetually contemplated by yogins.
By this, all these three worlds, including the moving and the non-moving, are pervaded;
through this, the yogi attains perfection, and omniscience proceeds. || 35 ||
The bindu and nāda have been fully described, as well as the śakti, in brief;
that secret has been told to you, for it was not hidden from you by me. (36)
"Listen, O Goddess, as I speak of the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth;
she of great renown, shining from above a white lotus. (37)
Having meditated on the Earth as bearing such a form— a youthful woman with a dark complexion and a splendor equal to the sun— one should place her at the two feet. (38)
Through the practice of continuous meditation, he shall swiftly destroy all calamities;
the teacher of all beings shall become just like the earth itself. (39)
Becoming intent on the meditation on Śyāmā, one should cause her to reside within oneself;
one should contemplate the wind as yellow in color in the region of the knees.
By this yoga and by this ritual placement (nyāsa), one who is well-composed attains success;
yogis should always meditate upon space as the form of the earth. 41.

O Great Goddess, at the time of performing the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should contemplate the ego-principle (ahaṅkāra) as red upon the pair of thighs; likewise, one should place it in the secret place and within the self. 42.
At the time of the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should contemplate [the deity] resembling the rising sun,
with a complexion like saffron-red, four faces, and four arms. (43)
One should contemplate [the deity] illuminating all directions with rosaries;
O Goddess of Gods, at the time of ritual placement (nyāsa), one should perform the placement of the intellect in this manner.
The Prakṛta has been previously described, as well as the Pauruṣa in particular;
these have been known by you, O Goddess. Now hear the detailed account of the Kalās.
Nivṛtti is white in color; extending from the feet up to the hips, it shines all around with rays as cool as snow.
Pratiṣṭhā, having a yellowish luster, should be meditated upon at the time of ritual placement (nyāsa) from the heart down to the waist; thus, yoga is always produced.

But one should contemplate the Vidyā, O lady of beautiful hips, as being red in color and situated in the heart extending to the ears, illuminating [all], at the time of the ritual placement (nyāsa). (48)
One should always perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) for peace as far as the root of the ears,
[visualizing her] resembling moonlight and constantly emitting nectar.

Yogis should meditate [on this] constantly; at the time of ritual placement (nyāsa), one should contemplate it as extremely subtle, reaching as far as the heart, for it must indeed be meditated upon perpetually.
At the time of placement, one should contemplate [the seed-syllable] as resembling the morning sun, blazing with many rays and resting upon the ear of Amṛta. 51.
At the time of depositing [the seed-syllable], one should contemplate it as being like a place sheltered from wind and sun;
it is the digit of nectar, indeed incomparable and free from disease. 52.
O Goddess, by meditating upon her, one is liberated from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra;
indeed, this divine [goddess] should always be meditated upon by those seeking the conquest of death. (53)
That which is to be known as "Amṛta-Amṛta," the destroyer of old age and death—
this deity-installation (nyāsa) must be performed upon the pericarp by one desiring spiritual accomplishment.
The form of that great-souled one has thus been fully described;
