indeed, O Goddess of the gods, these [signs] should be understood by the teachers as hunger. 55.
The face should likewise be understood and known with diligent effort.
Listen, O Goddess, as I describe the placement within the heart-lotus. 56.
The lotus previously described is infinite; O lady of excellent complexion, one should contemplate the foot of Dharma as white and the foot of Jñāna as red. (57)
They say that detachment is yellow, and sovereignty resembles darkness;
likewise, the limbs here, as well as the coverings, are the same. (58)
The filaments of the lotus should be fashioned from red powder and resemble the color of dawn;
one should thus contemplate the arrangement of the lotus at the time of sacrifice. (59)
O Goddess of gods, at the time of initiation one should always contemplate in this manner;
O Goddess, when performing the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa), one should then contemplate that very principle.
By him all this reality is pervaded, indeed everything;
all those who have been mentioned whatsoever are known as his splendors.
By its splendor, all principles (tattvas) shine forth; of this there is no doubt.
When each individual [mantra] has been deposited, one should cause each one to be recited by him.
Then all the groups of principles (tattvas), which bestow the fruits of both spiritual perfection (siddhi) and liberation (mukti),
as well as the mantras and the constituent parts (kalās), are to be understood in their entirety. (63)
Having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) in this manner, one gains the capacity for all rites,
O fair-faced one, whether it be for expulsion, killing, or even striking.
With tridents in hand, most terrible, their eyes red with wrath, and their faces made fearsome by frowning brows—such [deities] one should employ for cruel rites. 65.
O Goddess, one should always contemplate the deity of the mantra as having upward-pointing hair, exceedingly fierce, black in color, and terrifying, causing [the world] to wither away. 66.
[He saw them] with mallets as weapons in their hands, bearing tridents and skull-topped staffs (khaṭvāṅgas), likewise carrying stones and holding pieces of wood in their hands. 67.
Joined with the syllable *huṃ* at the beginning and illuminated by the syllable *phaṭ* at the end, it performs acts such as killing and uttering [mantras]; of this there is no doubt. (68)
Listen, O Goddess, as I speak concerning both pacifying and nourishing rites:
O Great Goddess, she is gentle and white, seated upon a white lotus. (69)
All of them held white lotuses and likewise carried water-pots in their hands;
they were gentle, as white as the rays of the moon, and held the temple with their right hands.
O Goddess, the deity should be meditated upon during rites for nourishment, pacification, and libation;
in rites of subjugation and attraction, she should be visualized as holding a noose and a goad.
All of them should be meditated upon as red in color by the practitioner;
however, for the purpose of paralyzing (staṃbhana), one should always contemplate them as black in color.
Having first performed the *mūrtinyāsa*, one should thereafter commence the [other] *nyāsa*.
O Goddess, this *nyāsa* has been fully described; it is most difficult to attain. (73)
But because you are a devoted follower, I have told this to you;
thus has the Nyāsa been declared here as the most excellent among all mantras.
One is liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin merely by [the rite of] nyāsa;
even after consuming forbidden food or having destroyed the world of moving and non-moving beings. (75)
Having performed the ritual deposition (nyāsa), even the lowest of men is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Having offered gold, the gift of a cow, and many other oblations, he is likewise freed. (76)
O Goddess, by performing this ritual placement (nyāsa), one is liberated at that very moment; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus performed the rite of placement, the preceptor, being well-composed, [proceeds].
One should liberate [the disciple] by mere sight; no deliberation is required here.
532) If the Guru performs the sacrifice according to the procedure for the Kālayāga, [then liberation occurs]. 78.
O Goddess, I am unable to describe her continuous abundance of qualities;
even for a single day, that best of practitioners performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) by means of me.
He who practices this ritual placement (nyāsa) with concentration for seven days is liberated from the bonds of birth and saṃsāra; of this there is no doubt. (80)

He who contemplates [this] at the three junctions of the day shall, within a month, attain the Yoga that quickly leads him from hell to the auspicious state of Śiva; this occurs within twenty-one kalās.
Whatever dharma one who is engaged in yoga contemplates in the mind for six months,
he accomplishes all of it, both the beneficial and the harmful for the world.
O Lord of Gods, through the practice of this for a year, one shall attain equanimity;
there is no doubt that one may then recount the events of the three worlds. (83)
The practitioner who is well-composed and endowed with yoga travels through the Lokāloka mountain and the world of moving and non-moving beings within two years; of this there is no doubt.

When the fields are being consumed by the fire of the *nidāna* in various ways through the resonance of the field (*kṣetra-nāda*), the yogi attains perfection; of this there is no doubt, indeed no uncertainty. || 85 ||
And [the practice of] concealing one's impurities, foot-ointment, and elixirs;
as well as traveling through the sky, and the staff and sacred grass-bundle. (86)
Yoga and the accomplishments attained by people are perfected; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, having understood this placement (nyāsa), any other placement is like straw.
Indeed, the lakṣas are to be known right here; the principles (tattvas), O virtuous one, are to be known right here.
Indeed, the Self (ātman) is to be known right here, and especially the gods as well. (88)
O Goddess, O fair-faced one, this must not be given even to one's own son;
it should be given only to a practitioner and likewise to a teacher. (89)
"It shall not cause even the welfare of other wicked mortals to fall.
The Goddess said:
"Tell me the forms of the five Brahmās, Īśa, and the limbs [of the mantra]. (90)
Without them, one does not attain success, nor likewise through the ancillaries of the Vidyā.
The Lord said: "O Supreme Goddess, this is the common [rule] for the five Brahmans and the limbs of Śiva. (91)
O Goddess, he is born everywhere endowed with beautiful form and auspicious marks;
O Shobhane, those very forms have been previously described in the Navasūtra. 92.
The application of the mouth has been fully explained; it must be understood by the teacher.
O fair-eyed one, listen as I shall describe the form of the heart. 93.
Resembling pure crystal and filled with rays of light,
it illuminates both below and above, situated in the region of the heart.
O Goddess, when one is intent on meditation in the heart, it is deposited there; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, the deposition on the head is performed on the head, which resembles a pearl necklace, a kunda flower, or the moon. 95.
At the time of the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should contemplate [the deity] illuminating all directions;
one should contemplate the goddess Śikhā as resembling ten million moons.
One should meditate upon this [goddess] as flowing with streams of nectar, flooding [everything]. By that ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and meditation, the practitioner becomes well-composed. (97)
One succeeds here, of this there is no doubt, being freed from old age and disease;
[this] armor, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, [should be placed] upon all limbs. 98.
It removes all obstacles and blazes with faces on every side;
by means of this ritual placement (nyāsa), O Goddess, it is perfected—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. || 99 ||
One should employ the weapon in the region of the hand, but not upon one's own limbs;
O Great Goddess, one should visualize the obstacles as being terrified. 100.
Having first recited the Astra-mantra ten thousand times (ayuta), one should then perform the ritual practice (sādhana); thus, one shall attain success free from obstacles. || 101 ||

Having gathered everything by means of that [mantra] in the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should perform the recitation (japa) in the midst of the weapons; then it succeeds, and not otherwise. || 102 ||
Thus, O beautiful one, the ancillaries of knowledge have been described to you;
therein is the Pāśupata weapon, the limb of Śiva known as Ghora. (103)
O Goddess, ten thousand recitations of the ancillary mantra (vidyāṅga) should be performed by those who are well-composed;
then, O Goddess, the supreme practitioner attains success without obstacles. (104)
The practitioner should always contemplate the enclosure wall at the time of recitation;
then the practitioner proceeds without obstacle—of this there is no doubt. || 105 ||
Being well-composed, one should perform the Jaya-Saṅkarṣaṇa within the limbs of the Vidyā;
having performed the yoga of the five sounds, one should begin the recitation in the center. 106.

The *arghya* should be offered with the eleventh [verse] inserted in the midst of the recitation; the mantra, having been recited according to the prescribed measure, should then be performed again in the well-prepared [manner]. (107)
Having worshipped according to the rule, one should perform the ritual as described in the Kalpa; then one attains success from the goddess, even those [powers] created by humans. 108.
The accomplished ministers sport according to the sequence of those previously mentioned;
the glorious one performs all actions through deed, mind, and speech. 109.
Having perceived the reality, O fair-faced one, one should mutter that reality one hundred thousand times;
thus one attains perfection in yoga, and the mantras become effective, not otherwise.
If, however, one should recite it a hundred times at the time of going to bed at night, O Goddess, he shall even recount lost things and various scriptures. || 111 ||
That very God is the impeller and will speak; of this there is no doubt.
Having recognized the Guru, O Great Goddess, he becomes [qualified]; of this there is no doubt. (112)
The Goddess said:
"In which place should those [senses], beginning with sound and touch, as well as the sense organs themselves, be purified for one who perceives them as being in a single direction? (113)
"O Goddess, listen; O beautiful one, I shall explain that in which [practitioners] attain perfection.
I will tell it to you accordingly; listen with a one-pointed mind. (114)
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—
these five should be properly joined by the high-souled preceptor.
One should purify those qualities which belong to earth and so forth that reside within the earth; likewise for water, fire, and indeed for air as well. (116)
On earth, the subtle element of smell is known as the object called "fragrance";
it resides within the sacrificial oblation of the organs of action and is considered the sense organ of hearing. (117)
In this very sequence, the wise one should perform the purification;
likewise, Śiva [should be purified] within Śakti, each one individually and in due order. (118)
Likewise, O beautiful one, one should purify the five elements beginning with earth;
then, one should purify the sixth, the ego (ahaṃkāra), in the forward order.
This initiation has been declared to you in its entirety, along with the extraction of mantras,
the determination of the kalās, and likewise the determination of the tattvas.
O beautiful one, the meaning of the words has been explained to you in brief.
Having recognized the disciple as being filled with devotion, you should now explain the initiation (dīkṣā). (121)
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of the gods of gods, O Master, I have heard everything in detail."
I wish to hear about the partless [Brahman], which stands pervading all that has parts. || 1 ||
Therefore, O Lord, I shall hereafter proclaim the eternal Śiva-dharma,
by which one who is liberated, being of virtuous soul, is called a "Dharmotsanna."
He is eternally independent as the Lord, forever possessed of all auspicious attributes,
immeasurable, omnipresent, pure, and endowed with the power of all energies.
Pervading all the worlds from Ananta up to Śiva, he remains stationed;
for he stands in a state of absolute unity, endowed with the power of Śiva (Śiva-śakti). || 4 ||
At the beginning, that Lord Śiva, the imperishable,
rules over the entire universe through his sovereign powers, by means of his great yoga, his yoga of power, and his rays of light.
And he is established in the twentieth [tattva], because by his own powers he protects the bound souls (paśu),
due to his tranquility, his status as the agent, his possession of power, and his great majesty.
By means of their power of instruction and pacification, those powers of the Great-Souled One bestow grace upon the individual soul (kṣetrajña) and bring about the entire universe.
Since the entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is presided over by Śiva—who is of every form yet formless, incomparable and free from affliction—[he is the ultimate reality]. (8)
Pervading all through all arts, subtle, having attained identity with that [reality],
consisting eternally of the splendor of mantra, inconceivable, he is Supreme Śiva. (9)
Standing far beyond all means of valid cognition, he is beyond the fourth state (turyātīta), both supreme and non-supreme;
pure of speech, the supreme light, his own splendor is the firm object of perception.
Immeasurable, indescribable, incomparable, and free from disease;
exceedingly subtle, imperishable, eternal, the cause, the supreme light. (11)

That splendor stands pervading [the universe], having been condensed a thousandfold from the brilliance of the moon, the sun, and fire, and [surpassing] ten million times a parārdha of lightning flashes.
The lightning, the moon, the sun, the stars, and the fire—all shine by his splendor; he is remembered as the one of great luster. || 13 ||
Like a gem [containing] a gem, or like brilliance enveloped by its own radiance,
so is that supreme deity, whose vow is such, the brilliance even of all brilliant things.
Abiding in the sky, eternal like the sky, possessing a form with qualities similar to the sky;
resembling a stainless mirror, with a luster like autumnal water. || 15 ||
Like the simultaneous rising of many suns,
they illuminated the ten directions with upward-shining light that utterly destroyed all darkness.
Having reflected in various ways upon the Lord, who is imperceptible, whose form is inconceivable, eternal, omnipresent, subtle, immovable, unwavering, and fixed; (17)
All-pervading, the doer of all, the all, the indweller of all, the knower of all, the Lord;
the self of all beings, residing within all beings, the supreme ether, Śiva, the imperishable. || 18 ||
The food, the eater, and the giver—all these have Śiva as their supreme body, for he is the essence of all reality;
having determined this, Śiva is both the agent and the non-agent, the Lord of all beings. (19)
There are thousands of various Śivas and tens of millions of Padmas;
all are pure and eternal, abiding within the sphere of Śiva.
All possess the radiance of ten million suns and are pure by their very nature;
yet that which has been described as having distinct forms was spoken by practitioners who contemplate the scriptures. (21)
The great abode, the great knowledge, and indeed the great departure;
he of great splendor, of great prosperity, of great luster, and of great fame. || 22 ||
It is beyond reasoning and unknowable, firmly established in its own nature;
it is ungraspable, abiding in all beings, and likewise unshakeable and immutable.
It is without sound and without tone, to be personally realized, immutable,
established in the self, to be known as formless and without support. (24)
He is without affliction and indeed imperishable, all-encompassing and of pervasive form; unborn and of infinite forms, he has no lineage, father, or mother.
Indeed, it is a body without bones, sinews, blood, or skin;
it is without beginning, middle, or end, immovable, unshakable, and eternal.
Unextended yet vast, uninterrupted on all sides,
equal toward all beings, and with its body perpetually spread throughout.
It is all that is external and internal, the abode of all and yet without abode;
it is stainless, devoid of ego, without intellect, and without sense organs. || 28 ||
It is devoid of qualities, immovable, free from conceptual proliferation, and without affliction;
it is eternally manifest, without appearance, free from discursive thought, and without affliction. (29)
It is beyond doubt, incomparable, eternal, and likewise perpetually manifest;
it is neither low nor high, neither crooked nor straight. (30)
It is neither long nor short, neither gross nor subtle;
it is neither triangular, nor quadrangular, nor even circular.
Nor indeed does it possess any form whatsoever; it is devoid of all shapes and free from form.
It is neither hidden nor manifest, and it is neither movement nor stillness.
Neither above nor below, neither in front nor behind;
it is neither existent nor non-existent—what is that which stands pervading all? (33)
The body is not established as something separate, nor is it situated as a single entity;
it is said to be neither an external object of cognition nor anything else whatsoever. (34)
Śiva is to be known as subtle and devoid of creation and dissolution;
therein no creation arises, nor does dissolution ever occur. (35)
The fire is likewise without beginning, unproduced, and inexhaustible;
it is imperishable, stable, eternal, incomparable, and free from affliction.
It is said to be without support and without beginning, unchanging, eternally peaceful, perfectly extinguished, and completely satisfied in every respect. || 37 ||
It is completely free from all entities, devoid of action and time; it is neither to be consumed nor has it been consumed, and it is transparent and utterly pure.
It is immeasurable and unknowable, all-knowing and facing in every direction;
it is devoid of the qualities of merit and demerit, and is not dependent upon anything. (39)
It does not shine forth by being thought about, nor can it be made manifest;
for it is stainless, free from passion, pure, auspicious, and sacred.
It is free from both existence and non-existence, devoid of illusion and the illusory, and is without fault or defect; it is neither moving nor moved.
But it cannot be revealed by means of perception and the other instruments of knowledge,
for it is infinite, ungraspable, subtle, and characterized as transcending all measures.
It is inaccessible to all scriptures, yet it abides both externally and internally;
it possesses the nature of being the cause of all things, yet its characteristic is to transcend all causes. || 43 ||
In this very way, the Great Reality stands with qualities that are beyond comparison;
and it cannot be known without its grace as well. (44)
And because it is produced through inferential cognition and by means of the conceptualization of scriptures, that [reality] is obtained from the mouth of the Guru, impelled by his power. (45)
Since the supreme is the true nature of reality, which is beyond reality and devoid of all conceptual constructs,
he who realizes all this has understood everything in its entirety.
That state which is pure at the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end—
that is proclaimed here as the non-dual [state] by means of the mind within the Manonmanī.
Pervading all entities, it is characterized by both purity and impurity;
yet the pure reality is that which arises from the state of the nectar of space.
Therefore, it cannot be said that the pure, partless object of knowledge is something to be known;
for that supreme self-luminous reality does not manifest through anything else. (49)
Just as a man perceives his own objects by means of his own power,
so too does that Supreme Lord perceive by means of His own power alone.
He is omniscient, perfectly complete, pure by nature, and auspicious; he is entirely free from all defects and is the source of extraordinary qualities. || 51 ||

This is not the Lord of Pārvatī, who wields the skull-topped trident; nor is this the destroyer of Tripura, whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon. He is devoid of absolute tranquility, yet he is a constant, flowing stream.
The Lord is another, a Sovereign who is devoid of both anger and favor. || 52 ||
Auspicious in the beginning, auspicious in the middle, and always auspicious at the end—
the Lord, whose body has transcended the net of the great collyrium.
Since birth, death, old age, delusion, desire, anger,
and worldly existence do not exist for him, his state is therefore peaceful and auspicious.
Because that state of Śiva is seen even in the lords of causes such as Brahmā, the auspiciousness of the great-souled Śambhu is eternally celebrated as his very nature of Śiva. (55)
Auspicious, exclusively benevolent, incomparable, and free from disease;
the most auspicious of all auspicious things, eternally bestowing well-being, the propitious one. (56)
But the Arhat, the Lord of Beings, endowed with all ornaments, is to be known as the Teacher of the World and is worthy of worship by the twice-born. (57)
His limbs are smeared with the ashes of compassion; he carries a peaceful khaṭvāṅga staff;
he wears matted locks due to his lack of worldly attachment; and he bears the moon of Śiva as his crown. (58)
He eternally wields the trident of knowledge, with a serpent at the tip of his tongue of compassion;
with divine vision, he perceives the three worlds as food, free from all obscuration.
O God, you are the one who has cast off the nature of desire, adorned with the power of will;
you are immovable, eternal, all-pervading, unborn, constant, and self-existent.
Inactive yet perfectly restrained, he is the eternal knower and doer;
he is the omniscient creator of all, possessing eyes, heads, and faces on every side.
It is without syllables, unproduced, inexpressible, and free from affliction.
That which eternally illuminates reality is called sovereignty and knowledge;
it stands forever like a witness over the threefold types of action. (63)
Having pierced through that center of the navel, one should not reflect upon that cycle of existence (saṃsāra),
nor upon whatever movement of the mind there may be, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
Pervading all beings on every side, he is the nature of consciousness;
in an instant, he perceives everything—pleasure and pain, the beneficial and the harmful.
One should perceive the entire circle of saṃsāra, situated in its beginning, middle, and end, all within oneself; yet the omnipresent one is not bound.
It hears and perceives everything created by all beings, which consists of volition and determination; yet it is eternally not joined to anything anywhere.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell— whether auspicious or inauspicious— as well as the hearer, the speaker, the enjoyer, and the thinker of pleasure and pain. (68)
Seeing and hearing everything, he bestows [liberation] everywhere;
pervading all worlds, he is the one who brings about the complete release from bondage.
He is omniscient, the performer of all actions, the agent of creation and dissolution;
without beginning, middle, or end, he is the source and the one who pervades all principles.
The Lord is the sovereign who, by means of play, is the agent of creation and destruction;
he is omniscient, fully awakened, the primordial light, and likewise the awakener.
He is the protector and the one to be protected, the lord of restraint and favor;
he is the progenitor and the unprocreated, the one to be desired and likewise the ruler.
Perceivable by all the luminaries, he is eternal, peaceful, and stainless;
by his own will the Lord is possessed of all forms, and by his will he is devoid of parts. (73)
By his will he creates this [world], and by his will he also withdraws it;
he is the adversary of worldly activity, the cause of both destruction and origination. (74)
He is stainless, free from pride, immeasurable, and the knower of all measures;
he is the cause of the origin of all things, yet he is himself the eternal causeless one.
Sudhāmā is eternal, constant, the source, and the Lord of causes;
he is the essence of all causal attributes and is manifested through his powers.
The Blessed One is by nature the Dharma, characterized by the absence of resistance; he is beginningless and endless, immovable, yet the mover of all. || 77 ||
The Supreme Lord is both the enjoyer and the pervader;
the Blessed Śiva is immeasurable through his powers and is eternally satisfied. (78)
He is Akṣobhya (the Unshakeable) and the Shaker of all things, especially of the principles (tattvas); the Lord whose actions are inconceivable, the Sovereign even of those who possess power.
The Lord, who is preceded by intelligence, is the supreme ether, higher than the highest;
impelled by Him, he indeed spat out [the world] through mere knowledge. 80.
Just as a medicinal herb acts through its potency, and as the powerful one [acts] through the weak; for he is indeed the impeller who is both with parts and without parts.
O Supreme Goddess, because of its extreme subtlety, its immeasurability, and its sovereignty, the primordial,
utterly pure Śakti is distinguished from [ordinary] power and cannot be obstructed.
Just as a well-kindled fire burns up the grass on the ground,
so too is the blazing state of having "Bhava" as the tongue of power (śaktijihvatva) brought to cessation. (83)
The characteristic of the Lord’s means for bestowing grace, which brings about the maintenance of those things subject to arising and dissolution, is proclaimed. 84.
Time, though formless, brings about the gathering of flowers upon the trees.
And likewise, he heard the falling of the remaining fruits exactly as it occurred. || 85 ||
In the same way, the formless Śambhu is the agent of their arising and destruction;
like the power residing in a magnet, his formless energy performs all actions.
Just as the stainless Śiva-śakti grasps reality below,
so too do the powers, being utterly pure, function under the control of Śaṅkara.
He alone is the creator of the world, and he is also called "Supreme" here;
because he does not act by himself, he is therefore described as "Peaceful. (88)
For the eternal Lord Sadāśiva is neither the doer nor the instigator [of actions], just as He is not for farmers and others who follow their own respective duties. (89)
However, through the grace of birth and old age, they do indeed yield fruit;
so it is with all actions, including certain recitations and meditations. (90)
Without the grace of Maheśvara, however, they do not bestow fruit;
he transcends all states of being and is devoid of inconceivable qualities. || 91 ||
The eternal one is the doer of all, being the self-nature of all;
yet he is not graspable by the senses, nor by the hand, nor by the eye.
The Lord, the Sovereign, who is formless yet possesses all forms, is to be grasped by himself through himself in every way;
he fulfills everything without exception. (93)

This one alone is the cause of the binding and liberation of all fettered beings (paśu), as well as of dissolution and creation; hidden and devoid of sound and other sensory qualities, He presides over all beings.
He is entirely peaceful, omniscient, the Lord, the Sovereign, and imperishable;
having pervaded all things with his powers, he abides as that which is woven warp and woof, without beginning or end.
By his power, he is this entire universe of moving and unmoving beings, facing in every direction;
he is everywhere, within all creatures, both stationary and moving. 96.

Pervading the entire range of all seeds, it remains having permeated everything; because it reveals [all things] first, it is called "Agra" (the Foremost) in the Śiva-sacrifice, as it is the word for Śiva.
Because all principles (tattvas) are non-existent, fire indeed has faces on all sides;
it abides in the internal samādhi and is within the range of the internal organ. || 98 ||
That which is perceived as subtle at the beginning by yogins is worshipped;
it is the Self of all, yet devoid of all beings. (99)
The self of all beings, devoid of all beings, the withdrawer of the primary qualities (guṇas)—that reality is remembered by me as the supreme boon. 100.
Abiding in the qualities of all beings, taking refuge in the cave of all beings, established as the self of all beings, he is omnipresent and imperishable. || 101 ||
Having fully accomplished the cycle of victory, pure and established in his own self,
thus the Supreme Śiva, the master of his own māyā, attains supreme nirvāṇa.
Without beginning, middle, or end, free from duality, with all doubts severed—this is the one who has transcended suffering; this is the cause, the bringer of security, the auspicious one. (103)
Free from comparison with any object of transformation, likewise devoid of resemblance, and stripped of all conditioned form;
it is distinct from the intellect by virtue of its non-existence.
Śiva is the eternal cause, distinct from all other causes. || 104 ||
Because there exists no other such entity anywhere whatsoever, he is Nirvāṇa, the supreme purity, the illusion-free, and the ultimate Śiva. || 105 ||
This partless God is endowed with parts; always remembering Him through meditation, you should keep Him in mind with your intellect and thought.
O Mahādevī, it has been told to you in the *Kārikā*, O virtuous one:
"In the supreme *Niśvāsa* Tantra, however, [the deity] is without parts (*niṣkala*) for the sake of the one with parts (*sakala*). (107)
This essence of the Śiva-dharma, the most excellent among all tantras, should be given to one consecrated in the Śaiva tradition; it should not be given to one who has received another initiation.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, whose banner is marked by the bull!"
O Lord, you who are omniscient and the creator of all, be gracious toward me.
O Maheśvara, O Mahādeva, O Lord, tell me the collection of all mantras and the practice of those mantras. (2)
O Lord of Gods, please graciously tell me how to perform the five limbs (pañcāṅga) beginning with Vyomavyāpin, as well as those of the Brahmas.
How indeed does the Self abide within the matrices, both in the differentiated and the undifferentiated?
What is the number of its parts? The Lord, possessing sprouts, scatters them forth.
How indeed is the self established within the number of syllables of the mantras?
Having first set aside ten for the self, [the remainder is for] its limbs in due order.
O Lord of Gods, tell me in its entirety and exactly as it is:
what is the number of steps that the Lord constantly traverses?
O Lord of Gods, O Śaṅkara, tell me: how does he who is devoid of internal organs move within all the arts and all mantras? (7)
"O Lord of Gods, O Master, speak to me concerning the inner self.
Listen, O Goddess, to that great knowledge which you have inquired about. (8)
It has not been told to anyone; I shall relate it to you in its entirety, the sequential course of the movement of all mantras.
O Great Goddess, merely by knowing which, one is liberated and also attains success; this movement of the mantra is difficult to obtain even for the gods.
O you of excellent conduct, I shall explain, without any doubt, even down to each single word and syllable, along with my very life, for you who are most distinguished.
As previously explained, the number of breaths is stated to be twenty-one thousand six hundred in their proper sequence. (12)
O Goddess of the gods, having divided those vital breaths in successive order,
one should determine by means of the syllables how many breaths there are for each individual division.
And how the embodied soul moves— I shall tell you all of that,
as well as the number of each caste that resides within the Lord.
O Goddess, hear now the number of the *kalās* in their proper order;
one who knows this method of differentiation is said to be "one whose body is divided. (15)
That wise one is eternally a liberator upon the earth and shall lead [others] to Śiva;
for by whatever mantra a person performs an action, [by that he attains his goal]. || 16 ||
And through the state of equanimity (*sāmarasya*), by virtue of its uninterrupted nature, he thus attains the mantra as his very self; of this there is no doubt. (17)

In whichever [syllable] one should join the deity of the mantra by means of that very syllable, the knower of mantras should release it through the middle of that; thus it is said, "one is released. (18)
At whichever specific time the mantra-practitioner becomes one whose body is the mantra, at that very same time the Guru who knows reality should effect liberation. 19.
By whichever caste a man may identify himself, by that very caste he shall liberate [others] and he himself is also liberated. (20)
O Beloved, by whatever reality one forms the body,
by that very same reality one may release it, and is even liberated.
p.
568) As many syllables as there are in the mantras, so many [deities] are said to be meditated upon through that.
By means of that, when one sacrifices and offers oblations, one attains accomplishment and is even liberated. || 22 ||
As many as are the letters of the Mātṛkā, so many are the paths (adhvans) remembered;
by worshipping and offering oblations with them, one attains success and is even liberated. (23)
All this regarding the mantras has been told to you, O virtuous one;
having understood it all in its entirety, perform the initiation, the yoga, and the recitation.
Having rendered the syllables auspicious, one should worship them in due order;
those syllables which are short or long, and those which are known to be joined with vowels. (25)

Having understood those phonemes, joined with the deities and the principles (tattvas) in their proper order through the various methods of extracting the Praṇava, one should then recognize the very words within this [system].
The knower of mantras should worship each individual letter in successive order;
the officiating priest must perform for them the fire-oblation previously described. (27)
O Goddess of gods, if the preceptor performs the sacrifice according to the division of the *kalās*,
he should place them upon the petals of the *kalās* and install them with the *mantra* at the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

O beautiful lady, the master of adepts who desires spiritual accomplishment must perform the worship, the fire-sacrifice (homa), and all other ritual actions for everyone using their respective mantras. (29)
All of these should be known without distinction by those who know the reality;
having thus worshipped according to the rule, the preceptor should perform the initiation.
All this has been declared by me in brief, O fair-faced one;
it should be understood with diligence by practitioners who desire liberation. (31)
I shall once again proclaim the unsurpassed nectar of the divisions, knowing which one is inevitably liberated from the bondage of worldly existence. (32)
This should be understood by the wise through internal application;
it is to be known, starting from the beginning, for each one in due order. (33)

O sinless one of excellent complexion, having divided [the teachings] into eighty-one according to their absence [of certain qualities], I shall relate them to you in their entirety without any doubt. (34)
When the vital breaths are divided individually for each [part], it should be known that there are two hundred breaths, and likewise for those established in the breath. (35)
Furthermore, O Goddess, the six breaths are to be known as two *nimeṣas*; thirty *tṛṣṭis* make one *lava*, O beautiful lady of the gods—this is how it should be understood. (36)
O Goddess, the Lord moves constantly through each individual step;
O Queen of the Gods, this should be understood by those who are well-composed throughout a day and night. (37)
And hear now how the Lord moves through the syllables on the left path:
in the case of the syllables pervading the void, sixty vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed proclaimed.
But devoid of these three, O Goddess, it lasts for half a nimeṣa; such is the thirst of each of the five elements individually, O fair-faced one. (39)
Knowing this, they are indeed liberated from the bonds of all fettered beings (paśus).
Thus it has been told to you, O Goddess of gods, O beautiful one, regarding the syllables of the words.
The Vyomavyāpin has been declared; now I shall tell you about Sadyojāta and the others—namely Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, and likewise Aghora. (41)
O Goddess of gods, I shall explain the nature of Puruṣeśa; listen to how each one of them comes to be through the eight kalās.
I shall relate in due order how the Sovereign Lady constantly moves, joined with two thousand and seven hundred [verses]. (43)
It must be constantly known by the great-souled yogi who understands the spies; likewise, it should be understood by the great-souled teacher as being within the Aghora [direction]. 44.
I shall fully declare the Vāma [Tantra]; listen with a one-pointed mind. It consists of five hundred and thirty-six [verses]. (45)
Furthermore, O Goddess, sixty breaths (prāṇas) must be known by the teacher;
one breath is likewise declared to be equal to one lava. (46)
O Goddess, one should diligently understand that the width [of the nose] is three parts;
O Goddess, listen as I shall briefly explain the [proportions] of a man. 47.
Five thousand and four hundred [verses] are to be known;
this, O Goddess, has been fully declared as that which should be understood by one who knows reality.
I shall tell you of the Lord; listen, O Goddess of excellent complexion, in brief: they are declared to be four thousand. (49)
It should be known without doubt that there are three hundred and twenty [units] for each single portion (kalā) of Brahman as it is traditionally recorded.
O Goddess of the gods, by that number the Lord moves eternally;
thus has the conduct of the *kalās* been fully explained in brief, but not in detail. (51)
It should be understood with effort by yogis who contemplate reality.
I shall fully declare the limbs of Śiva; listen attentively, O beloved. (52)
By the mere knowledge of which one would certainly obtain both supernatural powers and liberation—this is declared to be the Heart of the Supreme Self, known as the Soul of All. (53)
The six-syllabled mantra becomes equal [in power] through its recitation.
Suśiva is said to consist of eight syllables; listen, O beloved, to its ultimate limit. 54.
Two thousand [verses] are joined for each one in due order;
seven hundred are to be known, and this must be understood by the teacher. (55)
O fair-faced one, this movement of Suśiva has been declared to you.
O Goddess, listen as I shall now explain that of Jvālinī in brief. (56)
One thousand and nine hundred are declared, along with sixty breaths (prāṇas) that are to be known, as well as three breaths. || 57 ||
Likewise, three *nimeṣas* constitute one *lava*;
and each one of these, O fair-faced one, is joined with a *tṛṭi* and a *viśva*. (58)
O Goddess of the gods, thus one practices in the collection of syllables of Jvālinī.
I shall now declare that of Piṅgala; listen as I speak. (59)
O Goddess, understand that number which moves;
O Sovereign of the God of Gods, the Lord moves eternally within this.
The movement of the vowels has been fully explained for Piṅgala, O lady of beautiful countenance.
576) I shall now proclaim the [movement] of the weapon of Indra; listen, O Goddess, in brief. || 61 ||
O beautiful goddess, I shall describe the deity for each caste in brief: there are five hundred vital breaths (prāṇas) [per day]. 62.
Fourteen breaths are said to constitute a *nimeṣa*, and likewise, a *tṛṭi* is a fourth part of that; the Lord moves constantly through these.
Thus has the conduct regarding the colors of this Aghora-weapon been proclaimed to you;
O Goddess, this has been fully explained concerning those who abide in the Śiva-pīṭha.
O Goddess of the gods, this has been told in due order according to their divided states;
yet when undivided and united with Śiva, the mantras bestow the arising of knowledge.
Thus has their movement been described; those who are known as the eternal entities are the mantras of Śiva’s throne and assembly hall, proclaimed by the Omniscient One. (66)
Indeed, they are immeasurable, incomparable, indescribable, and free from affliction;
they abide through the differentiation of words and syllables, and through the differentiation of artistic branches.
O Goddess of gods, the wise should always understand the mantras by means of the movement of the eyes;
if the practitioner recites the mantra word by word, [he attains success]. 68.
The great-souled practitioner should recite it according to that procedure;
I shall now declare the Mātṛkā, which is perfectly endowed with all the scriptures. (69)
Since mastery over the lord of practitioners is accomplished merely by knowing this, one should therefore practice the conduct of the Mātṛkās with every effort. (70)
Bestowing success one by one in the sacrifice, it is accomplished very quickly.
The Mātṛkā is proclaimed to consist of the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*. (71)
Listen, O fair-eyed one, how the Soul of All operates through these:
for each individual caste, there are exactly four hundred [syllables].
The practitioners should always know that there are thirty-two breaths;
however, the great-souled practitioner should know that one [breath] is indeed a thirst.
One-third of a *tṛṭi* should be understood as the measure for each color; the master should proceed accordingly.
However, for one who worships with undivided [oneness], no such movement exists.
This supreme conduct of the Mātṛkās has been told to you, O Goddess;
I shall now describe the body consisting of ten aspects—listen with a one-pointed mind. (75)
Two thousand, one hundred, and likewise sixty breaths (prāṇas) should be known here for each individual, O fair-faced one. (579) 76.
And for one who is divided, movement has been declared by Śiva, the Supreme Self;
but among those who are undivided, O lady of excellent hips, the Lord is eternally arisen.
I shall explain the movement of the heart; listen, O fair-eyed one!
O lady of beautiful countenance, it should be known that there are three thousand [breaths] for each [vein]. (78)
Likewise, eighty-five breaths and two nimeṣas—these two and one [nimeṣa], O Goddess of Gods, are proclaimed as a single *tṛṭi*. (79)
One-third is declared for the well-rounded [body], and even a third part is for the heart; thus the heart is fully described. Now I shall tell you about the head. (80)
O fair-faced one, the enumeration of the principles (tattvas), beginning with the Sakala, is indeed declared to be that same number for the head; of this there is no doubt. (81)
In the same way, the weapon should be understood by the high-souled one who knows the movement;
O fair-eyed lady, listen as I shall explain the movement of the eye. 82.
Seven thousand and two hundred;
this is declared to be the movement of each one individually, O fair-faced lady. (83)

O Goddess, this which resides within the phonemes has been declared by the Lord of Teachers for one who desires the goals of spiritual perfection and liberation; it constitutes the discourse on the distinct modes of conduct. 84.
O Goddess, when one does not direct any fault toward the Śiva-pīṭha, that Blessed One is indeed the primordial source; for He is the inexpressible and the stainless. 85.

O Mistress of the Gods, the seat (pīṭha) of one who abides in the phonemes (varṇa), one who abides in the words (pada), and one who is both distinct and non-distinct has been described; it has been told to you in due order. (86)
Thus, one who knows the distinctions of the movements is liberated; of this there is no doubt.
O beautiful one, the collection of mantras has been told to you. 87.
Furthermore, the yoga and the recitation (japa) arising from that yoga must be understood by the teacher;
for if the Guru is engaged in worship, he is the Lord whose body is the year. (88)
The high-souled instructor should understand this through a single arising;
the practitioner of mantra should worship the six syllables and then begin their recitation of that very [mantra]. (89)
O lady of excellent hips, one attains perfection through the very hardship of the partless [state];
having divided the differentiated state into three, one shall no longer be subject to birth. (90)
Through the placement for accomplishment (*siddhinyāsa*), one attains success; through the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), indeed liberation.
Having understood both origination and dissolution, one achieves perfection—of this there is no doubt. (91)
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter of the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said: [Tell me] the origin and dissolution, as well as the coming and going of living beings.
I wish to understand this, O Blessed One; you should deign to explain it.
O fair-faced one, I shall fully explain this great and excellent question regarding the origin and dissolution of the Lord, for the sake of your pleasure.
Origination is to be known as partless, while dissolution is remembered as having parts.
This is the divine state of knowledge, which encompasses gods, asuras, and humans. (3)
He is born only from above and does not die from below;
they call this "sūtaka" (birth-impurity), which exists among all living beings.
That which pertains to the deceased (preta) has been declared above; it should be understood with diligent effort.
He who abandons both of these shall become one who has reached the further shore of reality (tattva). || 5 ||
This entire world is joined with impurity from birth and death;
yet one does not recognize the impurity of death and birth within one's own body.
And since he cannot be known by cognition, how could there be any cognition of him?
O Goddess, one should enjoy [all things] from every side, having abandoned [the concern for] death and birth-impurity.
O Goddess, favor must be bestowed; it has been understood that there is birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and likewise death-impurity (*mṛtaka*).
Birth-impurity resides within the body, and death-impurity is exactly the same. (p. 584) 8.
Furthermore, having investigated individually that which resides within the body,
[one understands] the origin and dissolution, as well as the coming and going of the elements.
He who contemplates for the sake of knowledge shall become one who has reached the further shore of reality.
O Lord, O Goddess, I wish to hear what is beneficial and what is harmful for living beings.
How does the movement and the very re-movement of the vital breath occur?
O Lord, tell me how many vital breaths are said to be in a year. (11)
At what time does one attain long life, and how indeed does one become short-lived?
How does one attain long life, and how even for women and children? (12)
"O Lord of the gods of gods, explain destruction according to authoritative proof.
Īśvara:
Listen, O Goddess; a question concerning another has been raised by you, O Goddess. (13)
Two tens of thousands, one thousand, and likewise six hundred;
this was previously declared by me, and it is known by you as well. (14)
In the same manner, I shall explain to you by dividing the calculation of breaths according to how many breaths there are in each year, as well as in each month and each fortnight. (15)
O Goddess, however many breaths there are in a day, and whatever the number at death may be, they are calculated by the calculators according to the measure of the objects of cognition.
I shall tell you everything exactly as it is, O one of good conduct;
by day and by night, it should be understood by the high-souled one who knows the proper time. (17)
Having analyzed in every way the vital breaths previously described and proclaimed, these vital breaths have been declared by me as divided into a hundred parts. || 18 ||
O Goddess, when divided according to each individual part, O lady of excellent complexion, two hundred breaths are to be known [for each]. (19)
And sixteen of those [moments] are known as one *śabda* by measure;
eight *tṛṭis*, O virtuous one, are to be understood as one day for a living being.
The night is said to be of that same duration; it should be known by one who understands the movement [of the breath].
A fortnight is not considered to consist of [that many] breaths, nor is a month [considered so] by doubling that [fortnight]. (21)
A fortnight consists of exactly four guṇas, and these are proclaimed as the seasons;
by this, which is headed by the syllable *a*, it should be known by the knower of reality. (22)
Three hundred and sixty such years are declared to be one year;
and in this [cycle], there are thirteen years in each watch (prahara).
When doubled, twenty-five years are to be known;
by this sequential method, it should be understood with diligence. (24)
Listen now, O Goddess of beautiful countenance, to this which is extremely secret;
I have never been questioned by anyone, nor have I spoken of it anywhere. (25)
Therefore, I shall explain that; listen to me with a one-pointed mind.
What kind of boy would one designate as born at the very moment of the sun's rising? (26)
In the second year, and likewise in the third, the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and so on up to the twelfth year and beyond. (27)
In the first and second [cases], one should designate it as "puruṣa" (man); one should predict the lifespan of young men to be as many years as the number of years [indicated]. || 28 ||

O Goddess of the Gods, in the worldly and profane [states], one imagines the acquisition of sesame seeds; however, those corpses which have been described as numbering according to the vital breaths (prāṇas)—|| 29 ||
One should cause the beginner, the intermediate, and the advanced to practice according to their respective levels.
Among those who possess the vital breath of the object of knowledge, that which is embodied in the beginner is designated as "tam" (darkness).
If it is divided by three parts, one should not designate it as medium or large;
O Goddess of gods, this sequence must be understood by the knower of reality.
In the second watch, one should designate him as "trijātā.
O Goddess, having thus given the fourth instruction, one should then command [the following]. (32)
Or, O Goddess of the gods, it should be diligently understood when [the teacher] has died;
thus becoming intent on meditation, the yogin indeed remains well-concentrated. (33)
One sees everything like a myrobalan fruit on the palm of the hand; there is no doubt in this.
He who reaches the auspicious, immeasurable deity through the opening in the Veginī [river] alone— || 34 ||
O Goddess who moves within perception, one is liberated from this; there is no doubt in this matter.
One should likewise instruct a woman regarding the carrying of grain. (35)
Listen, O Goddess, I shall now speak by the power of the lower channel (nāḍī):
at the first equinoxal conjunction (viṣuva-lagna), there occurs the birth known as that of a male. (36)
At the end [of the breath] there is a woman, and in the middle-born [breath] there is a neuter;
when, however, in the division of conduct, those who do not know the types are [instructed], the knower of yoga [should proceed]. (37)
Then it should be known as mine; by that, one should predict death. Sixty-four vital points (marmas) are recorded in the excellent body of embodied beings. || 38 ||
Some are external conditions, while others are internal;
whatever they may be, as well as others, should be understood according to their respective order. (39)
O Goddess of the gods, those internal signs are indeed difficult to discern;
I shall describe to you in brief those which are indicative of imminent birth. (40)
O Goddess, O best among those who bear bodies, all the limbs suddenly fail within the body; there occurs burning, emaciation, and wasting away. (41)
O Goddess of gods, for the yogin who is afflicted by pain, [the practice] is performed through the natural process;
he knows the reality of the movement within the channels and has exerted himself in the discernment of the hundred thousand [subtle divisions]. (42)
The wise one should begin with the rites of creation and so forth for the paths of those who are to be born;
then, at the proper time, he should again [perform them] through yogas such as Mṛtyuñjaya.
The vital point (marman) visibly flows; this must be understood by one who knows reality.
Listen as I tell you which specific [limb] will sweat. (44)
First, at the region of the ankles, then at the bases of the thumbs;
the third is at the joints of the arms, and the fourth is between the two breasts. (45)
The fifth is proclaimed by the yogis as being in the region of the lips;
the sixth is indeed celebrated as being right above the throat.
The head is declared to be one great vital point (*mahāmarma*);
the knee-joint is proclaimed as the eighth great vital point. (47)
The great vital points (mahāmarmans) of the penis and the hands should be understood with effort; O Goddess, those [great vital points] have been declared by you to be in the heart. 48.
I shall describe them, O Mistress of the Gods; listen to me as they truly are.
I shall tell you those which are spiritual (ādhyātmika); listen to me. (49)
Having heard that [sound] again according to the very sequence of its resonance, O Goddess, one should then know that death has immediately arrived. (50)

One should observe externally those things previously declared to be defective; furthermore, if the sense of taste does not perceive flavors on the tongue for more than six months, [it is a sign of death].
Other such [omens] as these should be understood by men on earth;
and that man who carries a corpse is likewise remembered as being [under the influence of] Māra. (52)
When one [side] comes into a state of rapid movement and the second is slow-moving, O beautiful one, it is indeed through the complete cessation of those vital points (marmans). 53.
Yogis should always know that death has arrived for him who, though a knower of reality, perceives the Self as not being the Self. 54.
Then the wise one should take recourse to the wheel of the three deaths;
then they indeed attain pacification—there is no need for deliberation on this point. (55)
Thus, O Goddess, I have told this to you out of affection;
it should be understood with effort and must not be given to just anyone. 56.
The Goddess said:
"O Supreme Lord, those vital points (*marmas*) which have been described by you are directly perceived."
How indeed should this be understood by yogins at the time of dissolution? || 57 ||
What is the primary point from which one should withdraw [the breath], and what indeed would be its characteristic?
O Blessed One, I wish to understand this; you should deign to speak. (58)
O Goddess, listen, for I shall tell you a supreme secret concerning the vital points (marmas),
by the mere knowledge of which one who understands the enemy does not come to grief. (59)
Having observed the characteristics of the vital points (marmans) every day, the wise man, having understood them, should perform what is beneficial; thus he does not come to grief.
The twenty-five vital points (*marmans*) are declared to be the *Kālacakra*;
from that time onward, one must perform the counter-measures against Time itself. (61)
Furthermore, I shall explain for twelve years the threefold [system] according to the yoga of the wheels;
having understood that therein correctly, one shall become a conqueror of death.
He shall further explain that division described in terms of fortnights and months;
and I shall also explain how the "revival of the dead" (mṛtasañjīvana) comes to be.
O Goddess, this secret concerning the examination of the vital points (marmans) among them, as well as the characteristic of how they are obstructed, has been told. 64.
In that way, I shall explain it for the benefit of all yogins;
listen now to the characteristics of that very [state] through the empty wrist-joint (maṇibandha). || 65 ||
If one's hands and fingers are always sluggish, cold, and elongated, and the *tilaka* mark on the forehead is scorched, one should designate such a person as being "withdrawn" (*saṃhṛta*).
Having understood this, O Goddess, one should perform the remedial rite for him;
otherwise, O virtuous lady, he shall meet his death within eleven months.
Pain in the shoulders arises, and it appears as if broken by wind;
there is frequent trembling, and one should cast that [body] which has been withdrawn. 68.
In exactly ten months, he meets his death; it cannot be otherwise.
Listen now as I describe the symptoms when the two temples (the temples of the head) are failing.
O beloved, if the head shakes suddenly and the eye rolls, one should know that it is obstructed;
this is indeed seen directly.
One who possesses such a sign indeed does not live for eight months.
Now listen to the sign when the channel above the throat is constricted: (71)
The tongue does not move about, yet clear speech proceeds; O lady of excellent hips, once the tongue has withered, one does not live beyond seven months.
Listen, I shall describe the symptoms of one whose vital points (marmas) in the throat are constricted:
there occurs a severe dryness of the throat accompanied by an absence of phlegm. (73)
Furthermore, food eaten like a stone does not digest;
he who possesses this characteristic indeed lives for four months.
Listen to the symptoms when the path situated at the base of the penis is obstructed:
the urine becomes red in color and it burns; of this there is no doubt. (75)
This indeed is the characteristic by which one lives for three months; however, he in whose region of the scrotum and the urinary tract such a pain arises [shall not live]. (76)
If, however, one sees a black spot in the middle of the penis, having recognized it by such a mark, he lives for two months. (77)
But if a throbbing occurs directly above the breast,
O Goddess, and it moves toward the right, he shall live for one month and a fortnight.
If the throbbing at the lower junction is suppressed, one will not live for even a single month; this is certain according to the scriptures. (79)
O Goddess, if one suddenly stops hearing sounds as one did before, one should know that person to be paralyzed; he shall live for half a month.
"O beautiful woman, why do her eyes shed tears without any apparent cause?
Then she will meet her death within ten days. (599) 81.
If, however, he should become paralyzed from above the foot, one should know his death will occur within five days; of this there is no doubt.
O beautiful lady, for one whose life is diminished, there occurs sudden trembling, as well as a sense of wonder, and even a discordant voice arises. (83)
Indeed, he who possesses such a characteristic lives for only three days;
his eyes will no longer perceive even the forms previously seen. (84)
Having observed it thus by its characteristics, he lives for two days;
however, when there is throbbing or lack of movement in the region of the ankle, [he lives for one day]. (85)
One who possesses only such characteristics lives for a single day;
he whose heart trembles and in whom fainting and shaking arise [lives for that same duration]. (86)
One should know that he is invincible; he lives for half a day.
If there is this "gur-gur" sound in the throat and it vibrates slightly in a well-closed [mouth], [he lives]. (87)
O Goddess of the gods, one should predict his death within a single watch;
when the vital air has entered the middle of the palate, it vibrates slightly in a well-guarded state. (88)
One should recognize that [life] as past; he lives for a hundred breaths.
Thus, the practitioner who knows the divisions of the vital points does not come to grief. (89)
One should examine [the breath] every day; he does not know otherwise.
[The counts are] eleven, one hundred, eight, nine, and likewise seven. (90)
Six, five, four, two, one month, and even half a month— these are the durations determined by the wise. (91)
One should know that ten, five, and three days, as well as two days, one day, half a day, and likewise a watch (prahara), [correspond to these durations]. || 92 ||
By half of half a watch—that is, by one hundred breaths—one should diligently understand [the movement] starting from the wrist. 93.
Having thus understood and realized this, one should perform the remedial measures for it:
visiting sacred fields and holy fords, as well as purifying acts such as the recitation of mantras and fire offerings.
O Goddess, Mistress of the Gods, these [mantras] beginning with Mṛtyuñjaya should be practiced with effort. O virtuous lady, I have explained these to you according to their respective order. 95.
Furthermore, I shall speak of another; listen, O Goddess, in due order:
if there should be a lack of throbbing in the vital points (*marmans*) on the left side by means of the *sama* [breathing], [it is a sign of death]. (96)
One should recognize the fault as being of the wind (vāyu) and perform a remedy for the wind;
O Goddess of the Gods, by means of phlegm (śleṣman), they then become motionless once again. 97.
One should examine those [symptoms] and perform the treatment for pitta.
O Goddess, listen; I shall tell you another most secret [instruction]. 98.
By the mere knowledge of which all suffering does not arise, that flow of the *iḍā* and *suṣumnā* should always be known by yogis. (99)
By this it is understood, O Goddess, that one discerns the welfare and non-welfare of the world, as well as one's own, according to the proper time and in their respective divisions. (100)
If the illustrious [Dakṣiṇāyana] flows to the south for even a single day, it portends some kind of portent; one should not predict fear in that case. (101)
If it returns after two days, having passed to the south,
one should know that misfortune will befall the lineage, but one should not predict death for him.
O Goddess, O virtuous lady, if it should indeed flow through the right [nostril] for three days, there will be great danger to the village and the lineage.
On the fourth day, O fair-faced one, he shall return through yoga;
he should know that his own [previous] misfortune has been overcome, and he lives with great ease.
Having carried him for five days along a single path, it turns back;
"one's own death is approaching"—this is the certainty of the scripture. (105)
But if a crow turns back from above the fifth [house],
one should know that it portends misfortune for the king and that he shall be deprived of sacrificial butter (ājya). (106)
O Goddess of the Gods, if after seven days the yogin should fail to return, and having observed the destruction of his mounts, the knower of the yoga of Śiva should speak [of this]. (107)
If it flows for eight days and then ceases thereafter, one should know that there is danger from kings; he lives with great suffering.
O Goddess of the gods, if it turns back after carrying [the offering] on the ninth day, one should know that the king is inauspicious; he lives only with great suffering.
O Goddess of gods, having carried [the corpse] for ten days, one turns back;
if indeed one turns back, the death of kings will swiftly occur.
Therefore, one should not predict fear for him based on the eleventh [day] alone;
rather, one should know that misfortune for people will occur until the fifteenth day. (111)
Just as it has been described for the right hand, so indeed it is for the left;
having understood this, the wise one who knows yoga shall neither falter nor despair.
Thus, one who knows the method of practice and understands yoga does not falter.
O Goddess, this has been fully declared as the supreme secret and mystery. 113.
You must act with extreme secrecy and not disclose this to anyone; for it will be discovered by a spy through the application of [esoteric] methods—of this there is no doubt.
"Victory is to be known in women; there is no doubt that success lies in the essence.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter in the Niśvāsakārikā.
The Goddess said:
By what measure should the manifestation be known by the teacher?
By what measure would the exit be, O Maheśvara, and likewise the entry? (1)
In the midst of this very inquiry,
O Goddess, I desire to know this great merit which has not been asked about by anyone before.
Therefore, I shall fully explain that which brings benefit to practitioners:
the teacher must remain in the state of the complete restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa).
O Goddess of gods, when the practitioner proceeds in this manner without interruption, in that very moment he becomes a perfected practitioner indeed. || 4 ||
O Goddess, there is no doubt in this; I tell you the truth:
when the cessation of breath occurs for the practitioner, [then he becomes a Siddha]. (p. 607) 5.
Then, having known that which is to be known, the object of knowledge shall belong to his sacrifice;
he should move in the upper portion as long as the void below is indicated.
The upper part is empty, the lower part is empty, and in the middle there is the victory. The subtle *kalā* is the *utkarṣaṇī*, and the second one is on the thread.
These two should be known by the knower of reality as situated in the lower part;
while that [breath] moves upward, Kālī is situated to the right.
Then, at dawn, the auspicious one who bestows all accomplishments appeared;
for him who had set out with face downward, two *kalās* were situated on his left.
(608) One should know that "niśānta" has been explained to you by Cārajña;
as long as it moves to the right, so long [is it auspicious], O beautiful one, when it moves to the left. 10.
One should know that the three [channels] are empty; however, O lady of excellent complexion, one should designate that central, motionless path as consisting of emptiness. || 11 ||
When the practitioner is joined with that through the state of contact, then he attains nirvāṇa; there is no need for deliberation in this matter. || 12 ||
O beautiful one, the nature of its contact has been described to you;
O beloved, listen attentively as I speak of the void locations. 13.
By the mere knowledge of which one attains the state of non-existence;
its cessation is in the middle part, while its establishment is in the horizontal and the north.
Vidyā is said to be in the south, and Śānti is situated in the eastern direction. Nāda, however, should be known as the fifth; it is proclaimed to be Śiva. (15)
The four kalās that have been described consist of the movement of nāda;
the fifth is said to be Śiva, who has been declared to you as extremely subtle.
O virtuous one, one performs the worship of Nāda through such meditation;
for the individual soul (jīva) is said to be Nāda, remembered as consisting of the power of touch.
O Goddess of the Gods, grace should always be bestowed in two ways: that which is free from the touch of the individual soul (jīva) and that which is established in the mouth of the Guru. 18.
O Goddess, this auspicious knowledge and its object must not be given;
it should be bestowed only upon one who is devoted to the Guru, devoted to Śiva, and wise. (19)
"Otherwise, it would cause the attainment of the highest good to fail for wicked mortals.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter in the *Niśvāsakārikā*.
The Goddess said:
Just as fire consumes water that is flowing swiftly, so does the Liberating Minister speak to the Pravaha wind. (1)
By what division of measures, and by what means, does one become a maker of auspiciousness?
O Blessed One, I wish to understand this; you should deign to explain it.
O Suvrata, I, the Lord, shall explain the threefold division of the Imperishable itself.
By the mere knowledge of which one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter. || 3 ||
When that which is peaceful is pierced by the letter *e* along with the *bindu* and *nāda*, O woman of excellent complexion, one should know that the swiftly moving water will roar.
Upon hearing it, they are liberated from sins; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
By the mere knowledge of it, one becomes fit for immortality.
When conjoined with the letter *ha* and the letter *su*, it resounds equally as if blazing;
when differentiated by the vowel *ā*, it is the eternal God of gods.
The wind Pravaha said: "I have previously declared that which one performs with a cool tremor and a short mouth. (7)
Thus, by knowing this within one's own body as the object of experience, there occurs the destruction of evil;
having heard it through the division of the syllable *ḍha* and the vowel *u*, one is liberated from sins. (8)
Having known [the self] through the analysis of its forms, one is released from bondage;
but by means of form, having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa), one certainly transcends through meditation.
The syllable *ī*, whose deity is Fire, is formed by the conjunction of living beings, stands face-to-face, and is ignited from below by the wind. (10)
